Description:
## Overview

Darbar Malik Ahmad Ayaz is an active Muslim shrine in the name of Malik Ahmad Ayaz, whom the survey identifies as "Slave of Mehmood Gaznavi - Governor Lahore"; the account given to the surveyor states that his tomb was built at this place after his death. The survey records the site's religion as Islam and its affiliation as "Ahl e Sunnat - Ghaznavi silsila" (*silsila*, a chain of spiritual transmission), reproduced as recorded.

The shrine stands in Shah Alam Market, which the survey describes as the largest market in Asia and reports as extremely crowded; the account given to the surveyor places the *mazār* (tomb, mausoleum) near Darbar Ali Hajveri Ganj Bakhsh. The site is small, and the surrounding congestion is reported to prevent many people from reaching it, gradually reducing both the figure's fame and the enthusiasm of visitors. Residents of this densely populated neighbourhood are largely unaware of the life of the figure buried there — a figure about whom, the survey states, Allama Iqbal, Kaniya Lal and other writers have written books.

The books consulted add a good deal to the survey's picture, and contest some of it. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* gives him an entry of his own as 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری', calls him the slave and beloved of Shah Mahmud Ghaznavi, follows him from tutor to the young prince who governed the Punjab to a renouncer in the company of *faqirs*, and has him die in 450 AH and lie buried inside the city of Lahore (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 192–193). Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* and Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* both make him the man who restored Lahore after Mahmud's conquest (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18; Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 525). Annemarie Schimmel's books on Islamic mysticism and its poetry know him as the Turkish officer whose devotion made the king "the slave of his slave" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 84, folio 74), and Nizami-i Arudi's *Chahar Maqala*, in Edward G. Browne's translation, tells of a carousal at which Mahmud bade him cut off his curls (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37). The editor of Lahori's Urdu edition, for his part, rejects the tradition that Ayaz refounded Lahore and treats the romance of Mahmud and Ayaz as a literary growth of post-Seljuq times (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed); and the year of Ayaz's death is given three different ways.

## The Life of Malik Ahmad Ayaz

The life narrated to the surveyor is long, and is given here in the account's own terms.

The survey relates that Malik Ayaz Ahmad was educated in Georgia in 993 AD, and that when "the infidels attacked your country" he was enslaved and taken for sale to the Baghdad slave market — the account notes that slave dealing was then the norm. Too weak to attract buyers, he was passed over until Mahmud Ghaznavi came through and asked his price. The minister questioned the purchase; the king answered that what he saw in the boy the minister could not see. The price asked was ten thousand dinars, greed having been raised in the seller's heart by the king's words; Mahmud paid it and enrolled him among his soldiers.

Tradition holds that the relation of master and slave turned into love, and that Ayaz spent his whole life in devotion to Mahmud. The account preserves the story of the melon: the king, feeding him a melon cut by his own hand, tasted it himself, found it bitter, and asked why Ayaz had said nothing; Ayaz replied that having had sweetness from his master's hand all his life, he had no cause to complain of one bitter piece.

The account states that Mahmud fought "almost 17 battles with Hindus", in which Ayaz "played the role of the mastermind", and that his faith was so firm that "he did not fall for the infidels". In one such story the king, attacking at the "Onkay temple", found the idol suspended in mid-air; Ayaz reasoned that a magnet in the temple held the clay figure up, and that demolishing the walls would bring it down of itself — which, the account says, is what happened, to the king's satisfaction.

The king's family and ministers, the survey relates, mocked the closeness between the two; when the minister tested them by summoning everyone at midnight to eat, Ayaz alone appeared fully prepared, the others arriving late or intoxicated and asleep. Mahmud made him his minister, and he continued always to regard himself as a slave, each night setting aside his costly clothes and taking out the old garments in which he had been brought for sale, so as to remember his past, sit alone and please his God. The last ten years of his life, tradition holds, were largely given to the remembrance of God (*dhikr*).

In Ayaz's last days, the account continues, Mahmud wished to hand his own place to him; Ayaz declined, asking that it go instead to one of his two sons, Saad, and the king relinquished his power. When Ayaz governed Lahore the city had been ruined by war, its systems of livelihood, food, trade and wages broken, and by his intelligence he gave it shape again and set it on its own feet. He fell suddenly ill and died; it is said he was poisoned out of resentment at the love shown him, and in some places it is said he died a natural death. The account gives his death as 8 August 1041, and states that his mausoleum was then built in Shah Alam Market.

## Origins and Career in the Histories

Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* tells another story of his origins, and introduces it with 'گویند', 'they say': 'این ایاز خلف والی کشمیر بود', this Ayaz was the son of the ruler of Kashmir. As a small child he went with his father to a hunting ground, where 'جمعی ازعیاران آدم دزد', a band of man-stealing rogues, seized him, carried him out of that country and sold him in Badakhshan to a merchant 'بقیمت خاطرخواه', at a price to their liking; and 'ازتقدیرات قادر مطلق شاهزاده بغلامی منسوب گشت', by the decrees of the Absolute Almighty the prince was given over to slavery (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410).

The merchant, 'نظر برحسن وجمال ایاز', with an eye to Ayaz's beauty and grace, valued him above all his slaves and saw to his upbringing, and came 'بقصد تجارت ازبدخشان درغزنین', from Badakhshan to Ghazni to trade (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410). In Ghazni word spread of a slave too beautiful to look at; great and small came to see him, likening him to the moon and, 'درحسن وخوبی به یوسف کنعان', in beauty and goodness to Yusuf of Canaan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 409–410). The Sultan summoned the merchant with him, bought Ayaz 'بقیمت گران انچه سوداگر میخواست بلکه زیاده بران', at a heavy price, what the merchant asked and more, and made him 'انیس انجمن خاص وجلیس مجلس اختصاص', the intimate of his private assembly and companion of his select gathering; 'اورا برتمامی خادم وحشم برگزیده', he preferred him above all his servants and retinue (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 409). 'وسلطان اگرچه چندین هزار غلام داشت اماسرامد ایشان ملک ایاز بود که سلطان درکمند عشق اوگرفتاری داشت': though the Sultan had many thousands of slaves, the foremost of them was Malik Ayaz, in the noose of whose love the Sultan was caught (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410).

Bhandari sets beside this a different view, introduced with 'بعضی شعرا نوشته اند', some poets have written: 'ایاز اگرچه حسن صوری وجمال ظاهری چندان نداشت لیکن دراخلاق پسندیده طاق ... بود', that although Ayaz had no great outward beauty he was matchless in praiseworthy character, so that the Sultan's devotion was to his 'سیرت نیک خصایل', his good disposition, and not to his looks (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 408).

Nizami-i Arudi's anecdote of Sultan Mahmud and Ayaz, in Browne's translation, calls the Sultan's love for 'the Turk' 'well-known and famous'; the opening sentence is garbled in the copy consulted, and Ayaz's name before 'the Turk' cannot be read (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37). Nizami's description of him can be read only in part in the copy consulted, and its reading is pieced together and uncertain: Ayaz was "not remarkably handsome, but was of sweet expression and olive complexion, symmetrically formed, graceful in his movements, sensible and deliberate in action, and mightily endowed with all the arts of pleasing" (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37).

Lahori's contents list him as entry no. 130, 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری', in the fifth chapter, on 'miscellaneous families' (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 18, folio 6), and the entry says of him: 'یہ شخص شاہ محمود غزنوی کا غلام و محبوب تھا۔ حق جل شانہ نے اس کو دولت ظاہری و باطنی عطا کی تھی', he was the slave and beloved of Shah Mahmud Ghaznavi, and God gave him both outward and inward wealth (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 192–193).

Lahori then follows him through the reigns after Mahmud's. After Mahmud's death Masud took the throne; in his reign his son Majdud, 'جو نو جوان لڑکا تھا', a young boy, was made governor of the Punjab, and Ayaz was appointed his *atalik*, his tutor, and came with him. When Masud died and his son Maudud took the throne, Majdud rebelled and set up a separate sultanate in Hindustan. Maudud marched against him, and 'جب لاہور کا محاصرہ ہوا تو بروز عید ناگاہ مجدود بمرگ مفاجات مر گیا': when Lahore was besieged, on the day of Eid, Majdud suddenly died, and Maudud established his hold over the Punjab (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). The edition's editor dates Majdud's governorship to 427–433 AH, though the reading of these figures is uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).

Maudud tried hard to take Ayaz with him to Ghazni, 'مگر اس نے منظور نہ کیا اور تارک الدنیا ہو کر صحبت فقرا اختیار کی اور بزرگان لاہور سے فیض کامل حاصل کیا اور بے انتہا دولت جو اس کے پاس تھی، براہ خدا فقرا و غربا کو دے دی': but he did not agree; he renounced the world, took to the company of *faqirs*, received complete *faiz* from the elders of Lahore, and gave away the boundless wealth he had to the *faqirs* and the poor for God's sake (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193).

'آخر سنہ چار سو پچاس ہجری میں وفات پائی اور شہر لاہور کے اندر دفن ہوا': he died in 450 AH and was buried inside the city of Lahore (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). The editor replaces the year with 449 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193), which he gives as 1057 CE on the authority of Ibn Athir, and reports Firishta as placing the death "a few days after Maudud's death" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).

## Governor of Lahore and the Resettlement of the City

The restoring of Lahore takes a large place in the books. Lahori records the tradition in full: 'یہ بزرگ بانی لاہور کا بھی شمار کیا جاتا ہے', this elder is also counted the founder of Lahore. When Sultan Mahmud Ghaznavi attacked Lahore and Raja Anangpal, son of Raja Jaipal, was overthrown and fled to Hind after the encounter, Mahmud's army plundered the city and all the subjects left — 'شہر میں کوئی متنفس باقی نہ رہا', not a breathing soul remained in the city. 'اس وقت ایاز نے سلطان سے اجازت لے کر اس شہر کو پھر آباد کیا اور رعایا کو دور دور سے طلب کر کے اس میں قیام پذیر کیا': then Ayaz, taking the sultan's permission, settled the city again and, summoning subjects from far and wide, settled them in it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193).

The edition's editor rejects this tradition outright (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). He calls the founding of Lahore "later writers' conjecture" and treats the romance of Mahmud and Ayaz as a literary growth of post-Seljuq times; in their place, citing Latif, he offers Ayaz as commander of the cantonment (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).

Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore*, which writes the name 'ملک ایاز' each time and never adds 'احمد' (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 17, 18, 21, 23; folios 12, 13, 16, 18), tells the story through the city's walls and gates. After Mahmud Ghaznavi's sack, 'چند سال یہ شہر غیر آباد رہا آخر جب ملک ایاز[OCR?] پنجاب کے انتظام کے لئے نامور ہوا تو اُس نے شہر کو دوبارہ آباد کرنا چاہا': for some years the city stayed unpeopled, until at last Malik Ayaz, named to the administration of the Punjab, wished to people it again (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 17, folio 12).

The resettlement was licensed, not private: 'جب ملک ایاز بادشاہ کے حکم سے پنجاب کا حاکم بنا تو اُس نے اس شہر کی آبادی پر توجہ کی اور فرمان اجازت سلطان سے حاصل کیا', when Malik Ayaz became *hakim* of the Punjab by the king's order, he turned to peopling this city and obtained a *farman* of permission from the Sultan (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18). He went about it with such zeal — 'اس سرگرمی سے شہر بسایا کہ چند سال میں وہ ویرانہ علما و فضلا کا معدن بن گیا' — that in a few years that wilderness became a mine of *ulama* and the learned (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18). Kanhaiya Lal makes this resettlement the event by which he divides the city's history, and the setting into which Ali Hajveri arrives, the saint whose shrine is the survey's landmark for this tomb (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18).

Three of Lahore's gates are tied to him in the book. The settlement began from the *mohalla* 'جسکو لاہوری منڈی کہتے ہیں', which is called Lahori Mandi, and 'سب سے اول یہی دروازہ تعمیر ہوا جسکا نام لاہوری دروازہ رکھا گیا', this gate was built first of all and was named the Lahori Darwaza (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 17, folio 12). The Mori Darwaza is his victory monument: Mahmud had breached the walls at that spot, and 'ایاز نے جب بہر شہر کو آباد کیا تو فتح کی یادگار کے طور اس جگہ دروازہ قائم کر دیا', when Ayaz settled the city again he set up a gate at that place as a memorial of the victory (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 18, folio 13). The Bhati Darwaza dates from his settlement too, the Bhat *qaum* settling inside it 'بعد آبادی ایاز کے', after Ayaz's settlement (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 18, folio 13). And yet, Kanhaiya Lal adds, 'ملک ایاز کی آبادی کے بعد بھی یہ شہر کبھی ترقی اور کبھی تنزل کی حالت میں رہا': even after Malik Ayaz's settlement the city remained now in a state of progress, now of decline (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 21, folio 16). The book gives no date for his governorship.

Bhandari says the same in brief. After Sultan Mahmud Ghaznavi conquered Hindustan, 'ملک ایاز که منظور نظر سلطان و درخوبی و فراست بے همتا بود', Malik Ayaz, the favourite of the Sultan's eye and without equal in goodness and discernment, turned to restoring Lahore; he 'قلعه پخته احداث نمود', raised a fort of baked brick, and the city was rebuilt (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 525). Bhandari says nothing of his tomb.

## The Shrine

The account given to the surveyor states that the tomb was built at this very place after the death of Malik Ayaz, that the Ghaznavi Sultanate built the Darbar, and that it was later maintained in good condition by "Raja Maharaja". The account then relates a period of loss: the water of the Darbar was polluted, and — in wording the transcriber flags as unclear — "the area of crop was stolen for the special place of your Darbar which was spoiled by Sikh Raja Ranjit Singh", after which only the present small plot remained. The survey elsewhere states that some of the site's space was lost during the Sikh era and some to the surrounding market.

A mosque named after the figure stands in the vicinity of the Darbar, where the five daily prayers are offered. The shrine is under the supervision of the Department of Auqaf (Government Mehkama Auqaf), given consistently in the survey as both the present custodian and the body responsible for the site's current condition.

Of the books, only Lahori and Kanhaiya Lal speak of his grave, and neither names Shah Alam Market. Lahori has him buried inside the city of Lahore and names no quarter (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). Kanhaiya Lal's table of contents lists a 'مزار ملک ایاز' at printed page ۱۶۰[OCR?], within its Islamic section for inside the city, which opens with 'مسجد بادشاہی' at printed page ۱۴۱; by the book's own classification, then, the tomb is inside the city, unlike the shrines it lists from printed page ۲۳۶ onward (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 3, folio 2). The reading of that page number is uncertain, and the line stands out of sequence in the contents (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 2–5). Beyond that line, what the book has on him is the history of the city: it says nothing of his person, his death, his burial or his darbar, and does not mention Shah Alam Market (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18).

Lahori's book has, in an appendix, a line for 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری قدس سرہ', placed 'اندر شہر لاہور', inside the city of Lahore, at 'چوک رنگ محل' (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 289, folio 277). It may be the same site, but nothing in the book says so: the line gives a saint's honorific, no 'ملک' and no date, and a landmark other than Shah Alam Market. The book's index lists him as 'ایاز لاہوری | ۱۸۰', with neither 'Malik' nor 'Ahmad' (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 313, folio 301), and in the copy consulted its index of persons has no entry for a Malik Ayaz (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 330, folio 318).

Chishti and Kanhaiya Lal also list a mosque of a 'خواجہ ایاز'. Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* has in its contents 'حال مسجد خواجہ ایاز', numbered ۷۲۵[OCR?] (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 6), and Kanhaiya Lal lists a 'مسجد خواجہ ایاز[OCR?]' at printed page ۲۸۱, a second Ayaz building, entered separately from the tomb (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 4, folio 3). The Khwaja Ayaz of Kanhaiya Lal's history is a noble of Shah Jahan's reign who served in the buildings department under Ali Mardan Khan (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 278, folio 281) and as *mir-e-imarat* of Shalamar Bagh (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 279, folio 282). Neither book says that this mosque is the one the survey reports beside the Darbar.

## Devotion and Practice

Visitors come from distant places; the survey records that non-Muslims also visit and that some have made documentaries about the figure, his stories appearing in books. *Diyas* (oil lamps) and *prasād* (consecrated food) are offered daily, in the survey's terms.

The *ʿurs* (death anniversary observance) is held annually on 12, 13 and 14 Zil Hajj, its activities including the lighting of lamps, the changing of sheets, bathing, and the eating of food at the site. Attendance is given as 700 to 800 people daily and 40,000 to 50,000 at the annual *ʿurs*.

The place is held spiritually important, the survey states, because he fought alongside the king, served the people, protected their lives and property and instilled the spirit of Islam in them; because after Mahmud Ghaznavi's death he left his residence; and because it was his habit to spend nights in the remembrance of God.

On his teachings the survey is brief: he was generous, intelligent, loyal, hasty, daring, brave, kind and honest, a soldier and also a good and devoted person, who set the example of these qualities in his own life, and people were motivated by seeing it.

None of the books consulted describes the observances at the tomb.

## Legends and Stories

The books tell other stories of the king and his servant, each in its own setting.

Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* has a temple story of its own. At Somnath the amirs advised Mahmud to take the rajas' crores; 'جب ایاز سے پوچہا', when Ayaz was asked, he held that breaking the idol was better, for the renown it would bring among Muslim kings, and God would give more; and the sultan broke it with his own hand (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 805). The survey's account sets its own temple story at the "Onkay temple", where Ayaz's reasoning about a magnet brought the idol down. The books do not say that the two are one episode.

The survey's picture of Ayaz taking out, each night, the old garments in which he had been brought for sale stands beside a story that Schimmel tells from Rūmī. She counts among 'the finest allegories ever written' one by Rūmī, "who tells the story of Ayaz, Mahmud of Ghazna's favorite slave, who looked every morning at the out-worn shoes and shabby clothes he wore before Mahmud elected him for himself; it was necessary for him to remember his former lowly state so that he could appreciate the bounty that his lord had bestowed upon him" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 221, folio 190). The lesson, as Rūmī concludes it in her account, is that "man should likewise remember how weak he was created, and then he will recognize his nothingness before God" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 221, folio 190).

Schimmel retells the story of the Huma bird as well: "One day the Huma bird passed over Mahmud's army, and everybody rushed to be touched by the Huma's shade, which, in Persian tradition, conveys kingdom. Only Ayaz went into Mahmud's shade", "for here was his true kingdom: he is like the faithful, who does not seek glory and power from anything created but only from his eternally rich, beloved Lord" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292).

Nizami-i Arudi's anecdote, in Browne's translation, turns on obedience. Mahmud, Nizami writes, was a pious and God-fearing man, and "he wrestled much with his love for Ayaz so that he should not diverge" from 'the Path of the Law'. At a carousal, with the wine affecting him, Mahmud looked at 'the curls of Ayaz' and "lover-like he drew him to himself"; but the 'watchman' of the Qur'anic verse warned him not to mingle sin with love. Fearing that he could not withstand 'the hosts of Ayaz's locks', he gave Ayaz a knife and told him to cut off his curls 'in the middle' (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37). Ayaz "doubled back his locks to get the measurement, executed the king's command, and laid the two tresses before Mahmud"; "this ready obedience became a fresh cause of love", and Mahmud gave him gold and jewels 'beyond his usual wont' before falling into a drunken sleep (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37).

Next morning Mahmud 'saw the clipped tresses' and was seized by remorse. No courtier dared ask him why, until the Hajib 'Ali ibn Qarib, 'his Chief Chamberlain', sent 'Unsuri in to restore his temper (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 56, folio 38). 'Unsuri 'extemporized' a quatrain, of which Browne's English reads in part:

*Why deem it shame a fair one's curls to shear, … When clipped the Cypress doth most trim appear* (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 56, folio 38)

Mahmud had the poet's mouth filled twice with 'precious stones', and drank wine to those verses until nightfall, "whereby his melancholy was dissipated" (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 56, folio 38). The anecdote stands in Nizami's Second Discourse, on poets, and its moral is his: "improvisation is the chief pillar of the Poetic Art" (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 56, folio 38).

Bhandari also carries Zulali's dream version of the tale (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 408–409).

## Ayaz in Poetry

In the poetry Annemarie Schimmel describes, the pair became a model. "More surprising is the transformation of the great warrior king of Ghazna, Sultan Mahmud, into the model of the ideal lover", she writes in *As Through a Veil*. "This conqueror of northwest India is praised for his close relationship with his Turkish officer Ayaz, who appears as the exemplar of the 'servant.'" "But the king finally became 'the slave of his slave'" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 84, folio 74).

In *Pain and Grace* she returns to the theme: "the warrior king and conqueror of Northwest India, Mahmud of Ghazna, was completely enchanted by the obedience and loving veneration of his Turkish officer Ayaz so that he became 'the slave of his slave'" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 175, folio 175). She names the Persian theme as "Shah i gada, 'King and Beggar'", and notes that the word *niyaz* is "often used in the Mahmud Ayaz story for the sake of its fitting rhyme" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 175, folio 175).

In *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* she writes that "Mahmud of Ghazna, the warrior king of Afghanistan (d. 1030), famous in political history as the conqueror of northwest India, becomes in literary tradition the model of the lover, because of his inclination toward his slave Ayaz", and that "The story of Mahmud and Ayaz is a typical expression of this kind of love and shows, at the same time, how the poets of Iran used historical facts to point out eternal truth" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292). For the theme she refers to Gertrud Spies, *Mahmud von Ghazna bei Farīd ud-dīn ʿAṭṭār* (Basel, 1959), and adds that "several epics have been devoted to this topic, and lyrics abound in allusions to Ayaz" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292).

Bhandari, writing in Persian, points to this literature. 'قصه عشق ونیاز سلطان وحسن وناز ایاز مشهور هست[OCR?] ودراکثر کتب مسطور علی الخصوص مولانا زلالی': the tale of the Sultan's love and *niyaz* and of Ayaz's beauty and *naz* is famous and set down in most books, above all in Mawlana Zulali (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 409). Verses on this love are in the 'محمود نامه ودیگر رساله', the *Mahmud-nama* and other treatises; as Bhandari's sentence runs, the Sultan himself composed them, 'سوز درونی وراز نهانی خویش بعرصه ظهور آورده', bringing his inner burning and his hidden secret into view (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 409). In a digression on love he writes: 'بدرگاهش شاه ودرویش برابر ودرحضرتش خواجه وغلام همسر', at its court king and dervish are equal, and in its presence master and slave are peers (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 409).

## Setting: Shah Alam Market and Data Darbar

The survey's landmark for the tomb is Darbar Ali Hajveri Ganj Bakhsh. Of that shrine, and not of this one, Schimmel writes: "His shrine, called that of Data Ganj Bakhsh, is still a popular place of pilgrimage in Lahore" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 119, folio 88); and "his tomb still provides a place of pilgrimage for the Panjabis" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 376, folio 345).

Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail* records a memory of Partition in Lahore that may concern the same bazaar, though the book does not mention the shrine and its 'Shah Alami' is not certainly the survey's Shah Alam Market. From his house Bishna Ram saw "the burning of the Hindu dominated market of Shah Alami, still one of the largest wholesale markets in the city" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 67, folio not stated). According to Ram, "The Hindus had their shops in the front, while they lived at the back. Using the gutters, the Muslims entered that area and burned everything" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 67, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **His name.** The survey gives Malik Ahmad Ayaz, and also Malik Ayaz Ahmad and Malik Ayaz. Lahori names him 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری', and his contents and index give neither 'Malik' nor 'Ahmad' (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 18, folio 6; Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 313, folio 301). Kanhaiya Lal writes 'ملک ایاز' and never 'احمد' (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 17, 18, 21, 23; folios 12, 13, 16, 18), as Bhandari too writes 'ملک ایاز' (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410). Schimmel prints only Ayaz, "his slave Ayaz" and "the Turkish officer Ayaz" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292).
- **His origin.** The survey has him educated in Georgia in 993 AD and enslaved when "the infidels attacked your country". Bhandari reports, as something 'they say', that he was the son of the ruler of Kashmir, seized as a child at a hunting ground and sold in Badakhshan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410). Schimmel calls him Mahmud's "Turkish officer" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 84, folio 74), and Nizami's anecdote calls him 'the Turk' (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37).
- **Where and how Mahmud bought him.** The survey places the sale in the Baghdad slave market, where he was too weak to attract buyers, and gives the price as ten thousand dinars. Bhandari has the merchant bring him from Badakhshan to Ghazni, where his beauty drew crowds, and the Sultan pay a heavy price, what the merchant asked and more (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 409–410).
- **His looks.** The survey's Ayaz was passed over as too weak. Bhandari's Ayaz was too beautiful to look at and likened to Yusuf of Canaan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 409–410), though Bhandari also reports poets who wrote that he had no great outward beauty and was loved for his character (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 408). Nizami's Ayaz, in lines only partly legible in the copy consulted, was "not remarkably handsome" but "mightily endowed with all the arts of pleasing" (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37).
- **His office.** The survey makes him a soldier, Mahmud's minister and governor of Lahore. Lahori makes him *atalik*, tutor, to Majdud, who was governor of the Punjab (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193); Kanhaiya Lal makes him *hakim* of the Punjab by the king's order (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18); Bhandari, the Sultan's intimate and the foremost of his slaves (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 409–410). Schimmel gives him no office but "his Turkish officer" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 175, folio 175), and the editor of Lahori's edition makes him commander of the cantonment (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).
- **The order of their deaths.** The survey has Mahmud, in Ayaz's last days, wish to hand his own place to Ayaz, who asked that it go instead to 'one of his two sons', Saad; it also says that after Mahmud Ghaznavi's death Ayaz left his residence, and it gives Ayaz's death as 8 August 1041. Lahori has Ayaz outlive Mahmud and live on through the reigns of Masud and Maudud (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). Schimmel gives Mahmud's death as 1030 (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292).
- **The year of his death.** The survey gives 8 August 1041 and names no calendar era. Lahori gives 450 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). His editor gives 449 AH, 1057 CE, on the authority of Ibn Athir, and reports Firishta as placing the death "a few days after Maudud's death" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed). The survey's date agrees with neither year.
- **Where he is buried.** The survey places the mausoleum in Shah Alam Market, near Darbar Ali Hajveri Ganj Bakhsh. Lahori says only that he was buried inside the city of Lahore (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193), and Kanhaiya Lal's contents class the 'مزار ملک ایاز' among the buildings inside the city (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 3, folio 2). Lahori's appendix places a 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری قدس سرہ' at 'چوک رنگ محل', a line the book does not tie to this tomb (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 289, folio 277).
- **The refounding of Lahore.** The survey remembers him as the man who gave Lahore a new shape and "made a new map of Lahore". Lahori counts him the founder of Lahore, who settled it again after Mahmud's army had emptied it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193); Kanhaiya Lal has him resettle it under a *farman* from the Sultan (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18); Bhandari has him restore it and raise a fort of baked brick (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 525). Lahori's editor rejects the tradition outright and calls the founding "later writers' conjecture" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).
- **The romance of king and slave.** The survey names "the love and romance" of king and slave as what should be remembered, and Schimmel's books trace the bond through mystical poetry (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 84, folio 74; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292). Lahori's editor treats the romance as a literary growth of post-Seljuq times (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).
- **The old clothes.** The survey has Ayaz take out his old garments each night. Rūmī's allegory, as Schimmel tells it, has him look "every morning at the out-worn shoes and shabby clothes he wore before Mahmud elected him for himself" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 221, folio 190).
- **Ayaz's counsel at a temple.** The survey's story is set at the "Onkay temple", where Ayaz reasoned that a magnet held the idol in the air and that demolishing the walls would bring it down. Chishti's is set at Somnath, where Ayaz advised breaking the idol rather than taking the rajas' crores, and the sultan broke it with his own hand (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 805). The books do not say that the two are one episode.

## Legacy

Asked what should be remembered, the survey names the bond between Mahmud Ghaznavi and Malik Ahmad Ayaz — in its own words, "the love and romance" of king and slave — a slave sacrificing his life for his king, and loyalty so complete that he could answer for it before God on the Day of Judgement; poets and travellers of that era and of the present, it states, have written of these qualities. It adds that he is remembered as the person who gave Lahore a new shape, and known still because he "made a new map of Lahore".

For Schimmel, "The complete surrender of the Turkish officer Ayaz, for whom only Mahmud exists, results in perfect love of the king, who becomes, in a wonderful transformation, the slave of his slave. Ayaz is the symbol of the loving soul" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292). Kanhaiya Lal, for his part, makes his settlement of Lahore the turn from which the city's later history runs (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18).

His name also served as a figure of speech. Chishti's history says of Raja Hira Singh that 'مہاراجہ کلان اسکو اپنا ایاز خیال کرکے [illegible] فرزند کہا کرتی تہی', thinking him 'اپنا ایاز', one's own Ayaz, and calling him son (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 868).

Description:
## Overview

At Jhok Sharif, in the Sujawal region of Sindh, lies the shrine of Sufi Shah Inayat Shaheed (d. 1718) — a Sufi saint remembered not only for his mysticism but for a remarkable social experiment and a martyr's death. Shah Inayat gathered around him a community that farmed the land in common under the principle that the one who sows should eat, and this challenge to the entrenched order of landlords and rulers led, after a long siege, to his execution. He is honoured today as a saint, a martyr, and — in modern eyes — a pioneer of social justice, and his darbar at Jhok is a place of pilgrimage and remembrance.

The books bear out the outline of that story from several sides. Annemarie Schimmel, who devoted a study of her own to him, tells of his preaching, the denunciation at court, the siege of his *khanqah* and his execution "in January 1718" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21), and records that "Large armies were sent to Jhok, which surrendered after four months' siege" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). Christopher Shackle, translating the *Risalo* of Shah Abdul Latif, calls him "the famous Sindhi" Sufi "martyr Shah Inayat of Jhok (d. 1718)" and finds his Persian verse quoted in that great Sindhi classic (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 325). Michel Boivin, writing of the Hindu Sufis of Sindh and their descendants in India, places "Sufi Shah Inayat's dargah" at Jhok Sharif and shows the dargah as a living centre of initiation, custodianship and song, finding that "most of the Hindu Sufis were in touch with Jhok, directly or indirectly, often through their own Sufi Master" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206; p. 60, folio 47).

## The Life of the Saint

Shah Inayat belonged to the tradition of *wahdat al-wujud*, the mysticism of the unity of being, and was schooled in the Sufi currents of his age, travelling in his search for knowledge before returning to his native Jhok in lower Sindh. There, in the early eighteenth century, he established a *khanqah* whose community held and cultivated land collectively, sharing its produce — a way of life summed up in the Sindhi maxim *jeko kheré, so khaé*, "whoever sows, eats." The gathering of the poor and the landless around him, and the implicit challenge his commune posed to the great landholders (*zamindars*) and to the Mughal-appointed authorities of the region, provoked their hostility. His settlement was besieged; after a long resistance he was taken by treachery and put to death in 1718. He is remembered ever after as *Shaheed*, the martyr of Jhok.

The books know him by several forms of the name. Schimmel writes "Shah Inayat of Jhok" and calls his establishment "his Khanqah Jhok" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21); the index of her *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* enters him, with the epithet that the site's name also carries, as Shah ʿInayat Shahid, "(d. 1718)" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 517, folio 486). Boivin writes "Sufi Shah Inayat" and "Shah Inayat of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206; p. 124, folio 111), and one of Shemeem Burney Abbas's informants speaks of "Shah Inayat of Jhokevale", the Shah Inayat of the people of Jhok (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 63, folio not stated). Schimmel dates him in the title of her article on him as "A Sindhi Mystic of the early 18th century" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 293, folio 293).

Of his own spiritual descent the books say little. Boivin names his master: "Sayyid Shah Mehmud Shah al-Qadiri was the Master of Shah Inayat of Jhok Sharif." That master, he writes, was "a Sufi Master from Jhok Sharif" who had been buried in Bijapur, in Karnataka (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 124, folio 111). Boivin gives no birth or death date and no chain of succession for Shah Inayat himself, though he repeatedly ties the lodge at Jhok to the Qadiri order through its *sajjada nashins*, and the chart of Sufi orders in an annex to his book sets down "Jhok Sharif (Qadiriyya)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 227, folio 214).

Boivin also counts him in a short list of masters, the "'three great Sufi teachers'", who are "Shah Inayat, Shah Abd al-Latif and Sachal Sarmast" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 49, folio 36). The name stands there without a place, and the company it keeps is the only sign that this Shah Inayat is meant. Boivin keeps him apart from an earlier poet with a similar name, "Shah Inat, a Sindhi Sufi poet of the seventeenth century", whom he dates 1623–1712 and calls Sayyid Inayat Allah Rizvi (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 105, folio 92; p. 211, folio 198); the nearness of that man's death year to 1718 does not make the two one.

## The Commune, the Siege and the Martyrdom

Schimmel's *Pain and Grace* gives the fullest account of his end among the books, and sets it in the politics of the province. "The first obvious sign of the struggle for power in the Lower Indus Valley becomes visible in 1717, when a mystical rebel was persecuted under the pretext that he tried to overthrow the established rule." She goes on: "The tragic story of Shah Inayat of Jhok, whose successful mystical preaching attracted many disciples from the mystical centers of the country, but also laborers from the neighboring big farms led his adversaries to denounce him at court; for during the confused situation in Delhi between the reign of Farrukh Siyar and that of Muhammad Shah it was easy to sow mistrust" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21). Two streams of followers thus came to him, adepts from the established centres and labourers from the great farms, and it was their coming, in her telling, that turned his enemies against him.

The siege followed. "The Kalhora clan from Upper Sind, particularly active in the struggle against Inayat, soon afterwards became independent in Sind. Shah Inayat was besieged in his Khanqah Jhok, and had to surrender to the overwhelming army that came from various places in Sind and Hind. He was executed in January 1718" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21). Later in the same book she gives the date again in a parenthesis: "Shah Inayat of Jhok (exec. 1718)" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 228, folio 228).

In *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* Schimmel tells the story a second time, placing Jhok as "not far from Hyderabad" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). There the dargah draws followers away from its neighbours: "His way of life, spirituality, and justice attracted a large number, not only of Sufi adepts, but also, according to the sources, of slaves and husbandmen from the neighboring villages." "The Sufi sheikhs and the feudal lords in the country lost large numbers of disciples and workers, whereas the dargah in Jhok flourished." She records that "A considerable amount of land was distributed among" Shah Inayat's followers "after an unjustified attack on Jhok, led by the Sayyids of Bulrri" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397); she does not say who those Sayyids were beyond the name of their place, printed so.

Then came the charge and the end: "the pious mystic was accused of conspiracy against the Mogul throne, the easiest method of blackmail, since the throne was in constant danger after Aurangzeb's death. Large armies were sent to Jhok, which surrendered after four months' siege", and Shah Inayat "was executed in January 1718" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). In *As Through a Veil* she writes that he was "called the first social reformer in Sindhi Islam, who was executed by the Moghul governor in early 1718" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157); the governor is not named. Shackle gives the same year, "(d. 1718)", and calls him "the martyred" Sufi saint (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 325; p. 321).

Schimmel is careful about how much of the commune can be known. To what extent Shah Inayat "really aimed at something like a land reform in the modern sense of the word cannot be detected from the sources, which are mostly unfriendly to him; positive evaluations, on the other hand, are strongly mixed with legends" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). She places his case among others in which mystical leaders of the lower Indus valley took a political part: "This was not the first time that mystical leaders in Sind, or in other parts of the Muslim world, were engaged in politics or in social reforms" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).

## The Shrine

The shrine of Sufi Shah Inayat at Jhok Sharif is a revered darbar of lower Sindh, drawing pilgrims who honour the saint and martyr. The books say little of its fabric: none of them describes the tomb, its building or its date. Boivin's glossary gives the place its most precise location: "Jhok Sharif: a village with an important Sufi Centre in Taluqa Mirpur Bathoro in Southern Sindh where Sufi Shah Inayat's dargah is." In the body of his book Jhok is "a great Sufi centre located in the extreme South of Sindh", and "Jhok, contrary to Daraza, is located in Southern Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206; p. 141, folio 128; p. 60, folio 47). Schimmel names "the dargah in Jhok" as an institution that drew disciples and workers away from the neighbouring sheikhs and lords (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).

The custodians of the dargah are the *sajjada nashins*, the holders of the seat, and Boivin names several. A disciple "spent many years in Jhok Sharif, and he was initiated to the Qadiri tariqa by the sajjada nashin, Sufi Abd al-Sattar Shah", who set him to "cleaning the stable of his Master's mare" and, when he had reached "the highest spiritual degree, that of salvation", allowed him to give *nam*, the initiatory name, to disciples of his own (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107; pp. 120–121, folios 107–108). Elsewhere he writes of "Sufi Hazrat Abdul Sattar Shah of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 101, folio 88), and his glossary makes the name a recurring one: "Abdul Sattar: the name of several Sufi masters at the dargah of Jhok Sharif." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 218, folio not stated). He also cites "the official website of Sufi Ataullah Sattari, the sajjada nashin of Jhok" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 128, folio 115). He gives no dates for any of them.

Jhok is, for Boivin, one of three seats in Sindh whose holders still keep the lineages of Hindu Sufis now in India: "They are the sajjada nashin of Daraza, of Tando Jahaniya and of Jhok Sharif. At each of them, a great Sufi poet is attached: Sachal Sarmast, Qutub Ali Shah and Nasir Faqir" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 27, folio 14). The poet who stands third in the list, against Jhok Sharif, is Nasir Faqir, though the book does not pair the two lists in so many words; Boivin elsewhere calls Nasir Muhammad Faqir "a Qadiri who was the disciple of the Master (murshid) of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 141, folio 128), without naming that master.

The dargah's reach crosses the border. Boivin reports that "the official website devoted to Jhok Sharif claims to have a dargah in Bijapur which is affiliated with Jhok", and that under the heading 'affiliated dargahs' it names a Hazrat Soofi Abdul Malik; he adds at once that "I do not know what the relations were between Molchand and the sajjada nashin of Jhok" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 124, folio 111). Boivin tells of Molchand, who after Partition "was worried that it was difficult for Hindu Sindhi Sufis to pay a visit to the Sufi places in Sindh, now in Pakistan", and of the search for the Bijapur grave of Shah Inayat's master: "he decided to look for his grave" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 124, folio 111). Of the pilgrimage that grew from the claimed tie to Jhok, Boivin judges that "this attempt at creating a Muslim Sufi pilgrimage from Sindh in India is unique, but, unfortunately, it does not look to be very successful." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 128, folio 115).

## Devotion and Practice

The shrine's annual *ʿurs* gathers devotees for prayer, Sufi music, and remembrance. Of one Sindhi Sufi poet Boivin writes: "His Sufi poetry in Sindhi is voluminous and his verses (kafis) are still a part of the main poetry, which is sung in the urs of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 59, folio 46). He gives no date, month or length for the *ʿurs*. Other Sindhi poetry is sung at Jhok too: the *kalam* of Dalpat Sufi is sung "in several dargahs located in Sindh and run by Muslim sajjada nashins, as for example in Jhok Sharif", and "It is also sung at Jhok Sharif in Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 118, folio 105).

Jhok's calendar travelled with its followers. The yearly *melo* at Bijapur is kept "every year from the 17th to the 19th of Moharram, as it is celebrated in Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 124, folio 111); Boivin does not say whether those days at Jhok are the *ʿurs* or whose memory they keep. One Hindu Sufi path counts Shah Inayat among the four masters whose death anniversaries (*versi*) it keeps: one of the four is "Shah Inayat (from Jhok Sharif)", and "the dates… are taken as sacred: the 11, the 15, the 17 and the 27" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 122, folio 109). The list of dates is not matched to the list of names, and nothing in the book says which day is Shah Inayat's.

A performance tradition carries his name. Naseer Mirza, speaking to Abbas of Sindhi poetry, says: "The sūng—the manānā—is done on the capṛi [castanets]—this is the tradition of Shah Inayat of Jhokevale—but we do not find this in Shah Latif's poetry", and, of Shah Latif, "his moods are more mellow" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 63, folio not stated).

Omar Kasmani, writing of the Sindhi publications of the state, which until the late 1960s hardly mentioned the saint or the shrine of Sehwan, records that "other saints of Sindh (especially Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, Sachal Sarmast, and Shah Inayat) were regularly featured during this time, and their annual fairs were marked by special editions" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 70, folio 53). He names no place for this Shah Inayat; only the phrase "saints of Sindh" and his companions in the list point to the saint of Jhok.

Jhok was a place of initiation for many. Boivin writes that "It was at about the age of forty that Rakhiyyal Shah adopted the Sufi path and went to the dargah of Jhok Sharif, where he stayed under the guidance of his Master" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 59, folio 46), the master unnamed. Rohal Faqir "was a disciple of Shah Inayat from Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 107, folio 94); the guru Asardas "was himself a follower of the Sufi masters of Jhok Sharif", and Dalpat Sufi was "Himself a follower of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 118, folio 105). Bedil, Boivin notes, "also visited Jhok Sharif and Daraza" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 97, folio 84). "It is interesting to observe," he concludes, "that the Sufi centre of Jhok Sharif plays a pivotal role since most of the Hindu Sufis were in touch with Jhok, directly or indirectly, often through their own Sufi Master", and "the two main Sufi traditions that were very popular among the Hindus were Daraza and Jhok." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 60, folio 47).

## Legends and Miracles

Schimmel warns that the favourable accounts of Shah Inayat "are strongly mixed with legends" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397), but the books themselves record few. The one vision they tell is of Jhok rather than of its saint: a disciple, as the published *kalam* of his own path relates, "from his early childhood on, he had visions involving Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani. In one of them, the founder of the Qadiriyya told him it was time for him to reach Jhok Sharif, to take nam from the Sufi Master" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107).

## In Verse

Shah Inayat wrote in Persian, and his verse is quoted in the *Risalo* of Shah Abdul Latif. Shackle's notes to his translation trace two Persian lines in it to him. The half-verse *bar khez ba-dih sāqī* is, he writes, "a half-verse from a ghazal by the martyred" Sufi saint Shah Inayat of Jhok, and he points the reader to "another quotation from this poet" elsewhere in the poem (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 321). The second is *sar dar qadam-e yār fdā shud chi ba-jā shud* (printed so, with *fdā* for *fidā*), "a verse from a poem by the famous Sindhi" Sufi "martyr Shah Inayat of Jhok (d. 1718)"; it is, Shackle adds, "one of the very few Persian quotations in the Risālo, but compare 2.49" (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 325).

Schimmel, too, notes that Shah Abdul Latif "has quoted a Persian line usually connected with Shah Inayat", and that "It is possible that Shah Abdul Latif alluded to his fate in some of his verses" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 26, folio 22). She gives that line in English, citing it as Sohn. II:

*The head is sacrificed at the Friend's foot, / which is in order* (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 228, folio 228)

Schimmel does not print the Persian of this line, and neither book refers to the other, so whether her English renders the line Shackle transliterates is not stated; the two stand side by side here as each book gives them.

Another Persian verse was tied to his martyrdom by a Sindhi writer, Qani. Schimmel discusses a quatrain on the 'kitchen of love' attributed to Sarmad, "one of the Sufis of 'Hallajian succession'", though it is, she says, "much older"; and "It is typical that this very verse has been quoted by Qani", in his *Maqalat ash-shuʿara*, "in connection with the martyr-mystic Shah Inayat of Jhok" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, pp. 182–183, folios 182–183, footnote 41).

Verse about him followed his death. Schimmel writes that "his fate has inspired many Sufi poets, Hindus and Muslims alike, to write touching poetry"; "he becomes 'the Hallaj of Sind' due to his death at the hands of the establishment, and to his overwhelming mystical 'state.'" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, pp. 25–26, folios 21–22). Again: "Both Muslim and Hindu admirers have composed songs extolling him or describing his martyrdom"; among them was the Suhrawardi mystic Janullah of Rohri, "one of the outstanding Persian poets of Sind from the second half of the eighteenth century" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).

The Sindhi poet Sachal Sarmast names him too. "Sachal also speaks of" Shah Inayat of Jhok, Schimmel writes (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157), and her translation of Sachal's litany of the afflicted includes the words "hast killed" ʿInayat "in the fighting arena"; her footnote identifies him as 'the martyr-mystic of Jhok' (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 426, folio 395).

At Jhok itself, one of the holders of the seat spoke in the same language of unity. Boivin reports that "Sufi Hazrat Abdul Sattar Shah of Jhok Sharif, speaks of jam wahdat jo, 'the cup of unity'", citing a work of Nasir Faqir of 1972 (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 101, folio 88).

## Setting

The epithet 'the Hallaj of Sind' draws on a long memory in the province. Schimmel writes that Hallaj traversed Sind "shortly after 900", and that "It is moving to listen to illiterate folk musicians in remote corners of Sind" who repeat his name in ecstatic songs, and "claim that he was the true lover who paid with his life for his love" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157). Boivin agrees: "In Sindh, Hallaj is a very popular figure, and many Sufi poets mention his name in their verses" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 102, folio 89). Of Sindhi poets at large, and not of Jhok, Schimmel adds that Hindu writers composed poems in the imagery of the Muslims and "devoted ballads to the fate of famous Sufi martyrs" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387).

The Sind in which he preached was a Mughal province in a time of change. Schimmel writes that "Sind was, since 1595, part of the Mughal Empire, and although representatives of the Delhi court came there, the indigenous rulers enjoyed much freedom" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio not stated). H. T. Sorley writes that "Sind was added to the Moghul Empire by Akbar in 1592" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 18, folio 9), and dates the rule of the Kalhora as governors from 1701 (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 35, folio 26). Of the province's social order in that century Sorley writes that "The system of land tenure in Sind, so far as is known, has always been feudal", and that the Kalhora's deference to the priestly class "led to the extraordinary reverence for pirs, Sayids and holy men, which may be said to have been the predominant characteristic of eighteenth century Sind" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 163, folio 154); "The social religion of Sind was built up round the reverence of the murid for the murshid" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 166, folio 157). In southern Sind, Schimmel notes, a strong Naqshbandi influence at the beginning of the eighteenth century "changed the spiritual climate of southern Sind to a certain extent" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). These passages speak of the province, not of Jhok.

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Where Jhok lies.** The site's account places Jhok Sharif in the Sujawal region of Sindh, in lower Sindh. Boivin puts it in "Taluqa Mirpur Bathoro in Southern Sindh" and "in the extreme South of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206; p. 141, folio 128). Schimmel says it "is not far from Hyderabad" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).
- **Who came to him.** The site's account speaks of the poor and the landless. Schimmel's *Pain and Grace* names two streams, "many disciples from the mystical centers of the country, but also laborers from the neighboring big farms" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21); her *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* names Sufi adepts and "slaves and husbandmen from the neighboring villages" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).
- **The land.** The site's account has the community hold and cultivate land collectively, under the maxim *jeko kheré, so khaé*. Schimmel records that land "was distributed among" his followers after an attack on Jhok, and holds that how far he aimed at a land reform "cannot be detected from the sources, which are mostly unfriendly to him" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). She also observes that progressive writers tend to read figures such as Hallaj, Bishr al-Hafi and Shah Inayat of Jhok 'in the light of' modern social ideals (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 288, folio 270).
- **How the end came.** The site's account says that after a long resistance he was taken by treachery and put to death. *Pain and Grace* says that he "had to surrender to the overwhelming army that came from various places in Sind and Hind", and names the Kalhora as "particularly active in the struggle against Inayat" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21). *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* says that Jhok "surrendered after four months' siege", after he was accused of conspiracy against the Mughal throne (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). *As Through a Veil* says he "was executed by the Moghul governor" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157).
- **The date.** The site's account gives 1718. Schimmel dates the persecution to 1717 and the execution to "January 1718" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21), to "January 1718" again (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397), and to "early 1718" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157); Shackle gives "(d. 1718)" (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 325). The year agrees throughout; only the start of the persecution is set a year earlier.
- **The holder of the seat.** Boivin names the *sajjada nashin* who initiated a disciple as "Sufi Abd al-Sattar Shah" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107) and elsewhere names "Sufi Ataullah Sattari, the sajjada nashin of Jhok" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 128, folio 115); his glossary calls Abdul Sattar "the name of several Sufi masters at the dargah of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 218, folio not stated). He gives no dates, and does not say whether these are one man or several.
- **The Bijapur dargah.** "the official website of Sufi Ataullah Sattari, the sajjada nashin of Jhok" claims Abd al-Malik's dargah in Bijapur as affiliated to Jhok, while "in the narrative found in Molchand's biography, there is no mention that Abd al-Malik's dargah in Bijapur is affiliated to Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 128, folio 115).
- **Boivin's article on Jhok.** Boivin's own bibliography lists his chapter 'The Sufi Centre of Jhok Sharif in Sindh (Pakistan)' as published at New York by Continuum in 2012, pages 94–109 (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 233, folio 220); Kasmani cites the same title from London, Continuum, pages 95–110, its first word damaged in the printed text (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 204, folio 187).
- **When Sind became Mughal.** Schimmel gives 1595 (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio not stated); Sorley gives 1592, under Akbar (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 18, folio 9).

## Legacy

Sufi Shah Inayat Shaheed holds a singular place among the saints of Sindh — a mystic of the unity of being whose commune of shared land and labour, and whose martyrdom in its defence, made him a saint of the poor and a byword for social justice. In the modern age his memory has taken on a further dimension: writers, poets, and social reformers have celebrated him as an early martyr for the rights of the peasant and the poor against feudal power, so that his shrine is honoured both as a place of mystical devotion and as a symbol of the struggle for justice. His darbar at Jhok Sharif keeps alive the memory of a holy man who joined the inward path to the cause of the landless, and who paid for it with his life.

The books show that double memory at work. Schimmel reports that he was "called the first social reformer in Sindhi Islam" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157), and that "his fate has inspired many Sufi poets, Hindus and Muslims alike, to write touching poetry", so that "he becomes 'the Hallaj of Sind'" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, pp. 25–26, folios 21–22); she also cautions that modern readers interpret him in the light of their own social ideals (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 288, folio 270). She devoted an article to him, published in the *Liber Amicorum* in honour of C. J. Bleeker at Leiden in 1969, pp. 151–70 (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 338, folio 320; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 493, folio 462). Boivin wrote his own study of the Sufi centre of Jhok Sharif (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 233, folio 220), and in his book Jhok stands at the heart of a network that outlived Partition: "Again, the invocation of Jhok Sharif contributes to the construction of a network of sacred territories which are all located in Sindh." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 141, folio 128).

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
- General established histories of Sufism in Sindh and of the Jhok movement.
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Pain and Grace: A Study of Two Mystical Writers of Eighteenth-Century Muslim India* (1976; 1997 edition).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, 2011).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *As Through a Veil: Mystical Poetry in Islam* (New York: Columbia University Press, 1982; Lectures on the History of Religions, New Series 12).
- Shah Abdul Latif; Christopher Shackle (tr.), *The Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif: Sufi Poetry from Sindh* (Murty Classical Library of India, 2025; an English-only reprint of the 2018 volume, with the Sindhi text removed and the introduction slightly edited).
- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, first published 2019).
- Shemeem Burney Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual* (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2002; Modern Middle East Series).
- Omar Kasmani, *Queer Companions* (Durham and London: Duke University Press, 2022).
- H. T. Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit: His Poetry, Life and Times — A Study of Literary, Social and Economic Conditions in Eighteenth Century Sind* (Lahore, Karachi and Dacca: Pakistan Branch, Oxford University Press; London: Oxford University Press; first published 1940, reprinted 1966).

Description:
## Overview

Data Darbar, in the old heart of Lahore, is the greatest and most beloved shrine in Pakistan — the resting place of Hazrat Ali ibn Usman al-Hujwiri (c. 1009–1072/77), the eleventh-century saint and scholar known to all simply as *Data Ganj Bakhsh*, “the Master who bestows the treasure.” He was the first great Sufi to make his home in Lahore, the author of *Kashf al-Mahjub*, the earliest treatise on Sufism written in Persian, and, in the devotion of the Punjab, the very patron of the city, which is often called *Data ki Nagri* — “the city of Data.” His tomb is more than a shrine: it is a vast devotional complex where prayer, learning, music, and above all the free kitchen (langar) come together in the daily life of hundreds of thousands, and it stands at the fountainhead of the whole tradition of Sufism in South Asia. To understand Data Darbar is to begin with the life of the saint whose blessing (baraka) is believed still to fill it.

The books that describe the shrine all speak of its standing. Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore counts it among the famous and adorned mazars of the city, to which Muslim devotees come from far for its *ziyarat*: "یہ متبرک و قدیمی مقبرہ لاہور کے مشہور و مزین مزارون و مقبرون سے ہے دور دور سے مسلمان معتقد لوگ اس مزار کی زیارت کو آتے ہین" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 288, folio 291). Annemarie Schimmel writes that his "tomb in Lahore is still a place of pilgrimage for the people" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 8, folio 4), and again: "His shrine, called that of Data Ganj Bakhsh, is still a popular place of pilgrimage in Lahore." (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 119, folio 88). Scott Kugle calls it "the shrine of Lahore's patron saint" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 206, folio 185); Omar Kasmani, "Lahore's most prominent shrine complex" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 65, folio 48); Haroon Khalid, "the most important shrine of Lahore" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated), and, in another book, "one of the most popular Sufi Shrines in the city, revered by people from different religions" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 207, folio not stated).

The older accounts set it by the Bhati gate. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* places the grave "اپنی خانقاہ میں", in the saint's own khanqah, and gives its present location as "بیرون بھاٹی دروازہ" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 289, folio 277). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* sets the khanqah by the same gate, "یہ خانقاہ باہر دروازہ بہاٹی[OCR?] کے غرب رو یہ", on ground that was formerly a graveyard (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 165). Kanhaiya Lal lists the "مزار داتا گنج بخش لاہوری[OCR?]" among the buildings outside Lahore connected with Islam (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 4, folio 3). Khalid places "the shrine of the eleventh century Sufi, Ali Hujwiri" "near the walled city of Lahore" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 207, folio not stated), and Robert Rozehnal "in the old city of Lahore" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 206, folio 198). Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian history says simply that the tomb is in Lahore: "درین مصر خوابگاه زبدة اولیاے عظام میر علی حجویریست" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 524).

The shrine goes by many names in these books. Rozehnal never calls it Data Darbar: it is "the tomb complex of his patron saint 'Ali Hujwiri", "Hujwiri's shrine" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 75, folio 65) and "al-Hujwiri's tomb", and to the disciples he interviewed its saint is "Hazrat Data Sahab", "Data Sahab" or "Data Ganj Bakhsh" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 207, folio 199). A woman interviewed by Ewing says simply, "I went to Data Sahib" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 178, folio 167). Shemeem Burney Abbas uses "Data Sahib" and "Data Darbar" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 162, folio not stated; pp. 20–21, folios not stated); Sharib's tazkira names it "حضرت داتا گنج بخش رحمۃ اللہ علیہ کے مزار", twice with the epithet "مزار پر انوار", the radiant mazar (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 250, folio 246); and Chishti's table of contents gives it a heading of its own, "حال مقبرہ داتا[OCR?] گنج بخش لاہوری" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 1).

## The Life of Ali Hujwiri

Ali Hujwiri was born around the turn of the eleventh century in Ghazni, in what is now Afghanistan, into a learned and pious family — his own epithets, *al-Jullabi* and *al-Hujwiri*, recall the quarters of Ghazni from which he came. He grew into a scholar and mystic of the first rank — a Sunni of the Hanafi school — uniting deep intellectual study with an inward devotion, and in the manner of the seekers of his age he travelled widely across the Muslim world — through Iran, Iraq, Syria, and Central Asia — sitting at the feet of the masters of the day. His own spiritual guide was Abu’l-Fadl Muhammad al-Khuttali, who linked him to the “sober” Sufism of the school of Junayd of Baghdad, that tradition which insists that the mystical life be lived in full obedience to the Sharia and the example of the Prophet, rather than in intoxicated excess.

The books add a birthplace, a family and a pedigree. Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi writes: "As his name implies, Hujwiri was born in the Ghazna suburb, about 1009" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). Zahur ul-Hasan Sharib says "آپ غزنی میں پیدا ہوئے", that he was born in Ghazni, without giving a year; that his forefathers were residents of Ghazni; that his grandfather's name was Ali; and that "آپ کے والد ماجد کا نام عثمان ہے", his father being Usman (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 21, folio 17; p. 21, folio 17, حاشیہ 1). The editor of the 1974 Urdu edition of Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, following Muhammad Musa Hakim Amritsari's *Muqaddama Kashf al-Mahjub*, writes "آپ کا سال ولادت غیر متعین طور پہ ۴۰۰ھ [OCR?] ہے", a year of birth that he himself calls indeterminate (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 196).

On the names he bears from Ghazni, Chishti records "ہجویر[OCR?]" and "جلاب" as mohallas of "غزنین" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 163). Sharib explains, without citing a source: "ہجویر شہر کا نام نہیں ہے، بلکہ غزنی کے ایک محلے کا نام ہے۔ اس لئے آپ 'علی ہجویری' کہلاتے ہیں" — Hujwir is not the name of a city but of a quarter of Ghazni, and that is why he is called Ali Hujwiri (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 21, folio 17). Chishti gives his father as "حضرت عثمان ابن علی جلالی غزنوی[OCR?]", his madhhab as "مذہب امام اعظم کوفی" and his silsila as "سلسلہ انکا جنیدیہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 163); Schimmel notes that "Hujwiri praised Abu Hanifa the Kufian" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 201, folio 201).

The Urdu accounts make him a sayyid of the line of Imam Hasan. Lahori's text says "حضرت حسنی سید تھے", a Hasani sayyid, and sets out the descent: Makhdoom Ali Ganj Bakhsh Hujwiri bin Sayyid Usman bin Sayyid Ali bin Abd al-Rahman bin Shah Shuja bin Abu al-Hasan Ali bin Husain Asghar bin Sayyid Zaid Shahid bin Imam Hasan bin Ali, a genealogy the edition's editor contests (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 194). Kanhaiya Lal, also calling him a Hasani sayyid, "یہ بزرگ یعنی علی گنج بخش ہجویری حسنی سید ہے", prints the descent in full: "شیخ علی بن سید عثمان بن سید علی بن سید عبد الرحمان بن سید عبد اللہ [OCR?] بن سید ابو الحسن علی بن سید حسن بن سید زید شہید بن امام حسن بن علی مرتضی" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 291, folio 294). Chishti writes "حضرت علی مخدوم گنج بخش ہجویری سید حسنی ہیں" and gives yet another line, several of its names uncertain in the printed text: "حضرت علی گنج بخش بن شیبان[OCR?] بن علی بن سکر[OCR?] بن سعد بن عبد الرحمن[OCR?] بن سید عبد الفتح[OCR?] ہجویری بن سلام[OCR?] الوارث[OCR?] بن سید حسن بن سید زید شہید بن حضرت امام حسن بن علی المرتضی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 172). Sharib says only "آپ سادات حسنی سے ہیں", that he was of the Hasani sayyids, the line running "چند واسطوں سے", through a few intermediaries whose number he does not give, to Zaid Shahid, son of Imam Hasan (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 21, folio 17).

Sharib relates that "آپ علوم ظاہری کی تحصیل سے فارغ ہو کر علوم باطنی کی طرف متوجہ ہوئے", that having finished the outward sciences he turned to the inward (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 22, folio 18). He names as his teacher (*ustad*) Shaikh Abu al-Qasim, whose saying on attending a murshid he quotes: a murshid "وہ ہوتا ہے جو کہ غواص ہو نہ کہ متصل [OCR?]", one who is a diver and not متصل[OCR?]; one should take *bai'at* only "اگر اپنے میں قوت پائے", if one finds strength in oneself, "اور اپنے میں قوت نہ ہو تو دونوں خراب ہوں گے", and if not, both will be ruined (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 22, folio 18, حاشیہ 4). Rizvi draws the teachers from the saint's own book: "He studied under several sufi masters, some of whom he names in his Kashf al-Mahjub were Abu'l-Qasim Gurgani, Khwaja Muzaffar, Abu'l-‘Abbas Ahmad bin Muhammad al-Ashqani. However, Khattali of Syria was his main teacher", that is, "Abu'l-Fazl Muhammad bin al-Hasan Khattali, a disciple of Husri (d. 371/981-82) of the school of Junaid" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). Schimmel makes him "One of Qushayri's colleagues, who had attended his meetings and had visited almost every leading Sufi of his time" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 119, folio 88), and a contemporary of ʿAbdullah-i Ansari, "whose work, like that of Hujwiri, was written in part in his Persian mother tongue" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 120, folio 89).

His initiation is traced through a short chain. In Lahori's account he took *bai'at* with Shaikh Abu al-Fazl bin Hasan Khuttali Junaidi, who had taken it with Shaikh Husri, who had taken it with Shaikh Abu Bakr Shibli; and when his training was complete his pir gave him leave to guide the people of Hind (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 194). Sharib makes him the murid of "شیخ ابو الفضل بن حسن ختلی", and continues: "وہ مرید حضرت خضری [OCR?] کے، اور وہ مرید حضرت شیخ شبلی کے ہیں" — Khuttali the murid of حضرت خضری[OCR?], and he of Shaikh Shibli (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 22, folio 18, حاشیہ 6). Kanhaiya Lal runs the chain from "خواجہ ابو الفضل بن حسن ختلی [OCR?]" through "شیخ علی حقیری [OCR?]" and on through Shibli and Junaid of Baghdad to Ali al-Murtaza (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 291, folio 294); Chishti's chain, ending likewise with "علی المرتضی", is uncertain at several points in the printed text and names no order (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 172).

His travels are given in two lists. Sharib writes "آپ نے خراسان، ماوراء النہر، مرو، آذربائیجان وغیرہ کی سیر و سیاحت فرمائی" — Khurasan, Transoxiana, Marw, Azerbaijan and others — where he met many darwishes and drew benefit from the spiritual graces of Shaikh Abu al-Qasim Gurgani, Shaikh Abu Sa'id Abu al-Khair and Shaikh Abu al-Qasim Qushairi (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 22, folio 18, حاشیہ 7). Rizvi writes that "Even after settling in Lahore, Hujwiri kept in contact with sufis in Transoxiana, Khurasan and Syria" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112).

Sharib gives him the titles "سلطان الطریقت ہیں۔ گنج حقیقت ہیں۔ برہان الشریعت ہیں" — Sultan al-Tariqat, Ganj al-Haqiqat, Burhan al-Shariat (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 21, folio 17) — and sums up his character: "آپ قطب زمانہ تھے", he was the *qutb* of the age, engaged in zikr and fikr, *muraqaba* and *muhasaba*, *ibadat* and *riyazat*; "دنیاوی آلائش سے پاک و صاف تھے", clean of worldly taint; and "تصرفات آپ کے بے شمار ہیں", his *tasarrufat* are countless (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 23, folio 19). Chishti calls him "قطب[OCR?] الاقطاب" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 164).

## The Coming to Lahore

In time, in the middle of the eleventh century — by the usual reckoning around 1039 CE (431 AH), in the age of the Ghaznavids — Hujwiri came to Lahore, then a frontier city newly brought within the Muslim world, and there he settled. He built a small mosque, taught, preached, and served the poor, living in humility and voluntary poverty even though the doors of royal circles were open to him. His presence transformed the city: under his teaching Lahore became a centre of Sufi learning and devotion, and the seed he planted would flower into the whole later history of Islam in the north-western subcontinent. He died in Lahore between about 1072 and 1077 CE (465–469 AH), and his grave, from the first, drew those who had loved him.

He went to Lahore, Rizvi, Chishti and Sharib agree, at his pir's command; two of them add that he objected. Rizvi writes that his pir "asked a young disciple … to follow Husain Zinjani" to the Panjab, and that "Hujwiri objected on the grounds that already an eminent sufi was there. His pir, however, ordered him to obey" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). In Chishti's account he was told by his pir to go to Lahore although his pir-bhai Husain Zanjani was already there (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 163). Sharib tells the command as a dream, for which he footnotes no source: "مرشد کے حکم سے ہندوستان تشریف لائے", he came to Hindustan by his murshid's command; one night his pir appeared to him in a dream and said "تم کو لاہور کا قطب بنایا گیا ہے۔ لاہور تمہارے سپرد کیا گیا ہے۔ لاہور جاؤ" — you have been made the *qutb* of Lahore, Lahore has been entrusted to you, go to Lahore. He objected in the dream that Khwaja Hasan Zanjani was already there, "ان کی موجودگی میں میرا لاہور جانا بے کار ہے", and the pir replied that there was no need for argument and that he should set out quickly (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 22, folio 18).

All three tell of the funeral that met him. "Hujwiri reached Lahore after dark. In the morning Shaikh Husain Zinjani's coffin was carried out for burial—he had died during the night" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). Chishti has him reach the city at night, meet "جنازہ حضرت حسین زنجانی" the next morning, and see to the shrouding and the burial (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 163). In Sharib he stayed outside the city because night had fallen, and entering in the morning saw a bier and learned "کہ حضرت شیخ حسن زنجانی رحمۃ اللہ علیہ کا جنازہ ہے", that it was the funeral of Shaikh Hasan Zanjani; "اب آپ کو معلوم ہوا کہ پیرو مرشد کے فرمان میں کیا مصلحت تھی" — now he understood what the expediency in his pir's command had been (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 23, folio 19, حاشیہ 9). Lahori's editor separates two men of that name: "فوائد الفواد میں مذکورہ آپ کے برادر طریقت شیخ حسین زنجانی، معروف شیخ حسین زنجانی ف ۶۰۰ [OCR?] ہجری (مدفون چاہ میراں) سے مختلف شخصیت ہیں" — the brother-in-the-path named in the *Fawaid al-Fuad* is a different person from the well-known Shaikh Husain Zanjani who is buried at Chah Miran (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 196).

When he came, and with whom, the books tell differently. Kanhaiya Lal writes that "یہ بزرگ سلطان مسعود سلطان محمود کے بیٹے کے ہمراہ لاہور مین آیا", that he came to Lahore in the company of Sultan Masud, son of Sultan Mahmud, and that "سنہ ۴۳۱ ہجری مین اس نے اپنے قدوم [OCR?] میمنت لزوم سے لاہور کو مشرف کیا اور سنہ ۴۶۵ مین مر گیا چونتیس برس برابر لاہور مین رہ کر ظاہری باطنی علم پہیلایا" — he honoured Lahore with his arrival in 431 AH, died in 465, and spread outward and inward knowledge through thirty-four years in Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 289, folio 292). Sharib sets two accounts side by side and judges neither: "بعض لوگوں کا خیال ہے کہ آپ سلطان مسعود بن سلطان محمود غزنوی کے لشکر کے ساتھ ہندوستان تشریف لائے", some think that he came with the army of Sultan Masud son of Sultan Mahmud Ghaznavi; "اور بعض لوگ اس سے متفق نہیں، ان کا کہنا ہے کہ آپ شیخ احمد جماوی [OCR?] سرخسی اور شیخ ابو سعید ہجویری کے ہمراہ ہندوستان تشریف لائے", while others disagree and say he came in the company of Shaikh Ahmad Jamawi[OCR?] Sarakhsi and Shaikh Abu Sa'id Hujwiri (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 22–23, folios 18–19, حاشیہ 8).
