Sharib gives Friday, 27 Ramazan 566 AH, at Kot Karor (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 49, folio 45). Lahori's editor gives 566 AH / 1170 CE at Kot Kahror (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 158, folio 146, حاشیہ 1), but Lahori's text gives 578 AH and no place (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 160–161, folios 148–149). Bhandari gives 565 AH at Kot Karor (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 528). Rizvi's index gives 1182-83 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 461, folio 437); Khalid gives 1170 (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated).
- **Where his seat was.** The site's account and nearly every book place him at Multan. Rozehnal calls him "the well-known Suhrawardi saint of Uch Sharif", and in the same passage calls Makhdum-i Jahaniyan "the famous fourteenth-century Suhrawardi master of Multan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 57, folio 47).
- **Whether Multan is in the Punjab or in Sind.** The site's account sets him in the Punjab. Schimmel's *Pain and Grace* sets Multan "at the border of Sind and the Panjab" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 8, folio 4), and has him establish the Suhrawardi centre "at the northernmost border of the country, in Multan", the country there being Sind (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21).
- **His descent.** The site's account calls the family Qureshi, of Arab descent. Sharib gives four accounts, Qurashi, Asadi and Hashimi; of the progeny of Mahyar[OCR?] bin Aswad; only al-Qurashi al-Asadi; and of Asad of Quraish, the maternal grandfather of Ali; and then rules that he is Hashimi beyond doubt (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 48, folio 44, حاشیہ 1; p. 48, folio 44, حاشیہ 5).
- **His mother's father.** Lahori names Maulana Husam al-Din Tirmizi of Kot Karor (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 160, folio 148). Sharib gives Husam al-Din Tirmizi and also, as "it is also said", Hazrat Isa of the progeny of Shaikh Jilani, and does not choose (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 49, folio 45).
- **His kunya.** Sharib gives Abu Muhammad, and reports that some wrote Abu al-Barakat (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 49, folio 45, حاشیہ 8).
- **When he learned the Quran.** Sharib: at seven, with the seven readings (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 50, folio 46, حاشیہ 10). Lahori: at twelve (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 160, folio 148).
- **How long he stayed with his master.** The site's account says he completed his training with remarkable speed. Lahori gives eighteen days to the *khirqa* of *khilafat* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 160, folio 148). Sharib, quoting Nizam al-Din Auliya, gives seventy days in his master's service, the number uncertain in the printed text (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 50, folio 46, حاشیہ 11).
- **His place in the order.** The site's account calls the Suhrawardi order one "he founded", and Rafat calls him "the founder of the Suhrawardiya school" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 39, folio 19). Lahori traces the line from Junaid Baghdadi through Shihab-ud-Din Umar Suhrawardi to him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 158, folio 146); Sharib makes him the murid and khalifa of Shihab-ud-Din (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 48, folio 44); and in the story Schimmel quotes he is Shihab-ud-Din's "favoured pupil" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 384, folio 353).
- **A Qadiri threshold.** Sharib makes him a Suhrawardi murid and khalifa (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 48, folio 44), and prints, as his, a *manqabat* to Abd al-Qadir Jilani whose last couplet calls Baha al-Din Multani "a stone of the threshold of Jilani" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 53, folio 49). The book does not reconcile the two.
- **How he became Shaikh al-Islam.** The *Hadiqat al-Awliya* has him accept the office at Iltutmish's request, after supporting him against Qabacha (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 159, folio 147). Sharib has him appointed in place of Najm al-Din Sughra[OCR?], removed for a false slander (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 51–52, folios 47–48, حاشیہ 14).
- **Why he parted from Jalal al-Din Tabrizi.** Sharib: he rebuked Jalal al-Din for not naming Shihab-ud-Din Suhrawardi before Farid al-Din Attar (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 35, folio 31, حاشیہ 6). Rizvi: he prayed and meditated on the road while Jalal al-Din visited dervishes and went sightseeing (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 217, folio 199).
- **His table.** The site's account speaks of hospitality on a grand scale. Sharib writes that his *langar* was open to all (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 52, folio 48, حاشیہ 17). Rizvi writes that the food "was offered to only a select few" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 236, folio 216). Schimmel writes that he kept fixed hours for invited visitors, as opposed to the open Chishti table (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 383, folio 352).
- **Who came to him.** Lahori: the kings of the time and high and low alike, and lakhs who benefited (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 160, folio 148). Rizvi: he "was concerned only with the élite", and Rizvi thinks it unlikely that people came to him for faith cures (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 240, folio 220).
- **What sustained the house.** The site's account speaks of endowments and gifts. Sharib speaks of agriculture and trade on a large scale (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 52, folio 48, حاشیہ 17); Rizvi, of gifts from merchants and trade guilds (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 242, folio 222); Schimmel, of a well-to-do landlord (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 383, folio 352).
- **Music and poetry.** Sharib: he was fond of *sama'* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 52, folio 48). Rizvi: he "was opposed to poetry and music", tolerating them in Iraqi alone (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 224, folio 204). Ernst and Lawrence and Abbas report qawwals in his gatherings (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 171, folio 159; Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 193, folio not stated).
- **Lal Shahbaz Qalandar.** Sharib lists him among the five eminent khalifas (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 52, folio 48, حاشیہ 16); Rizvi has Bahauddin adopt him and name him (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 328, folio 306); Kasmani reports a tradition that he was initiated at Multan by him (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 184, folio 167, intro n. 34). Khalid writes that both Bahaudin and Farid "would have had serious differences" with him (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 282, folio 256).
- **The answer to Hamid ad-Din.** Rizvi says that Bahauddin replied, though not to Hamid ad-Din's satisfaction (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 146, folio 128). The letter Ernst and Lawrence quote says that he did not reply, or replied unsatisfactorily (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 184, folio 172).
- **The estate.** Sharib gives seventy lakh *tanka* as Sadr al-Din's share (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 74, folio 70), and the identical sum, spelled differently, as the value of the offering from the ship (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 54, folio 50). Rizvi has Sadr al-Din alone inherit property worth 700,000 *tankas* (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 220, folio 202). Lahori's notice records seven sons and the division of the estate (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 158–161).
- **Iraqi's years at Multan.** Schimmel gives twenty-five years (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 8, folio 4) and nearly twenty-five (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 383, folio 352); Rizvi, from about 1239 to about 1263 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 225, folio 205). Rizvi has him forced out by the other disciples' jealousy (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 225, folio 205); Schimmel has him leave for Konya soon after the master's death (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354).
- **Iraqi's investiture.** Rizvi: the master declared his training complete, gave him his own *khirqa*, then his daughter, and before he died made him khalifa (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 224–225, folios 204–205). Schimmel's story: on hearing Iraqi's poem sung in the bazaar and the taverns he declared "His affair is complete," and invested him with the mystic robe (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, pp. 383–384, folios 352–353).
- **Amir Husain.** Bhandari names میر حسینی among his students (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 528). Rizvi argues that the Amir Husain whom Jamali and modern scholars call his disciple was born ten years after his death (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 226, folio 206). The books do not say that the two are one man.
- **Pithoro Pir's master.** Boivin's legend gives Baha al-Din Zakariyya; sometimes, as with the *gaddi nashin*, it gives Shah Rukn-e Alam instead (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 187, folio 174).
- **The Five Pirs.** Shackle names Khwaja Khizr, Farid of Pakpattan, Baha ud Din Zakariya of Multan, Jalal ud Din Makhdum Jahaniyan of Uch and Lal Shahbaz Qalandar of Sehwan (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 186, folio 161, n. 2 on 122). Usborne's Waris Shah has "Shahbaz Qalandar, the holy saint of Uch", Zakaria of Multan, and Sayyid Jalal of Bukhara, called Makhdum Jahanian (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 10, folio 9; p. 11, folio 10).
- **Two items in the literature on him.** The editor of the *Hadiqat al-Awliya* dates Malik Latif's publication of the *Malfuzat* in *Sahifa* to 1970, the year uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 159, folio 147, حاشیہ 1); the book list dates it January 1971 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 305, folio 293). The book list gives the *Ahwal wa Athar* to Shamim Zaidi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 298, folio 286); the publisher's catalogue gives a book of that title to Hamid Allah Shah Hashmi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 353).
- **Lahori's own descent.** The author's pedigree from the saint is printed twice and the two printings differ at three links and in the number of generations (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 24, folio 12; p. 232, folio 220).

## Legacy

Bahauddin Zakariya stands beside Baba Farid as one of the two founding fathers of Punjabi Sufism — the Suhrawardi to Farid’s Chishti — and his khanqah made Multan a wellspring of the tradition. Through his descendants and disciples, and through the later saints of Multan who trace to his line, his influence runs through the whole later history of Sufism in the western subcontinent. His shrine anchors Multan’s ancient identity as the “City of Saints,” and his memory endures as that of the master who first gave the Suhrawardi order an Indian home.

The books carry that memory in several traditions at once. Khalid calls him the saint "who is now considered the patron saint of Multan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 282, folio 256). Shackle's Bulleh Shah and Usborne's Waris Shah count him among the Five Pirs (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 186, folio 161, n. 2 on 122; Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 16, folio 15, note 10). Kasmani names him, with Fariduddin Ganjshakr and Jalaluddin Surkhposh Bukhari, among "The other three figures" of a group he elsewhere calls "a quartet of mystics, chahar-yar or 'four friends'", and writes: "Their shrines are spread across southern Punjab in Pakistan." Chothanbi, a site between Lal-bagh and Sehwan that pilgrims visit, "is believed to be their place of meeting" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 17; p. 62, folio 45). In Sindh the legend of Pithoro Pir traces that saint's birth and discipleship to him (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 187, folio 174), and Nanak's hagiography, as Khalid and Rizvi report it, has Guru Nanak meet him at Multan, a meeting both writers reject (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 286, folio 260; Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 413, folio 389). Rizvi's judgement is that the continuous history of the Suhrawardi silsila in India "can be traced only through the khalifas of Shaikh Baha'u'd-Din Zakariyya" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 220, folio 202).

## Overview

At Pakpattan, on the old bank of the Sutlej in southern Punjab, stands the shrine of Hazrat Baba Fariduddin Mas‘ud Ganjshakar (c. 1173–1266) — "Baba Farid," one of the founding saints of the Chishti order in South Asia and among the most beloved holy figures of the Punjab. A disciple and spiritual heir of Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki of Delhi, and the master of the great Nizamuddin Auliya, Baba Farid made the town then called Ajodhan into a centre of Sufi devotion so important that it came to be renamed Pakpattan, "the Holy Ferry." He was also a pioneer of Punjabi as a language of spiritual poetry, and verses attributed to him were later gathered into the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib — a mark of how far his memory reaches across the communities of the Punjab. His shrine remains one of the greatest pilgrimage places of Pakistan, most of all at the annual celebration of the Bahishti Darwaza, the "Gate of Paradise."

The books bear out that standing from many sides. Richard Eaton gives two whole essays of his *Essays on Islam and Indian History* to this one shrine, "The Political and Religious Authority of the Shrine of Baba Farid" and "Court of Man, Court of God: Local Perceptions of the Shrine of Baba Farid, Pakpattan, Punjab" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 9), and calls it "perhaps the most famous such tomb-shrine in the Punjab" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 16). The devotees whose depositions he read saw it as "the supreme shrine of the Punjab, to which others were subordinate" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 241–242). Robert Rozehnal, whose *Islamic Sufism Unbound* opens with the shrine, calls Baba Farid "Pakistan's most famous Sufi saint" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 26, folio 15) and "the patron saint of Pakistan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 215, folio 207), and writes that since Partition "Pakpattan now stands as the unrivaled center of a distinctly Pakistani Sufism" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 36, folio 26). Carl Ernst and Bruce Lawrence set the tomb beside Ajmer and Delhi on a pilgrimage itinerary (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 98, folio not stated), and Haroon Khalid, arriving in the town, found that "The shrine of Baba Farid is the focal point of the city of Pakpattan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 154, folio not stated).

On the years of his birth and death, on his family, on how he came by his name and on much else, the sources do not agree. Their readings are given side by side in the course of the article and gathered under "Where the Sources Disagree" below.

## The Life of the Saint

Farid was born around 1173 at Kothewal, near Multan, into a family of learned émigrés of Central Asian origin; his grandfather is said to have come from Kabul in the upheavals of the age. His mother, remembered as a woman of deep piety, first set him on the path of prayer, and he received a thorough religious education at Multan, where a chance meeting with Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki, the Chishti master of Delhi, changed his life. He followed Bakhtiar Kaki to Delhi, entered his discipleship, and gave himself to the severe austerities for which he became famous — long fasts and the arduous devotions of the Chishti way, including the *chilla-e-ma‘kus*, the forty-day "inverted" prayer suspended head-down in a well. It is from the sweetness that his long fasts are said to have miraculously produced — a pebble or a morsel turning to sugar in his mouth — that he earned the title *Ganjshakar*, "the Treasure of Sugar."

On the death of his master he became the head (*qutb*) of the Chishti order and, seeking distance from the intrigues of the capital, settled at Ajodhan in the Punjab. There he lived in poverty and prayer, keeping an open *langar* though his own family often went hungry, teaching, and drawing to himself disciples who would carry the Chishti way across India — above all Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi, through whom Farid’s spiritual line became the greatest in the subcontinent. He died at Ajodhan in 1266.

The year of his birth differs from book to book. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, which gives him entry no. 43 of its Chishti chapter (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 16, folio 4), says: "ولادت حضرت گنج شکر کی سال پانسو تیاسی ہجری میں بموضع کھوتوال علاقہ ملتان عمل میں آئی۔ پرورش بھی حضرت نے ملتان سے پائی" — he was born in 583 AH at mauza Khotwal in the Multan district, and brought up from Multan (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]). The edition's editor, in a footnote on the same page, calls a birth year of 582 AH entirely wrong, notes that *Sair al-Auliya* gives 569 AH and that *Fawaid al-Fawad*, which says Baba Sahib lived 93 years, gives 571 AH counted back, and concludes: "ہمارے نزدیک فوائد الفواد کو سیر الاولیا پر ترجیح حاصل ہے گویا بابا صاحب کا سال ولادت ۵۷۱ھ درست ہے" — *Fawaid al-Fawad* has preference, so 571 AH is correct (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]). The readings of the three numerals in that footnote are uncertain in the printed text, and the author's own 583 is not among the years the editor weighs. Zahur ul-Hasan Sharib's *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind* prints two years and chooses neither: "آپ نے 575ھ میں اس عالم کو زینت بخشی", he adorned this world in 575 AH, and "بعض نے آپ کی پیدائش 569ھ میں ہونا لکھا ہے", some have written his birth as 569 AH (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52). Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi writes that "Shaikh Farid was born in 569/1173-74 or 571/1175-76" and prefers neither (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139). Taufiq Rafat's selection of Bulleh Shah gives "(1175-1265)" in two places (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 25, folio not stated; Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 29, folio not stated) and "(1173-1265)" in two others (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 30, folio 10; Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222). Haroon Khalid writes that Baba Farid "was born in the year 1173 CE" at the village of Tibba Haji Deen, formerly Kothewal (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 150, folio 132), and Harish Dhillon gives his years as 1173–1266 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187).

The village of his birth is spelled three ways in Lahori's book: کھوتوال in the author's sentence (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]), کتہوال [OCR?] in the editor's footnote on the family (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 86–87, folios 74–75), and, in a later annotation, "قصبہ کہتوال کا صحیح نام کوٹھے وال ہے" — the correct name of qasba Kahtwal is Kothewal (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 345, folio 333). That annotation names no saint itself; it refers to an article by Muhammad Aslam whose title, "حضرت بابا فرید کا آبائی وطن", makes the link to Baba Farid (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 345, folio 333). Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* writes "زاد بوم ایشان قصبه کهوتوال نزدیک ملتان واقع است" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526). At Tibba Haji Deen a shrine official told Khalid's guide, the historian Iqbal Qaiser, "This is Kothewal. Kothewal was its old name" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated).

The family's origins are told at length, and contested. In Lahori's text his father, Jamal al-Din Sulaiman, said there to be a nephew of Sultan Mahmud Ghaznavi, came from Kabul to Lahore in the time of Sultan Shihab al-Din Ghori, resided چندے [OCR?] in qasba Kasur, then went to Multan and married Qursum Khatun, daughter of Mulla Wajih al-Din Khujandi; three sons were born of her, Shaikh Azz al-Din Mahmud, Farid al-Din Masud and Najib al-Din Mutawakkil, of whom the text says "کہ یہ تینوں بھائی اپنے زمانے کے یگانہ تھے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 86–87, folios 74–75 [markers 84–85]). The ancestral chain is said to reach Sultan Ibrahim b. Adham through seventeen links and Umar ibn al-Khattab through thirty, and is printed in full (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 87, folio 75 [marker 85]). After Farrukh Shah, king of Kabul, died and the kings of Ghazni took Kabul, sovereignty left the family though its progeny stayed on; then, when Chingiz Khan overcame the Sultan of Khwarazm and calamity struck Kabul, "حضرت کے جد بزرگوار لڑائی میں شہید ہوئے اور شیخ جمال الدین سلیمان ہندوستان کو چلے آئے" — his grandfather was martyred in the fighting, and Shaikh Jamal al-Din Sulaiman came away to Hindustan (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]).

The edition's editor rejects almost all of this. The migration story transmitted in *Sair al-Auliya*, *Mirat al-Asrar*, *Maarij al-Wilayat* and *Sair al-Arifin* "درست نہیں ہے", is not correct: Qazi Shuaib came to Hindustan before 1175 CE, about forty years before the Mongol occupation, indeed at the time of the غز [OCR?] invaders in 552 AH / 1157 CE (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 87, folio 75 [marker 85]). Mulla Wajih al-Din Khujandi is mentioned by no contemporary tazkira-writer, his name appearing only in four later books; and on the genealogy, "مفتی صاحب کا منقولہ شجرہ غلط ثابت ہو جاتا ہے", the Mufti's transmitted genealogy is proved wrong, and a corrected chain is printed from *Sair al-Aqtab* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 87, folio 75). The editor adds that after Qazi Shuaib's death Shaikh Jamal al-Din Sulaiman was appointed qazi of qasba کتہوال [OCR?], between Multan and Ajodhan — "اس وقت ایک معمولی قصبہ ہے جسے مشائخ کی جھاولی [OCR?] کہتے ہیں" — and was buried there (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 86–87, folios 74–75).

Sharib's account runs differently again. It traces his paternal genealogy to "امیر المومنین حضرت عمر بن خطاب رضی اللہ عنہ" and places him in the family of Farrukh Shah, king of Kabul; his highest ancestor was martyred in the battle of Kabul, and his grandfather, حضرت قاضی شعیب فاروق, came with three sons and his goods to Lahore, went from Lahore to Kasur, was appointed qazi of Kahtwal and settled there. His father was شیخ جمال الدین سلیمان; his mother بی بی قرسم خاتون, daughter of مولانا وجیہہ الدین نجندی[OCR?]; his elder brother اعزا الدین[OCR?] محمود; his younger brother حضرت نجیب الدین متوکل, who was, in Sharib's words, "آپ کے مرید اور خلیفہ تھے", his murid and khalifa; and his sister ہاجرہ, famous by the title جمیلہ خاتون (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52). Rizvi writes that "Shaikh Faridu'd-Din's ancestors came from Kabul, but migrated to the Panjab in the middle of the twelfth century" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 156, folio 138), driven by "The orgy of Ghazna's destruction by 'Ala'u'd-Din Husain of Ghur in 1150-51, followed by the Ghuzz invasion six years later" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 156–157, folios 138–139). In his account it was "Baba Farid's father, Qazi Shu'aib" who "went to Lahore and later moved to Qasur, south-east of Lahore", and "The Ghaznawid Sultan of the Panjab made him the Qazi of Kahtwal, a town in Multan, between Maharan and Ajodhan"; there "Qazi Shu'aib married and had three sons, 'Izzu'd-Din Mahmud, Faridu'd-Din and Najibu'd-Din" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139). Bhandari names him "پسر جلال الدین سلیمان از نژاد فرخ شاه کابلی", the father's name printed there with جلال (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527).

His mother has an entry of her own in Lahori's chapter on righteous women, no. 194, headed "بی بی قرسم خاتون والدہ فرید الدین گنج شکر قدس سرہا", which says of her: "یہ بی بی عارف زمان و مستجاب الدعوات تھی۔ جو کچھ زبان مبارک سے فرما دیتی۔ وہی وقوع میں آ جاتا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 250, folio 238). Rizvi, who never gives her name, writes that "The Shaikh's father was a scholar, but it was his mother, an exceedingly pious woman, who prayed nightly at lengthy vigils, who exerted the greater influence on the future sufi saint" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139). Annemarie Schimmel writes that he "had been influenced in his early religious life by his pious mother" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346), and names "Farid Ganj-i Shakar's mother in India" among the women of whom "there is no doubt that many elderly women in the families contributed to the spiritual formation of some of the great Sufi leaders" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 461, folio 430). In Thanvi's account as Ernst and Lawrence give it, his mother is Bibi Sharifa: "Bibi Sharifa became a widow at an early age and had no children besides Farid ad-Din. Until her dying breath, she continued to remember God, and was considered to be a great perfected saint" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 135, folio 122).

His brother Najib al-Din Mutawakkil appears in Lahori as "شیخ نجیب الدین متوکل شیخ فرید الدین کے بھائی", whom the woman saint Bibi Fatima Sam "یہ بی بی اپنا بھائی کہتی تھی", and as the family's courier between Hansi and Ajodhan (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 250, folio 238); Rizvi calls him "Shaikh Najibu'd-Din Matwakkil (Trusting in God)" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 169, folio 151), and Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* names the brother "شیخ نجیب الدین متوکل" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 229). Of his own name Sharib writes that it was "مسعود"; that حضرت فرید الدین عطار bestowed on him the name Farid al-Din; and that "یہ بھی کہا جاتا ہے کہ فرید الدین لقب ہے' جو بارگاہ ایزدی سے آپ کو عطا ہوا" — it is also said that Farid al-Din is a title granted from the divine court (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 57, folio 53).

In Sharib's telling his father died before he came to his senses. He was taught at home, memorised the Quran at twelve, and at fifteen came to Multan, where he read the famous book of fiqh "نافع" with Maulana Minhaj al-Din Tirmizi and acquired the religious sciences; he then went to Qandahar, stayed five years, and attained high competence in tafsir, hadith, fiqh, sarf, nahw and logic (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 58, folio 54). He was sitting with his *Nafi* in a mosque in "محلّہ سرائے حلوائی", where Minhaj al-Din Tirmizi gave his lessons, when Khwaja Qutb al-Din Bakhtiar Kaki came to Multan and entered the same mosque. After the prayer the Khwaja asked him, "مسعود! تو چو می خوانی", Masud, what do you read?; the answer was "کتاب نافع"; the Khwaja asked, "میدانی کہ نفع تو از ین نافع خواہد بود", do you know that your benefit will be from this *Nafi*?; and the young man replied "مجھے تو حضرت کی قدم بوسی سے نفع ہو گا" and laid his head on the Khwaja's feet (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 58, folio 54). When the Khwaja left for Delhi he refused him leave to follow and ordered him to continue his studies, and the disciple went with him "تیس[OCR?] منزل تک", up to thirty stages, the numeral uncertain in the printed text (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 58–59, folios 54–55). Sharib dates the *bai'at* to 590 AH, when he was fifteen years old (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 59, folio 55). His studies done, he came to Delhi in 595 AH and lived in a *hujra* near the Ghazni gate (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 59, folio 55).

Rizvi gives the scene another age and doubts its place. "At the age of eighteen, Baba Farid settled in Multan to undertake further studies and joined a seminary at the mosque of Maulana Minhaju'd-Din Tirmizi. There he met Khwaja Qutbu'd-Din Bakhtiyar Kaki and asked to become his disciple. According to Jamali, Baba Farid was initiated by the Khwaja at Multan and was advised to complete his education there"; but "Jamali adds that the Baba then visited Qandahar to acquire further knowledge, but it is more likely that Baba Farid reached Delhi shortly after the Khwaja's arrival and was initiated into the distinguished group of sufis residing in the Khwaja's" *jama'at-khana* (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139). Bhandari has it that "درملتان اتفاق خواجه قطب الدین محمد بختیار را دریافته": in Multan he met Khwaja Qutb al-Din Muhammad Bakhtiyar, went with him to Delhi and became his disciple; and "بعضی گویند" that on the Khwaja's instruction he went from Multan to Qandahar and Sistan to study before rejoining him in Delhi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526). Ernst and Lawrence write that "The visit of Qutb ad-Din to Multan (a strategic commercial center in the Punjab) became the occasion" for his pledge of allegiance to the Chishti master, and give no year for it (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 80, folio 66).

Sharib sends him on long travels — to Iraq, Syria, Siwistan, Ghazni, Bukhara, Qandahar and غرہ[OCR?] — and has him benefit from the company of masters whose list runs from شیخ شہاب الدین عمر سہروردی through حضرت شیخ بہاء الدین زکریا to شیخ فرید الدین محمد عطار نیشا پوری (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 59, folio 55). In Delhi, Rizvi writes, "Baba Farid lived in a small cell near the jama'at-khana and, under guidance, performed severe ascetic exercises. His austerities so impressed Khwaja Mu'inu'd-Din during his visit to Delhi, that he took a special interest in Baba Farid, prophesied his later fame and asked Khwaja Qutbu'd-Din to join him in prayer for his disciple's future greatness" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 157–158, folios 139–140). Lahori says that in "ترک و تجرید و زہد و ریاضت و علم و عمل و کشف و کرامت میں ہر ایک سے سبقت لے گئے تھے" — in renunciation, austerity, knowledge, practice, unveiling and miracle he outstripped everyone of the Chishti family, with perfect occupation in *zauq*, *shauq*, love, *wajd* and *sama* — and that "روزہ آپ کا دائمی تھا جب افطار کرتے تو درختوں کی پتی ان کی خوراک تھی": his fast was perpetual and tree leaves his *iftar*, his days given to instructing the people and his nights to worship (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 86, folio 74 [marker 84]). Sharib quotes him, from the Urdu translation of *Rahat al-Qulub*: "میں بیس برس عالم تفکر میں کھڑا رہا' بالکل نہیں بیٹھا' میرے پاؤں سوج گئے تھے اور خون ان سے بہتا تھا" — twenty years he stood in contemplation, never sitting, his feet swollen and bleeding; and once he kept a روزۂ طے, once did a چلہ معکوس, an inverted *chilla*, and once kept a روزۂ داؤدی (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 60, folio 56). Ernst and Lawrence write that "His reputation for vigils, fasting, and penances extended back to his boyhood when he used to be regarded as" crazy for the severity of his observances, and that "Customarily he broke his fast by eating stale bread" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 81, folio 67).

The inverted *chilla* is described most fully by Rizvi. He asked "if he could perform a chilla which involved spiritual exercises and fasting for forty days. The Khwaja finally permitted him to perform a chilla-i ma'kus (inverted chilla)"; the details, obtained through Badru'd-Din Ghaznawi, were that "it required a man to tie a rope around his feet and remain suspended in a well, head down, for forty days and nights, while both fasting and praying. The Baba found a lonely mosque in Uch and, taking the mu'azzin into his confidence performed the chilla-i ma'kus" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140). The master's hesitation, Rizvi explains, "sprang from the fact that such devotional exercises gave the devotee unnecessary publicity" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140), and he later writes that "the first Indian sufi to perform it was Baba Farid" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 364, folio 342). Ernst and Lawrence's translation of the *Akhbar al-akhyar* locates it in the well of the Hajj mosque of Ucch: "For 40 days they would suspend him from a branch of the tree that overhung the well every night. At daybreak they would pull him out" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 168, folio 156). Scott Kugle writes that "He perpetuated in South Asia the Central Asian Sufi practice of the 'inverted prayer'", which "consisted of a spiritual retreat for prayer by hanging by one's feet from a rafter or in a dry well, remaining in an inverted state of contemplation from daybreak to sunset, often continued as an isolated retreat" for forty days in succession, and that "Though Farid al-Din never made this arduous exercise obligatory for his followers, it was integral to his own spiritual practice, and he saw it as crucial to forcefully dispel selfishness through such muscular ascetic practices" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). Schimmel: "He performed extremely difficult ascetic practices, among them the chilla ma'kusa, hanging upside down in a well and performing the prescribed prayers and recollections for forty days" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346). Ernst and Lawrence also report Thanvi's caution: "Baba Farid was reputed to have practiced this unusual form of meditation. How could this be justified? Thanvi concludes that if it is performed as a practice stipulated for drawing a person closer to God then it is not allowable, but if it is done in order to cure some moral defect, then it may be permitted" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 135, folio 122).

From Delhi he went to Hansi. Lahori writes that "بعد حصول خرقہ خلافت حضرت نے شہر ہانسی میں سکونت اختیار کی پھر اجودھن میں آ کر قیام پذیر ہوئے" — after receiving the *khirqa* of *khilafat* from Khwaja Qutb al-Din Bakhtiar Kaki Aushi Dehlvi he settled at Hansi, then came to Ajodhan (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]); and, from the side of the majzubs, that he left Delhi for Hansi for the sake of a majzub, Mian Saranga Hansvi, who wept, in the book's words, "اب جو آپ مسند ارشاد و ہدایت پر متمکن ہیں بسبب ہجوم خلق کے مجھ کو زیارت بھی نصیب نہیں ہوتی۔ … حضرت متاثر ہوئے اور اس کی خاطر دہلی چھوڑ کر ہانسی کو روانہ ہو گئے"; the majzub died "سال چھ سو چھیالیس", 646 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 236, folio 224). Rizvi writes: "After the Baba's fame in Delhi became an obstacle to prayer and meditation, he left for Hansi in the Hisar district. He was therefore absent from Delhi at the time of the Khwaja's death, arriving five days after the event" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140); and "It was mainly his deep affection for Shaikh Jamalu'd-Din which prompted Baba Farid to stay in Hansi for a period of twelve years. To Baba Shaikh Jamal was his jamal (beauty)" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 171, folio 153). Disciples of the Chishti Sabiri order told Rozehnal that "the saints Baba Farid Ganj-i Shakkar and 'Ali Ahmad Sabir both underwent twelve years of spiritual training before completing suluk" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 81, folio 71).

The inheritance he came to Delhi to receive is itemised in Sharib. Qutb al-Din Bakhtiar Kaki gave him "اپنا خاص مصلّیٰ اور عصا", his own prayer-mat and staff, and said: "میں تمہاری امانت یعنی سجادہ' دستار اور نعلیں جو کہ دست بدست پیران چشت سے مجھ کو پہنچی ہیں' قاضی حمید الدین ناگوری کے سپرد کر دوں گا اور جب تم پانچویں روز (وفات) کے ہانسی سے میری قبر پر آؤ گے' وہ یہ امانت پیران تم کو پہنچا دیں گے" — I shall entrust your *amanat*, that is the *sajjada*, the *dastar* and the *na'lain*, which reached me hand to hand from the pirs of Chisht, to Qazi Hamid al-Din Nagori, and when you come from Hansi to my grave on the fifth day after my death, the pirs will deliver this trust to you. In accordance with that order Qazi Hamid al-Din Nagori and Badr al-Din Ghaznavi handed over all the *tabarrukat*; he wore his pir's *khirqa*, prayed two rak'ats on the *musalla* and stayed in his pir's house (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 59, folio 55). Rizvi: "In accordance with the Khwaja's will, Qazi Hamidu'd-Din Nagauri gave Baba Farid relics from the Khwaja, including his" *khirqa*, turban, stick and wooden sandals; "Although this implied that the Baba was the Khwaja's successor in Delhi, the Baba's asceticism and total withdrawal from the world precluded any conflict with Shaikh Badru'd-Din" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140) — and elsewhere: "His successor in Delhi was Shaikh Badru'd-Din, who came from Ghazna" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 156, folio 138). Bhandari says that at his death Khwaja Qutb al-Din ordered that "خرقه و عصا و غیره انچه از پیر رسیده" be given to Farid, who came from Hansi to Delhi, took the trust, went back, and "درپتن طرح اقامت انداخت" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526). Schimmel writes that "because of the politically confused situation he left the capital and settled in the Punjab on the river Sutlej" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346).

## At Ajodhan

The town he chose is named by Sharib as "اجودھن میں جو آج کل پاک پٹن کے نام سے مشہور ہے", Ajodhan, which nowadays is famous by the name of Pak Pattan (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 59, folio 55), and by the *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* as "مقام اجودہن[OCR?] جو اب بنام پاک پٹن مشہور ہی", where he hid himself from people among a folk "منکر درویشان", under a *karir* tree (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 229). Ernst and Lawrence's translation of the *Akhbar al-akhyar* says: "After wandering from city to city, he at last settled in Ajodhan. At that time its inhabitants were harsh-mannered people who worshiped the world and had no faith in dervishes" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 167, folio 155). Eaton has him arrive "sometime in the early thirteenth century" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 217), and, citing *Siyar al-auliya'*, writes that "Baba Farid resided in Ajudhan only sixteen or twenty-four years" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 228, n. 43). Rizvi, who calls the town only Ajodhan, has him there "from about 1236 until his death", and writes: "His long stay on the Satlaj, along one of the main routes from Multan to Lahore and Delhi, was a spiritually rewarding experience" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140). Kugle notes that "Shaykh Farid al-Din lived far from the major urban areas where other Chishti masters were increasingly settling" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, pp. 259–260, folios 238–239). In Haroon Khalid's words, he "had shifted the centre from Delhi to Ajodhan", believing the order "should distance itself from the imperial authority" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated); and "Baba Farid moved from Delhi to Pakpattan because he did not want to associate with the rulers there. His madrassa was similar to poorly funded public schools, where the students could not even afford a proper meal" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 282, folio 256).

His life there is drawn in close detail. Rizvi: "Shaikh Faridu'd-Din lived near the Jami' mosque, in a small house of mud walls covered with a thatched roof. He had strictly forbidden the use of burnt bricks for the buildings which, according to Chishti tradition, were not simple enough for an ascetic's dwelling. The door remained open until midnight as a welcome to visitors" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 159, folio 141). "Among his few possessions, the Baba had a small rug which he used by night as a blanket, but which hardly covered him. During the day it was used as a sitting rug. Khwaja Qutbu'd-Din's stick rested behind his head as a pillow" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 159, folio 141). "His food consisted of wild fruit and millet bread. Abstaining from nourishment during the day, in the evening he broke his fast by taking sherbet. A bowl of it would be brought to the Baba and often mixed with dried grapes. Of this he drank never more than half, dividing the rest among his visitors. After prayers, two pieces of bread smeared with ghee were taken to Baba Farid. One was given away, the other he himself ate, sharing it with his favourite disciples" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 159, folio 141). Sharib's account runs close to it: he broke his fast "شربت کے ایک پیالے سے جس میں متقی[OCR?] ہوتی تھی", from one cup of sharbat, drinking a little and sharing out the rest; of two روغنی روٹیاں he ate one and broke the other for the company; when he first came to Ajodhan "آپ اور آپ کے متعلقین پیلو اور ویلہ[OCR?] پر گزارہ کرتے تھے", he and his dependants lived on *pilu* and *vela*[OCR?]; "آپ کے مریدوں نے سالہا سال زنبیل گردان کی ہے", his murids carried the begging bowl round for years; "کھانے میں نمک نہیں ہوتا تھا", there was no salt in the food; and "توکل کا یہ حال تھا کہ جو کچھ آتا وہ خرچ کر دیتے تھے", whatever came in was spent (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 63, folio 59). His clothing was tattered, and his one blanket was so small that covering his feet uncovered his head (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 63, folio 59). Ernst and Lawrence's translation adds that "Outside the town there was a grove of karil trees. One was especially thick, and Farid ad-Din used to spend his time meditating under that tree", and that "It was there in Ajodhan that his children were born. Often they suffered pangs of starvation and underwent hardships" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 167, folio 155); Nizam ad-Din remembered that "That night when I ate delah or the fruit of the karil tree was like a festival to me; it was a gift of grace" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 167, folio 155). Ernst and Lawrence quote another writer's judgement that he "was forced by his circumstances to permit his disciples to circulate a begging bowl and collect food" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 20, folio 5).

Ajodhan did not welcome him. Sharib writes that "قاضی اجودھن آپ کا سخت مخالف تھا' لیکن اس کی مخالفت کارگر نہ ہوئی' آپ برابر رشد و ہدایت فرماتے رہے" — the qazi of Ajodhan was his fierce opponent, but his opposition did not work and he went on guiding (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 59–60, folios 55–56). Rizvi: "Although he selected a lonely place to reside, Baba Farid was harassed by local officers of the Qazi of Ajodhan and by the rudeness of the people of the town. This was prompted mainly by the Qazi's hostility towards the sufi movement" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140); "On one occasion the Qazi requested the 'ulama' of Multan to issue a fatwa (legal decree) against anyone who lived in a mosque, was known as a dervish, listened to music or danced. The 'ulama' refused to comply, after discovering that such a fatwa would be used against the Baba" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 158–159, folios 140–141); "Nevertheless, official oppression continued, and an attempt was made on his life by a qalandar. At a later date, the Shaikh became convinced that a Muslim magician was employing witchcraft to kill him" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 159, folio 141). Sharib records that the son of شہاب الدین ساحر worked magic on him and that "آپ نے اس کا قصور معاف کیا" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 60, folio 56). Rizvi rejects a modern reading of the choice of Ajodhan: "The Baba did not, therefore, select Ajodhan in order to reform or convert 'backward Hindu tribes', as Nizami seeks to show, for it would appear that there was a great deal of work to be done among the Muslims of Ajodhan. Rather, through an example of sanctity and austerity, Baba Farid sought to reform the Muslims in the area of north-west India" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 159, folio 141).

Lahori tells of a land dispute that reached the royal governor. "حضرت نے ایک قطعہ زمین ایک شخص سے شمول خانقاہ کے لیے قیمت دے کر خریدا" — he bought a plot of land from a man, paying a price, for inclusion in the *khanqah*. Months later a second claimant "استغاثہ اس دعوے کا دیپالپور میں جا کر حاکم شاہی کے روبرو پیش کیا", filed suit at Dipalpur before the royal governor; the Hazrat was summoned "اصالتاً یا وکالتاً" and sent an attendant, and witnesses were demanded "جن سے زمین ملکیت بائع کی ثابت ہو". Wearied, he said "اس گردن ٹوٹے کو کہہ دو کہ خود اگر زمین سے پوچھ لے۔ اگر زمین گواہی نہ دے گی تو ہم گواہ بھیج دیں گے". The governor came in person, mounted, and "ہزاروں لوگ دیکھنے والے جمع ہوئے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 88–89, folios 76–77 [markers 86–87]); what followed is told under Legends and Miracles below.

Kings and their gifts he kept at a distance. Eaton writes that he "assiduously avoided contact with the mundane world of the court and its ministers", and quotes Barani's report of his warning to a Sufi leaving Ajudhan for Delhi: "Have nothing to do with maliks and amirs, and beware of their intimacy as dangerous; no darwesh ever kept up such intimacy, but in the end found it disastrous" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 219, n. 12). Ernst and Lawrence: "Farid ad-Din later refused land grants that were offered to him, and routinely gave away all money and other gifts brought to his lodge. As a consequence, his family is said to have literally faced starvation on numerous occasions" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 81, folio 67). Ernst and Lawrence note that he never performed the hajj: "Qutb ad-Din, Farid ad-Din, Nizam ad-Din, and Nasir ad-Din all failed to fulfill this critical obligation of Islam. It must be quickly noted, however, that they espoused poverty and, therefore, were not technically able to go on the pilgrimage" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 81, folio 67). Schimmel calls him the stern ascetic "who gave no thought to any worldly needs and refused all governmental grants for his family and his disciples" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 383, folio 352). Rizvi tells of one offer: "Ulugh Khan himself visited Shaikh Farid and offered a farman of four villages to the Shaikh and a cash payment for dervishes. The Shaikh returned the farman but accepted the money for distribution among the dervishes" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 162, folio 144). Sharib tells the same refusal of a different giver: "سلطان ناصر الدین جب اوچہ و ملتان گیا تو آپ کی خدمت میں حاضر ہوا' واپسی پر اس نے چارہ[OCR?] گاؤں کا فرمان اور کچھ نقدی آپ کی خدمت میں بھیجی۔ آپ نے گاؤں کی مثال واپس کر دی اور نقدی وصول فرما کر درویشوں پر خرچ کی" — Sultan Nasir al-Din visited him on his way to Uch and Multan and afterwards sent a *farman* for villages, their number uncertain in the printed text, and some cash; he returned the villages' deed and accepted the cash, spending it on the dervishes (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 61, folio 57). Rizvi, for his part, writes that "Ulugh Khan prevented Sultan Nasiru'd-Din from seeing Baba Farid in 650/1252-53 when the Sultan was marching towards Multan", and that "Ulugh Khan was too discreet to request the Shaikh to pray for his succession to the throne" but "paid close attention to the Shaikh's utterances for a propitious omen" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 162, folio 144). Sharib reports that it is said he gave النمان[OCR?] the tidings of crown and throne, "چنانچہ وہ بادشاہ ہوا", as Ghiyath al-Din Balban (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 61–62, folios 57–58); and that Balban "اس نے اپنی لڑکی بی بی نہرزہ[OCR?] کی شادی آپ سے کی", married his daughter to him (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 61, folio 57). Rizvi writes that "Later Chishti records give an exaggerated account of the intimate relationship between Baba Farid and Sultan Balban (1266-87)", and of this story: "According to the Jawahar-i Faridi, after his accession Balban married his daughter to the Shaikh, but this is hardly historical as the Shaikh died before Ulugh Khan became Sultan Balban of the Delhi Sultanate" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 162, folio 144). Lahori's list of sources includes an essay by Muhammad Aslam titled "کیا سلطان بلبن [OCR?] کی کوئی بیٹی بابا صاحب سے منسوب تھی؟" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 89–90, folios 77–78 [markers 87–88]). Asked for a letter to Sultan Ghiyas ad-Din Balban on a petitioner's behalf, he wrote, in Ernst and Lawrence's translation, "I entrust this man's fate to God and then to you. If you give him something, God is the giver but you will be thanked for it" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 170, folio 158); the *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* quotes a *ruq'a* of his to "سلطان غیاث الدین" in Arabic with a translation (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 233).

Rizvi makes his refusal the saving of the order: "Baba Farid, through his total rejection of government patronage, averted the crisis threatening the Chishti order and succeeded in convincing his disciples that the wisest course was not to accept any form of land grant. Holiness could only be obtained, said the Baba, by ignoring princes"; yet "non-involvement in government service was not compulsory for ordinary disciples, and applied only to khalifas" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 244, folio 224). He records too that "The verses recited by Baba Farid before Ulugh Beg, reminded him of Firidun's previous rule of justice and advocated a high degree of tolerance" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 244, folio 224); that when an *'amil* asked him to intercede with the *wali* of Ajodhan, "Baba Farid sent a message to the wali requesting that he treat the 'amil kindly. However, the Shaikh was unsuccessful and the wali refused to heed his advice" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 163, folio 145); and that his last years were hard: "As a result of Sher Khan's hostility towards Baba Farid, merchants and wealthy supporters appear to have stopped sending gifts to the sufis at the jama'at-khana. This action impoverished Baba Farid, his family and other members of his religious community, during the last years of his life, and they all were reduced to near starvation" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 163, folio 145).

Yet the crowds came. "Baba Farid was tremendously popular at this time. The soldiers of Sultan Nasiru'd-Din's army also visited him. The large crowd of men concerned him, so he left his house. A sleeve from his shirt was hung from the roof of his dwelling facing the street. Crowds of people came to kiss the sleeve and in the process it was torn to shreds. Baba Farid went to the mosque and on his instructions his disciples formed a circle around him, so his devotees could not come too close. A farrash (menial servant) broke the circle of protectors and falling at the Shaikh's feet, kissed them" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 162–163, folios 144–145). Amir Khwurd's grandfather, Saiyid Muhammad bin Mahmud Kirmani, a merchant on the road between Kirman and Lahore, would call on him at Ajodhan, became his disciple, "finally settled in Ajodhan and for about eighteen years loyally served his pir" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 23, folio 9). In Eaton's account the saint already had two constituencies in his lifetime: the full-time residents of the convent, "initiated into the Chishti order, who lived a communal life of a strongly ascetic nature", and the masses who received amulets (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 217). Kugle notes "elliptical textual references to discussions between Shaykh Farid al-Din and some Hindu Yogis who visited his retreat in the Punjab", which he calls "these tantalizing fragments of evidence" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 264, folio 243); Rizvi writes that "The topics discussed at the jama 'at-khana gatherings of Baba Farid were of great interest to visiting Siddhas whose beliefs were founded on Hatha Yoga" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 345, folio 323).

He married and had a large family. Rizvi: "Having had two or three wives, the Baba's family was large. Some of his children died of starvation in infancy, but five sons and three daughters survived and outlived him" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 167, folio 149). Sharib names four wives — بی بی نہرزہ[OCR?], the daughter of سلطان غیاث الدین بلبن; بی بی کلثوم, mother of شیخ نصر اللہ; بی بی شارو[OCR?]; and بی بی سکرے[OCR?] — and five sons and three daughters, with a further son, شیخ عبد اللہ, who died "کا مصغر سنی[OCR?] میں" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 61–62, folios 57–58). Schimmel writes that "He did not care for his wives or children, eight of whom survived" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 378, folio 347), and Ernst and Lawrence that "it is Farid ad-Din who poignantly attests to the tension peculiar to Muslim saints, the tension between bearing responsibility for one's family and abandoning all to God" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 81, folio 67). Rizvi names the sons: "The eldest, Nasiru'd-Din", who "lived as an agriculturalist"; "Baba's second son, Shihabu'd-Din"; "The third, Badru'd-Din Sulaiman" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 167, folio 149); "his fourth son, Nizamu'd-Din, who preferred the life of a soldier"; and "Baba Farid's fifth son, Shaikh Ya'qub, was a malamati and died in obscurity" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150). Of the soldier, "According to Amir Khwurd, Nizamu'd-Din was killed fighting against a Mongol army which had attacked Ajodhan. Later sources refer to his death during 'Ala'u'd-Din Khalji's invasion of Ranthambhor in 1301" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150). Khwaja Ya'qub is quoted on the *muwahhid*: "The muwahhid is he whose main concern is good action. Whatever he does aims at seeking divine grace. Water does not drown him and fire doesn't burn him" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 397, folio 373). "It was mainly due to Shaikh Badru'd-Din that the descendants of Baba Farid spread throughout all of India, and became a significant part of the sufi movement in the sub-continent" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 167, folio 149).

Of the daughters Rizvi writes that "Bibi Sharifa, who was widowed at a very early age and did not remarry, was the most pious", that "Her father often stated that if women could have become khalifas he would not have hesitated in making her one", and that "His third daughter was married to one of her father's disciples, Shaikh Badru'd-Din Ishaq" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150). Sharib names the daughters بی بی مستورہ، بی بی شریفہ، بی بی فاطمہ (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 61–62, folios 57–58), and in his chapter on Sabir says that Baba Farid married his daughter "خدیجہ بیگم عرف شریفہ" to Sabir at his mother's insistence (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 80, folio 76). Ernst and Lawrence name "a prominent daughter of Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar", Bibi Fatimah, through whose elder son the Faridi blood line runs, and write that "the descendants of Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar (the Faridis) have shaped the continuation of Chishti identity" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 126, folio 113). Ernst and Lawrence, through Thanvi, attach a like saying to Bibi Sharifa the mother: "Her son, Baba Farid, used to say," that "If khilafat and sajjada [deputyship and successorship] could be given to a woman, then undoubtedly she was worthy of getting the khilafat" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 135, folio 122). So numerous did his line become, Eaton notes, "that even in the seventeenth century Baba Farid himself was called 'the Second Adam'" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 230, n. 51).

He died at Ajodhan in the month of Muharram. Ernst and Lawrence's translation tells that after the evening prayers in congregation he fell unconscious, asked on waking whether he had prayed, and said the prayers a second and then a third time, asking 'Who knows what may happen?'; at the end he cried out, 'O Living one, O Eternal one!', "and gave up his soul to God" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 169, folio 157). The *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* tells of the night prayer said three times and of the words "یا حتی[OCR?] و ما قیوم[OCR?]" repeated thrice (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 232–233), and Sharib that he died saying "*Ya Hayy, Ya Qayyum*" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58). The year is given variously as 664, 663, 667, 670 and 634 AH and as 1265, 1266 and 1295 CE, as set out under "Where the Sources Disagree" below. Kugle, in a note on Sabir, gives the place where he died as "in Pakpattan in Pakistan", near which Sabir's cave retreat is preserved (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 331, folio 310, ch. 5 n. 30). Ernst and Lawrence give his age at death as 95 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 169, folio 157); Eaton writes of "Baba Farid, who died at the age of ninety in A.D. 1265" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241).

Rizvi tells how the grave came to lie inside the town. His fourth son Nizamu'd-Din "was with Balban's army in Patiali (approximately two hundred kilometres east of Delhi). When he reached Ajodhan, the coffin was being taken for burial outside the city walls. He suggested to his brothers that it be brought inside so that pilgrims could also receive spiritual guidance from members of Baba Farid's descendants. His advice was taken" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150). Sharib records how poor the house was at the end: "جب آپ کا وصال ہوا تو گھر میں کفن کے لئے پیسہ نہ تھا۔ مکان کا دروازہ توڑ کر اس کی اینٹیں قبر میں لگائی گئیں" — when he died there was no money in the house for a shroud, and the door of the house was broken up and its bricks set in the grave (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 63, folio 59).

## Disciples and Succession

Rizvi calls Nizamuddin Auliya "Baba Farid's most outstanding khalifa" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150), and dates his discipleship closely: "In 655/1257-58 Nizamu'd-Din left Delhi for Ajodhan"; "Nizamu'd-Din was immediately initiated and his head shaved"; he made three visits in all, and "In Jumada I 663/February 1265, the Shaikh made his third and final visit to the Baba" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 174, folio 156); "He received his khilafat-nama from Baba Farid on 13 Ramazan 663/29 June 1265" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 175, folio 157). Baba Farid "offered him a bed in the jama'at-khana" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 174, folio 156). Schimmel writes that "After his third visit to Pakpattan, he was appointed khalifa in Delhi", and that Nizamuddin was Farid's outstanding khalifa, "whom he met in 1257" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 379, folio 348). Bhandari writes that Nizamuddin "در بست سالگی بقصبه اجودهن رسیده از شیخ فرید الدین گنجشکر ارادت گرفت", and that having obtained "کلید گنجینه معنوی" he was given leave for Delhi to guide the people (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 556). Kugle: "Near the end of his life, Shaykh Farid al-Din delegated his authority to a young follower", Nizam al-Din; "Farid al-Din charged him to become the embodiment of love, through whom the comforting shade of divine mercy would pour forth in the capital city of Delhi, infusing all corners of the Islamic empire in India" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). Regula Burckhardt Qureshi's study of qawwali calls Baba Farid, in her glossary, "spiritual guide of Nizamuddin Auliya" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 262, folio 242).

The training was severe. "The method by which Baba Farid trained Shaikh Nizamu'd-Din Auliya' to take up his position as successor in the order became engraved in the latter's memory" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 175, folio 157), and Baba Farid justified it: "the pir is the mashshata (hairdresser) of the murids (disciples)" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 176, folio 158). His parting words, in Rizvi: "'You will be a tree under whose shadow the people will find rest… you should strengthen your spirits by devotion…I have handed over all these things to you for at the time of my death you will not be present.'" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 175, folio 157). Lahori tells that after eating the cowpeas Nizam al-Din had bought by pawning his turban, he blessed the disciple's kitchen: "ہم نے خدا سے مانگا ہے کہ تیرے مہمان خانے میں ہر روز تہتر من نمک خرچ ہوا کرے" — seventy-three maunds of salt a day (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 95, folio 83 [marker 93]). Nizamuddin later found himself unable to abolish prostration before the pir, because of "the traditions followed by Shaikh Qutbu'd-Din Bakhtiyar Kaki and Shaikh Faridu'd-Din, who had both permitted prostration" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 239, folio 219). He drew up his own disciples' diplomas "according to a strict procedure that Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar employed" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 194, folio 182).

How the tokens of succession reached Nizamuddin is told several ways. Kugle: "Upon his death in 1265, Farid al-Din sent his staff, sandals, and other tokens of his authority to Nizam al-Din in Delhi" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). Sharib: "آپ کی وفات کے بعد حضرت نظام الدین اولیاء اجودھن آئے تو آپ کے داماد حضرت بدر الدین اسحق نے آپ کی وصیت کے مطابق جامہ ان کو دیا" — when Nizam al-Din Auliya came to Ajodhan after his death, his son-in-law Badr al-Din Ishaq gave him the robe in accordance with his will (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58). Ernst and Lawrence's translation tells that "When Nizam ad-Din was laid in his grave, they covered his body with the cloak that he had received from Farid ad-Din and they put under his blessed head the prayer mat of the Shaykh" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 176, folio 164).

His khalifas are counted differently. Rizvi: "Later authorities give a long list of the khalifas of Baba Farid, but Amir Khwurd lists only seven. According to Baba himself, the khalifas were chosen in three different ways. The most outstanding were those whom God inspired the Shaikh to select. These were the Rahmani khalifas. The second category were those personally chosen by the Shaikh because of their own merits. The third group consisted of those disciples whom the Shaikh accepted as successors on the recommendation of others" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150). Schimmel: "Fariduddin invested seven khalifas with spiritual power; among his disciples, Jamal Hanswi and Nizamuddin must be counted as his special friends" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 379, folio 348). Sharib: "بعض نے لکھا ہے کہ آپ کے خلفاء پچاس ہزار سے زیادہ تھے" — some have written that his khalifas numbered more than fifty thousand (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58).

His deputies carried signed documents, countersealed at Hansi. Lahori: "حضرت فرید الدین گنج شکر کا یہ دستور تھا کہ جس خلیفہ کو کسی ملک کو روانہ کرتے۔ فرمان اپنے دستخط سے لکھ کر اس کو دیتے اور فرماتے کہ خواجہ جمال الدین ہانسویؒ کے پاس جا کر اس کی مہر کرا لو" — every khalifa sent to a country carried a *farman* over Farid's own signature, to be sealed by Khwaja Jamal al-Din Hansvi at Hansi before he set out (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 90, folio 78 [marker 88]). Sharib, in a chapter that places Baba Farid at Ajodhan and citing *Siyar al-Auliya*, has the same rule: if Shaikh Jamal sealed the *khilafat-nama* it was reckoned "مستند", authentic, and if he did not, Baba Sahib would not accept it either, saying "پارہ کردۂ جمال را نتوانیم دوخت", what Jamal has torn we cannot stitch (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 84, folio 80). Rizvi explains the rule by a forgery threat: "The Baba took care that his khilafat-namas were quite accurate and not forged as a disciple whom he considered unworthy of receiving a khilafat-nama threatened the Baba that he would prepare a similar document and use it for enlisting his own disciples" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 166–167, folios 148–149); "Maulana Badru'd-Din Ishaq who prepared copies of the khilafat-nama was required to sign them, and they were later endorsed by the Baba's senior disciple, Shaikh Jamalu'd-Din, who lived at Hansi" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 167, folio 149). Badr al-Din Ishaq was also "the steward of his jama'at-khana" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 170, folio 152). Jamal al-Din had a copy of the *'Awarifu'l-Ma'arif* "from Baba Farid at the time of receiving his khilafat-nama", which passed down to his grandson through Nizamuddin (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 196, folio 178). In Jamal al-Din's house, Sharib relates, there was a *kaniz*, "وہ پاک دامن خاتون تھیں", whom Baba Farid addressed as "مادر مومناں"; asked "مادر مومناں! جمال ماچہ می کند", she said that since meeting Baba Sahib he had wholly abandoned village, means, estate and the occupation of preaching, girding himself to starvation and labour, and Baba Sahib, delighted, said "الحمدللہ' خوش می باشد" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 84–85, folios 80–81). To Jamal al-Din's minor son Burhan al-Din Sufi he "ان کو خرقہ خلافت' مصلا اور عصا عنایت فرمایا", gave the *khirqa* of *khilafat*, the *musalla* and the staff (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 85, folio 81). Bhandari records at Hansi the "مزار شیخ جمال الدین خلیفه شیخ فرید الدین گنجشکر" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 554).

Sabir is told of in conflicting ways. In Lahori, Ala al-Din Ali Ahmad was given the title Sabir for twelve years' service in the kitchen without eating an unpermitted morsel, "اور دہلی کا قطب بنا کر فرمان لکھ دیا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 90, folio 78 [marker 88]); when Jamal al-Din tore up the first *farman*, Farid said "پارہ کردہ جمال را فرید نتواند دوخت", and later wrote Sabir a "فرمان تولیت", a *farman* of custodianship, for Kaliyar in his own hand (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 91, folio 79 [marker 89]). Sharib's chapter on Sabir, which places Baba Farid at Ajodhan, says that "حضرت بابا فرید الدین گنج شکر رحمۃ اللہ علیہ نے لنگر تقسیم کرنے کی خدمت آپ کے سپرد فرمائی", he entrusted Sabir with distributing the *langar*; that "آپ نے 12 سال کے عرصہ میں کچھ نہیں کھایا", over twelve years he ate nothing of it; and that when Baba Farid learned this he said "علاؤ الدین احمد صابر ہیں", and the title stuck (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 78, folio 74). Sabir had come to Ajodhan with his mother and lived with his *mamun*, his maternal uncle, Baba Farid (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 78, folio 74). Entrusted with the *wilayat* of Delhi, with the instruction to have his certificate sealed at Hansi first (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 78, folio 74), Sabir rode into Jamal al-Din's *khanqah* at Hansi still mounted on his palanquin (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 78–79, folios 74–75); Jamal al-Din "حضرت جمال الدین ہانسوی نے آپ کا خلافت نامہ پھاڑ دیا۔ خلافت نامہ پر مہر نہیں لگائی", tore the certificate up and did not seal it (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 79, folio 75); at Ajodhan Baba Farid said "پارہ کردہ جمال را فرید نتواں دوخت", and then "حضرت بابا صاحب نے آپ کو کلیر کی ولایت سپرد فرمائی' آپ کی مثال پر اپنے دستخط کئے اور اس مرتبہ آپ کو حضرت جمال الدین ہانسوی کے پاس جانے کی تاکید نہیں فرمائی" — he entrusted him with the *wilayat* of Kaliyar, signed the deed himself, and this time did not send him to Jamal al-Din (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 79–80, folios 75–76). Kugle tells it otherwise: Sabir's "ability to channel this force into performing miracles was so audacious that Shaykh Farid al-Din was wary of granting him leadership of the community and exposing the wider public to his spiritual heat. Instead, he sent the young Shaykh Sabir out to the wilderness" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). He calls Sabir "a follower and nephew of Shaykh Farid al-Din 'Ganj-i Shakar'" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 259, folio 238), and reports that Sabir's followers "regarded him as the true inheritor of Shaykh Farid al-Din's saintly authority and the only one of his followers to adhere closely to the saint's rigorous concentration on bodily control" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 261, folio 240). Rizvi writes that in later sources "the sufi whose khilafat-nama, Shaikh Jamalu'd-Din had torn was Sabir, and he was also depicted as the nephew of Baba Farid", and calls these stories legendary (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 172, folio 154). Ernst and Lawrence report that Shaykh 'Ali ibn Ahmad Sabir "is said to have been the Shaykh 'Ali Sabir who is briefly mentioned in Siyar al-awliya' as a disciple of Shaykh Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar. No less an authority than Shaykh 'Abd al-Haqq, however, questions the conflation of the two names and persons" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 74, folio 60).

Through these two the order divided. "The centuries-old division between the two branches stems from the time of Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar, and it is his two disciples 'Ala' ad-Din 'Ali Sabir and Nizam ad-Din Awliya', after whom these two branches are named" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 131, folio 118); "Both the major sublineages of the Chishtis derive from him" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 167, folio 155). Kugle: "not all Chishtis were followers of Nizam al-Din, even if the majority were, for Nizam al-Din was not the only follower of the passionate and ascetic Shaykh Farid al-Din" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). In Qureshi's table of the Chishti hierarchy, Baba Farid stands below Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar-e-Kaki and above the pair Ala'uddin Sabir and Nizamuddin Auliya (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 101, folio 81); in the Chishti Sabiri *shajara* that Rozehnal prints, "19. Farid ad-Din Mas'ud Ganj-i Shakkar (d. 1265)" is followed by 'Ala ad-Din 'Ali Ahmad Sabir, "eponymous founder of the Chishti Sabiri order" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 15, folio 4). Ernst and Lawrence count him the third of "the five human pillars on whom the Indian extension of the Chishti order was built" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 80, folio 66), one of "the three Chishti giants, Farid ad-Din, Nizam ad-Din, and Nasir ad-Din, who complete the first cycle of the Chishtiyya" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 183, folio 171), and write that "Shaykh Farid was in the first generation of Indian-born masters of the Chishti order" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 111, folio 98).

Other disciples pass through the books. Shams al-Din Turk was told at his leave-taking "کہ پانی پت میں مستقل سکونت اختیار کریں' کیوں کہ پانی پت کی ولایت ان کے سپرد کی گئی ہے", to settle at Panipat because its *wilayat* had been entrusted to him; and Baba Farid declared his own *khilafat* insufficient for him, "حصول نعمت و کمال تو موقوف بر مرشد دیگر است", and sent him to Sabir at Kaliyar (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 92, folio 88). Sabir sent away the qawwal حسن قوال with a few gular figs, which he brought to Baba Sahib at Ajodhan; "حضرت بابا صاحب نے وہ گولر حاضرین کو تقسیم فرمائے", and whoever ate of them "اس کی کثافت دور ہوئی' اس کو نور باطن حاصل ہوا" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 82–83, folios 78–79). Lahori records that a grandson, Shaikh Ala al-Din, received the Hindu Sohan Majzub "اجودھنی پاک پٹنی" into Islam (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 236, folio 224), and that Shah Kaku Chishti of Lahore was "حضرت خواجہ فرید الدین گنج شکر کی اولاد سے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 99–100, folios 87–88 [markers 97–98]). Generations later, Burhan ad-Din Gharib asked of Nizam ad-Din "the gift of being under the direct spiritual observation (nazar) of Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 192, folio 180).

## Teaching and Poetry

Baba Farid’s teaching was the pure Chishti gospel of love: of God to be sought through humility, poverty (*faqr*), patient endurance, and above all a boundless compassion that returned kindness for cruelty. He is remembered for counselling his disciples to answer harshness with gentleness — to give those who bring thorns the softest of replies. What sets him apart in the history of the Punjab is that he expressed this vision not only in the Persian of the learned but in the language of the common people, and he is honoured as one of the earliest and greatest poets of Punjabi. His *shlokas* (couplets) have such authority that the Sikh Gurus included a body of them in the Guru Granth Sahib. Their tone is unmistakable — the ache of the soul for God, and the memory of death that makes the world small:

کاگا سب تن کھائیو، چُن چُن کھائیو ماس
دوے نیناں مت کھائیو، مینوں پِیا ملن دی آس

*"O crow, eat all my flesh, pick and eat it piece by piece — but do not eat these two eyes, for I still long to see my Beloved."*

فریدا جے تُوں عقل لطیف ہیں، کالے لِکھ نہ لیکھ
آپنڑے گریوان مہ سِر نیواں کر ویکھ

*"Farid, if you are of subtle wit, write not against another’s account; bow your head into your own collar, and look there instead."*

Rizvi gives the teaching in his own summary: "To Baba Farid, sufism was a strenuous exercise leading one to a pious life within the society in which one lived. It demanded humility, modesty, patience, fortitude and a cleansing of the heart from all conceit. Self-abnegation involved careful concern for any offence to another, and in the event of such a situation, sincere and copious apologies were demanded" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146). "Five hundred aphorisms of Baba Farid were collected", and Rizvi prints sixty of those Amir Khwurd selected, which "give some insight into the Baba's broadly based, humanitarian teachings" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146). Among them is a parable of renunciation: "The zakat of Sharia'a [OCR?] [Shari'a] was five dirhams out of 200, the zakat of Tariga [Tariqa] involved the payment of 195 dirhams out of 200 and the retention of only five dirhams and the zakat of Hagiqa [Haqiqa] entailed the payment of everything, while retaining nothing" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146). "He encouraged education in his disciples and considered the 'ulama' to be nobler than the common people, though he disliked their self-satisfied indifference to others"; the *faqirs*, he asserted, were superior to the *'ulama'* "and occupied the same place among them as the full moon amongst a constellation of stars" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146). The *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* quotes the saying in Arabic, "العلماء اشرف الناس والفقراء اشرف الاشراف والفقیر من العلماء کالبدر فی الکواکب", together with "الآفتہ فی التدبیر والسلامت فی التسلیم" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 233). "Fasting was the first half of the way along the sufi path, said the Baba, and prayers and pilgrimages the other" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 174, folio 156).

Asked whether to give up study for prayer, he answered, in Rizvi's paraphrase, that the disciple should "continue both, as the two were necessary for the life of a dervish and he would then see which would emerge as the most dominant" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 174, folio 156); in Ernst and Lawrence's translation, "Do both till one predominates" — though they warn at once that "This anecdote is not found in Fawa'id al-fu'ad. It may or may not be true" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 87, folio 73). Sharib sets out his teachings at length: six kinds of *tauba*, of heart and tongue, eye, ear, hand, foot and *nafs*; that a dervish who seeks the eminence of this base world "درویش نہیں ہے' درویشوں کا نام بد نام کرنے والا ہے اور مرتد طریقت ہے' کیونکہ فقراء کو دنیا سے اعراض ہے", is no dervish but one who defames dervishes and an apostate from the *tariqa*; "محبت کے ساتھ سو مقام ہیں", love has a hundred stations, the first being patience under affliction from the Friend; that the *kulah* may not be worn until one guards the four worlds of eye, ear, tongue, and hand and foot; and four questions "چار چیزوں کے متعلق سات سو پیران طریقت سے پوچھا گیا' سب نے ایک سا جواب دیا", put to seven hundred pirs of the *tariqa*, all of whom answered alike — the wisest is he who abandons sins, the most alert he whom nothing troubles, the richest the contented, the neediest he who abandons contentment (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 64–65, folios 60–61). Among his sayings Sharib prints "تصوف مولیٰ کی صفا دوستی[OCR?] کا نام ہے" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 65, folio 61), and calls his teachings "آپ کی تعلیمات تصوف کا بیش بہا خزانہ ہیں", a priceless treasury of *tasawwuf* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 64, folio 60).

His prayers became remedies. Sharib gives *aurad* and *waza'if* in his name: Sura Baqara recited between the *sunnats* and *farz* of the dawn prayer for three days fulfils a purpose; Sura An'am recited seventy times fulfils a need; "لا الہ الا انت سبحانک انی کنت من الظالمین" frees one from grief and worry; and "حسب ذیل دعا اکثر پڑھنے سے معاش میں تنگی دور ہوتی ہے" — frequent recitation of the following prayer removes straitness in livelihood — "بسم اللّٰہ الرحمٰن یا دائم العز والملک والبقاء یا ذو الجلال و الجود والفضل والعطاء یا و دود ذو العرش المجید یا فعال ما یرید" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 66, folio 62). Ernst and Lawrence write that "Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar is the source of specific zikr formulas, including some in Indian languages" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 45, folio 31), and quote one, from Awrangabadi: "Say *wuhi hi* upwards, *hi hi* to the left side of the breast, *hin hi* toward the heart." These phrases, they add, "belong to a long tradition of adapting" hatha yoga mantras to Islamic themes and Sufi practices (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 47, folio 33). Nizamuddin traced his own amulet-writing to him, recalling "the fact that Shaikh Faridu'd-Din once gave me a pot of ink and ordered me to write amulets for the people" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 193, folio 175), and Farid had himself asked his master about amulets, receiving the answer that "the fulfilment of desires belonged to no-one; the amulets contained God's name and His words, and could be given to the people" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 154–155, folios 136–137).

He loved *sama'*. Sharib: "آپ کو سماع کا بہت شوق تھا", he was very fond of *sama'* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 62–63, folios 58–59), and his saying "سماع راحت دل ہے اور اہل محبت کو جنبش دینے والا ہے' جو بحر محبت میں شناوری کرتا ہے" — *sama'* is the heart's ease and sets the people of love in motion (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 65, folio 61). Asked about its lawfulness, "a topic disputed among the 'ulama", he replied, in Ernst and Lawrence's translation, "Praise be to God!" and then: "One group has been burnt to ashes, while the other is still arguing" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 170, folio 158). Ashraf Jahangir Simnani counted him among the Indian shaykhs who favoured music and "experienced empathetic ecstasy and danced" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 57, folio 43). Once, Rizvi writes, "the Baba wished to partake of sama' although no musician was present", and had the letters of Qazi Hamidu'd-Din Nagauri read to him instead, falling at once into an ecstatic swoon (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 216, folio 198).
