The qawwals of the Chishti order sing his name in Amir Khusrau's Hindi song, which Qureshi transcribes. Its second verse runs "Sadqa Baba Ganj-e-Shakar ka / Rakh le laj hamari (Nijam Piya)", which she translates (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 46, folio 26):

*In the name of Ganj-e-Shakar / Protect our honour (Nijam, Beloved)* (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 46, folio 26)

In another song, "Ganj-e-Shakar ke rup men, Mahbub piyara sowat hai" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 51, folio 31):

*In the likeness of Ganj-e-Shakar [see note 6 above], the dear Beloved is asleep* (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 51, folio 31)

Qureshi observed that the stanza naming him "is certain to yield offerings, since it constitutes an appeal to the saint in the very name of his own spiritual guide, Baba Farid", the saint being Nizamuddin (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 187, folio 167), and that the song, "both text and music, is part of the Qawwal Bachche's special heritage. It is widely sung within the entire Chishti" order (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 47, folio 27).

A qawwali in the United Kingdom that Abbas describes opens by invoking him. She transliterates the line "Sir devĩ te vafā na mangĩ-ehī pīr Farīd dā dāse" and translates (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 88, folio not stated):

*Give thy head, expect no loyalty in return— / O, this is Farid, the Saint's wisdom* (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 10, folio not stated)

Another line of the same performance, "Yār Farīd ābād thī vaṇ o jhok-rab phir vīrān basāe", she renders as running text:

*O lover Farid, alive were those habitations once—may God bring the wilderness to life again!* (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 88, folio not stated)

"Had it not been for the very sacred frame at the beginning, when his ensemble invoked Baba Farid, a researcher might have taken the performance for a secular love song where a lover seeks a beloved and serenades her" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 89, folio not stated).

When Sher Khan turned against him, Baba Farid is said to have recited:

*'Alas! You have no knowledge about me; / When you would gain knowledge about me, you would repent.'* (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 163, folio 145)

The older books carry verse about him. The *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* prints a versified Chishti chain in which he follows "قطب الدین" and precedes "محبوب الٰہی", with the lines "از کمال نور[OCR?] رخ و ہمچون فرید الدین شدی" and "صد ہزاراں [illegible] شکر بار[OCR?] آمدے" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 36–37), and a chronogram with the line "بامدادِ[OCR?] فرید الدین شکر گنج" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 38). After giving his death year as "سنہ ۶۶۳[OCR?] ہجری" it prints a *qit'a-e tarikh*, a chronogram verse, by "مفتی[OCR?] غلام سرور[OCR?]", with the words "گنج ٭ شکر ٭ گنج شکر" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 234–235). The Persian chronogram that follows Lahori's notice of the tomb ends both its couplets with "فردے یگانہ فرید" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 89, folio 77 [marker 87]). The saying on Jamal al-Din's torn certificate comes down in three forms: "پارہ کردہ جمال را فرید نتواند دوخت" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 91, folio 79 [marker 89]), "پارہ کردہ جمال را فرید نتواں دوخت" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 79, folio 75) and "پارہ کردۂ جمال را نتوانیم دوخت" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 84, folio 80).

Poets have made him a measure. Schimmel notes that in Panjabi there are *bārahmāsa* about Fariduddin Ganj Shakar of Pakpattan (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 287, folio 269), and that a biographer of Mir Dard wrote that the mountain of Dard's patience would have made Sheikh Farid Ganj-i Shakar "bite his fingers from amazement like sugarcane" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 411, folio 380). The Mughal grandee Bayram Khan "is said to have composed" a four-line poem on Farid's name (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 168, folio 156).

## Other Places Linked to Baba Farid

Several places beyond the Pakpattan shrine are linked to him in the books; none of them is this shrine.

Khalid places his birthplace at Tibba Haji Deen, the old Kothewal, and found there that the birthplace house "is preserved", its courtyard holding graves of the saint's ancestors "back seven generations", that "Baba Farid's parents are also buried here", and that the family of the caretaker Ghulam Shabbir "has been serving this shrine for the past seven generations"; nearby is "another shrine dedicated to the childhood of Baba Farid", a well within a house under an iron cage, on whose railing devotees tie thread (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 150, folio 132). "Because of his presence, this well and its water became sacred" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 150, folio 132). "The shrine at Tiba Haji Deen was older than the shrine of Baba Farid at Pakpattan, but it was less important. The importance, in this case, was determined by the number of followers each shrine had" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 145, folio 127). In *In Search of Shiva* pilgrims walk "barefoot on the dusty roads of the village, out of respect for the holy village"; "The well was covered by an iron cage, on which devotees had tied saffron-coloured threads", and a shrine official said, "Drinking water from this well will cure all your problems!" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated). In the birth-house "In an open courtyard were seven graves", which an old caretaker said were those of "Baba Farid's father, grandfather, uncles, and siblings" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated).

Chistian, Khalid writes, is "a small city which was established by Baba Farid's son and named after his school of thought, according to legend" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 154, folio not stated); a local book, the *Tajul Auliya*, says it was founded by his grandson, and that in a jungle outside an old fort "there was a spot where Baba Farid had spent some time in meditation. Later when the saint settled at Pakpattan, he asked his grandson, Tajuddin Chisti to populate the place of his meditation" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 16, ch. 10, folio not stated). Tibba Nanaksar, with its gurdwara, lies "about five kilometres from the shrine of Baba Farid", and a descendant of the saint, "Baba Fateh Ullah Shah Noori Chisti", has a shrine there (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 155, folio 137); Iqbal Qaiser told Khalid that pressure "even by the Diwan of the shrine of Baba Farid" led the government to renovate its gurdwara (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 156, folio 138).

In Lahore the *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* tells that he came for ascetic practice and sat on the mound now called Farid Astana, refusing to sit where his pir had sat — "پاؤں کی طرف چلہ کاٹوں" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 228). Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore names "خواجہ فرید پاک پٹنی" among the elders who came to the mazar of Data Ganj Bakhsh and "چلے کاٹے", kept *chillas* there (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 289, folio 292); its table of contents lists a "چلہ بابا فرید گنج شکر[OCR?]" in Lahore, the name and page uncertain in the printed text (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 5, folio 4), and it uses a "تکیہ[OCR?] بابا فرید گنج شکر" in Lahore as a landmark (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 443, folio 450). Lahori places outside Delhi Gate the mazar of Shah Kaku Chishti, of his progeny (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 99–100, folios 87–88 [markers 97–98]).

Further afield, Ernst and Lawrence record that "one chillah of Baba Farid abuts the shrine of Khwaja Mu'in ad-Din in Ajmer, while another associated with Farid is found outside the tomb of Qutb ad-Din in Delhi" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 109, folio 96), and a staff "which is called the staff" of Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar held at Khuldabad (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 218, folio 207). Rizvi writes that Gisu Daraz ordered a disciple "to perform forty days continuous meditation and penance in the Delhi cell of Baba Farid. The cell was later incorporated into the tomb of Shaikh Qutbu'd-Din" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 276, folio 256). Qureshi describes the Chilla of Baba Farid in Delhi as a working qawwali venue — "The Chilla Mahfil is perhaps the most exclusive or intimate Qawwali event at Nizamuddin Auliya" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 164, folio 144) — and as her example of "any other locality having an associational link with a saint (such as the Chilla of Baba Farid near the Nizamuddin Auliya shrine)" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 132, folio 112). Dhillon writes that the city of Faridkot, then known as Mokhalpur, was named after him by its ruler Raja Mokhal, and that the "Baba Sheikh Farid Agman Purb Mela" is held "each year for three days, from 21 to 23 September, commemorating his arrival in" the city (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 172, folio 188). At Uch, Khalid saw him on a banner at Jalaludin's shrine "in a simple white dress with a green shawl on his shoulders" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 282, folio 256).

Near Kallar Kahar in the Salt Range there is a spring and a cave shrine of a "Baba Farid", which Lukas Werth describes without saying whether this is the saint of Pakpattan. "A locally well-known spring near Kallar Kahar is also associated with a shrine: the spring of Baba Farid" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 95, folio 84). The local tradition tells that he asked girls carrying water for a drink; "they teased him and said: ‘The water is bitter.' Three times he repeated his request, with the same answer, at which point he turned the lake's sweet waters bitter (its waters are salty)"; "Then he disappeared into the mountain above, to a lonely place whence nowadays his spring emerges, flowing with sweet water containing healing powers" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, pp. 95–96, folios 84–85). "He is said to have vanished into a cave near the top of the mountain, above the spring, where there is also a small shrine, accessible only after some half-hour's climb" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 96, folio 85).

## Setting

Pakpattan was a river town long before the saint. Eaton places the shrine "on the right bank of the Punjab's most southeasterly river, the Sutlej, roughly halfway between Ferozepore and Bahawalpur" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 216–217): "The town in which the shrine is located, known since the sixteenth century as Pakpattan, is the ancient city of Ajudhan", and "As the principal ferry point on the Sutlej river, this town served from ancient times as a major nexus for east-west trade between the Delhi region and Multan" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 217). Bhandari's Persian places it in "سرکار دیپالپور" and calls it "پتن عرف اجودهن" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527). Ernst and Lawrence write that "One had to go to the desert to reach the tomb of Farid ad-Din at Pakpattan/Ajodhan, or that of Hamid ad-Din at Nagaur in Rajasthan" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 99, folio 86), and that the itinerary of Ajmer, Delhi and Pakpattan was "followed in 1352 by Shaykh Zayn ad-Din Shirazi, the main successor to Burhan ad-Din Gharib in Khuldabad" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 98, folio not stated). Khalid writes of the Pakpattan that had once been Ajodhan as "a small insignificant city", next to which "on top of an abandoned mound Baba Farid used to teach his students", while the Sutlej "snaked through" it (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 141, folio 123); in his own day the town lay "a journey of about four hours" by road from Lahore (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated), and Rozehnal puts it "120 miles southwest of Lahore" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 35, folio 25). Khalid also writes of "another shrine of phallic offerings also referred to as Aban Shah near Pakpattan" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of his birth.** The site's account gives c. 1173. Lahori's text gives 583 AH; its editor rejects 582 AH, notes 569 AH from *Sair al-Auliya*, and chooses 571 AH from *Fawaid al-Fawad* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]). Sharib gives 575 AH, and 569 AH as what some have written (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52). Rizvi gives "569/1173-74 or 571/1175-76" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139). Rafat gives 1175 twice (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 25, folio not stated; Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 29, folio not stated) and 1173 twice (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 30, folio 10; Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222). Khalid gives 1173 CE (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 150, folio 132), and Dhillon 1173 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187).
- **The year of his death.** The site's account gives 1266, as do Qureshi (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 101, folio 81), Omar Kasmani (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 17) and Dhillon (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187). Lahori gives 5 Muharram 664 AH, and his editor affirms it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 89, folio 77 [marker 87]). Rizvi gives "5 Muharram 664/17 October 1265" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140). The *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* gives "سنہ ۶۶۳[OCR?] ہجری" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 234). Bhandari gives Saturday 5 Muharram 667 AH, at Patan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526). Sharib gives 5 Muharram 670 AH, and 664 AH as what some have written (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58). Ernst and Lawrence print "d. 664/1265" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 159, folio 147), 1265 elsewhere (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 17, folio 2), and "5 Muharram 634 A.H." (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 169, folio 157). Eaton (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 218), Kugle (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239), Schimmel (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 8, folio 4; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346; Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 353, folio 335) and Rafat (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222) give 1265. Rozehnal gives 1265 in his text (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 29, folio not stated) and 1295 in his index (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 276, folio 270).
- **His age at death.** Ernst and Lawrence give 95 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 169, folio 157); Eaton ninety (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241); Lahori's editor cites *Fawaid al-Fawad* for 93 years (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]).
- **His century.** Qureshi calls him a "major thirteenth-century saint of the Chishti order in India" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 263, folio 243), and Rozehnal "his renowned thirteenth-century predecessor" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 175, folio 167); Rafat calls him "The 12th century poet" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 47, folio 27), and Khalid calls him a mystic "from the twelfth century" in one book (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated) and "a Muslim Saint from the twelfth century" in another (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 188, folio not stated), while also writing that he settled at Ajodhan "in the thirteenth century" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).
- **The name of his birthplace.** The site's account gives Kothewal. Lahori's book prints کھوتوال (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]), کتہوال [OCR?] (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 86–87, folios 74–75), and کہتوال corrected to کوٹھے وال (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 345, folio 333). Sharib and Rizvi have Kahtwal (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52; Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139); Bhandari کهوتوال (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526); Khalid Tibba Haji Deen, formerly Kothewal (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 150, folio 132).
- **Who came from Kabul, and who was Qazi Shuaib.** The site's account says his grandfather came from Kabul. Lahori's author has his father, Jamal al-Din Sulaiman, come from Kabul to Lahore, his grandfather having been martyred (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]); Lahori's editor has Qazi Shuaib come to Hindustan in 552 AH / 1157 CE (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 87, folio 75 [marker 85]). Sharib makes Qazi Shuaib his grandfather and the qazi of Kahtwal (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52); Lahori's editor makes Jamal al-Din Sulaiman, after Qazi Shuaib's death, the qazi there (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 86–87, folios 74–75); Rizvi makes Qazi Shu'aib his father and the qazi of Kahtwal (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139).
- **His father's name.** Lahori and Sharib give Jamal al-Din Sulaiman (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 86–87, folios 74–75 [markers 84–85]; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52); Bhandari prints "جلال الدین سلیمان" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527); Rizvi names the father Qazi Shu'aib (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139).
- **His mother's name, and who Bibi Sharifa was.** Lahori and Sharib name his mother Qursum Khatun (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 250, folio 238; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52), and Lahori's editor says her father is named by no contemporary writer (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 87, folio 75). In Thanvi's account as Ernst and Lawrence give it, his mother is Bibi Sharifa, of whom "Her son, Baba Farid" said that she would have been worthy of *khilafat* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 135, folio 122). Rizvi leaves his mother unnamed and makes Bibi Sharifa his daughter, of whom "Her father" said the same (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150); Sharib also lists a daughter بی بی شریفہ (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 61–62, folios 57–58).
- **His age, and the place, of his initiation.** Sharib has him come to Multan at fifteen (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 58, folio 54) and take *bai'at* in 590 AH, aged fifteen (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 59, folio 55); Rizvi has him settle in Multan at eighteen, reports Jamali's account of initiation at Multan, and thinks it "more likely" that he was initiated at Delhi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139). Bhandari has him meet the Khwaja at Multan and become his disciple at Delhi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526).
- **Whether he followed his master to Delhi at once.** The site's account says that after meeting Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki at Multan he followed him to Delhi. Sharib says the Khwaja refused him leave to follow and ordered him to go on with his studies, that he went to Qandahar for five years, and that he came to Delhi in 595 AH (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 58–59, folios 54–55; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 58, folio 54; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 59, folio 55). Rizvi reports Jamali's account of a visit to Qandahar and thinks it "more likely" that he reached Delhi shortly after the Khwaja (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139); Bhandari has him go with the Khwaja to Delhi, and reports that some say he first studied at Qandahar and Sistan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526).
- **Who succeeded Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki.** The site's account says that on his master's death Farid became the head of the order, and Schimmel calls him Bakhtiyar Kaki's successor (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346); Rizvi says the relics implied he was the Khwaja's successor in Delhi, yet "His successor in Delhi was Shaikh Badru'd-Din, who came from Ghazna" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 156, folio 138; Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140).
- **Where he performed the inverted *chilla*.** Rizvi places it in a lonely mosque at Uch (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140), and Ernst and Lawrence's translation in the well of the Hajj mosque of Ucch (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 168, folio 156). Khalid reports the tradition that "he hung himself inside a well not far from the shrine" at Tibba Haji Deen, and a shrine official's denial: "Baba Farid did not hang inside the well, as it is believed" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated). Schimmel says that he performed it (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346); Ernst and Lawrence, through Thanvi, that he "was reputed to have practiced" it (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 135, folio 122). The timing differs too: Rizvi has him suspended "for forty days and nights" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140); Ernst and Lawrence's translation has him suspended "every night" and pulled out at daybreak (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 168, folio 156); Kugle describes the practice as "remaining in an inverted state of contemplation from daybreak to sunset" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239).
- **How he came by the name Ganjshakar.** The site's account: a pebble or a morsel turned to sugar in his mouth during his fasts. Sharib gives two reasons, mud turned to sugar and a merchant's sugar turned to salt and back, and chooses neither (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 57, folio 53). Rizvi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140) and Schimmel (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, pp. 377–378, folios 346–347) give the pebbles; Ernst and Lawrence the pebbles and the merchant (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 168, folio 156); Bhandari earth turned to sugar under his gaze (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526); Khalid a myth that he was "extremely soft-spoken" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).
- **The renaming of Ajodhan and its meaning.** The site's account gives Pakpattan as "the Holy Ferry"; Eaton "('the holy ferry')", the name dating "by the sixteenth century" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 228); Schimmel "the ferry of the pure", the name in use "ever since" his time (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346); Khalid has the name changed after Baba Farid settled there (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 141, folio 123).
- **Where Pakpattan lies.** The site's account puts it on the old bank of the Sutlej in southern Punjab, and Eaton halfway between Ferozepore and Bahawalpur (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 216–217); Dhillon calls Pak Pattan "a town near Sirhind" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187).
- **How long he lived at Ajodhan.** Eaton, citing *Siyar al-auliya'*, says "only sixteen or twenty-four years" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 228, n. 43); Rizvi has him there "from about 1236 until his death" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140).
- **Who offered him villages.** Rizvi says Ulugh Khan offered a *farman* of four villages (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 162, folio 144); Sharib that Sultan Nasir al-Din, having visited him, sent a *farman* for villages whose number is uncertain in the printed text (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 61, folio 57). Rizvi also says that Ulugh Khan prevented Sultan Nasiru'd-Din from seeing him in 650/1252-53 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 162, folio 144).
- **The marriage to Balban's daughter.** Sharib states that Balban married his daughter to him, and names her first of four wives (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 61, folio 57); Rizvi calls the story "hardly historical as the Shaikh died before Ulugh Khan became Sultan Balban" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 162, folio 144).
- **His wives and children.** Sharib names four wives (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 61–62, folios 57–58); Rizvi says "two or three wives" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 167, folio 149). Rizvi and Sharib give five sons and three daughters, Sharib adding a further son, شیخ عبد اللہ; Schimmel says eight children survived (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 378, folio 347).
- **The tokens that passed to Nizamuddin.** Kugle: sent "Upon his death in 1265" to Delhi (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). Rizvi: handed over in his lifetime, "for at the time of my death you will not be present" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 175, folio 157). Sharib: the robe given at Ajodhan after his death by his son-in-law, under his will (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58).
- **The number of his khalifas.** Seven according to Amir Khwurd, as Rizvi reports (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150), and to Schimmel (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 379, folio 348); more than fifty thousand according to what "some have written", as Sharib reports (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58).
- **Sabir.** Lahori says Farid made him *qutb* of Delhi and later gave him a *farman* for Kaliyar (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 90, folio 78 [marker 88]; Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 91, folio 79 [marker 89]), and Sharib that he gave him the *wilayat* of Kaliyar, and makes Baba Farid his maternal uncle (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 79–80, folios 75–76; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 78, folio 74). Kugle says Farid was wary of granting him leadership and sent him to the wilderness, and calls him a nephew (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239; Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 259, folio 238). Rizvi calls the torn certificate and the nephew stories legendary (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 172, folio 154), and Ernst and Lawrence report Shaykh 'Abd al-Haqq's doubt that Sabir is the disciple named in *Siyar al-awliya'* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 74, folio 60).
- **His writings.** Sharib calls *Fawaid al-Salikin* his famous book and lists three *risalas* said to be his (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 63, folio 59). Lahori's editor (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 89, folio 77 [marker 87]) and Rizvi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 18, folio 4) call *Fawaid al-Salikin*, *Asrar al-Auliya* and *Rahat al-Qulub* spurious; Ernst and Lawrence give Nizam ad-Din's testimony that he wrote no book and list two works only attributed to him (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 178, folio 166; Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 241, folio 231).
- **Whether he composed in Punjabi.** The site's account calls him one of the earliest and greatest poets of Punjabi, and Khalid "the first poet of the Punjabi language" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 153, folio 135). Schimmel writes that "It is possible that Fariduddin composed a few lines of poetry in the local dialect" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 379, folio 348). Rizvi credits him with poetry in Arabic, Persian and Hindawi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146).
- **The *shlokas* in the Guru Granth Sahib.** The site's account calls them his, and Rafat calls him "the most important poet of the Granth" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222). Rizvi concludes that they "were not composed by one individual" but by "a number of different descendants, all using Farid as their nom de plume" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 351, folio 329). Rafat (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222), Khalid (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated) and Rizvi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328) have Guru Arjan compile them into the Granth, Rizvi in 1604; Dhillon has Guru Nanak "personally" include "134 hymns composed by Baba Farid in the Adi Granth" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187). Rizvi counts "more than a hundred" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328).
- **The building and the ground.** Nur Ahmad Chishti describes the tomb as lower than the ground of the town (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 233); Khalid as "located on the top of a mound that overlooks the entire city" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated) and as the highest point of the area (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 154, folio not stated).
- **Which building is the great one.** Eaton calls the grandson 'Ala' ad-Din's tomb "the most imposing structure in the entire shrine complex, dwarfing by far Baba Farid's own tomb" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 221), and elsewhere calls the shrine itself "a magnificent marble edifice constructed in the fourteenth century" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 239). Khalid calls the saint's shrine "a modest building" and the burial place of his progeny behind it "a splendid structure" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).
- **Whether every power honoured the shrine.** The site's account says the shrine has been honoured by every power to rule the Punjab. Eaton writes that the Khalji sultans "do not seem to have been interested in the shrine" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 220), and that in 1810 its holdings "were seized by Ranjit Singh" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 231); of the saint himself Eaton writes that he "assiduously avoided contact with the mundane world of the court and its ministers" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 219).
- **The name of the Gate.** The site's account calls it the *Bahishti Darwaza*, a silver-plated door. Eaton calls it "the southern door (shisha darwaza)" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 219, n. 11), the "Gate of Paradise" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 236) and the "Bahishti Gate" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 254); Rozehnal "the narrow Gate of Heaven (bihishti darwaza)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 36, folio 26). The *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* gives the door a name of its own, "اب سرور سی[OCR?] یہ دروازہ کہلاتا ہی", the reading uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 234).
- **Where the Chilla of Baba Farid in Delhi stands.** Qureshi places it "near the Nizamuddin Auliya shrine" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 132, folio 112) and, in her glossary, attached to Humayun's tomb (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 262, folio 242).
- **Ibn Battuta's visit.** Eaton dates it to 1334 (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 221–222); Ernst and Lawrence to "around the year 1340" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 105, folio 92).
- **Who comes to the shrine now.** Khalid writes that "Every year, hundreds of Sikhs and Hindus travel to Pakpattan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 153, folio 135), and also that Sikhs have petitioned for visas to attend the *'urs* "but in vain" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated); Rozehnal that "the shrine is now marked as exclusively Muslim space" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, pp. 35–36, folios 25–26).
- **Women at the qawwali.** Abbas calls qawwali at the Chishtiyya shrines, this one among them, "an exclusively male domain" where "women's presence at such performances is rare" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 84, folio not stated); Khalid, at the qawwali in the courtyard, writes "Here women and men sat together" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).
- **The court case of the 1930s.** Eaton's introduction calls it "a 1938 court dispute" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 16); his essay runs it from 6 April 1935 to 2 December 1938 (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 238), with the appeal record dated 1939 (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 239, n. 3). The colonial assessment report he quotes is "An 1897 British Assessment Report" in his text and dated 1896 in his note (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 230, n. 52).
- **The dead of 2001.** Rozehnal gives "more than one hundred" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 29, folio not stated); the newspapers, as Tahir Jehangir reports them, "over forty" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 37, folio 27). The state blamed the Diwan's four-hour delay over the Awqaf annuity (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 39, folio 29); the Diwan's family blamed crowd control, the tragedy coming "some two hours after the Diwan's arrival" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 39, folio 29).
- **Conversion.** Eaton reports that "the vast majority" of the Jat and Rajput groups that became Muslim in the medieval period "claim to have been converted either by Baba Farid or by his contemporary, Baha' al-Haqq Zakariya (d. 1263)" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 227), and Schimmel that "A number of Punjabi tribes still claim to have been converted by Fariduddin Ganj-i Shakar" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 381, folio 350). Eaton doubts the claim, among his grounds the shortness of the saint's stay (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 228); Rizvi rejects the view that he went to Ajodhan to convert "'backward Hindu tribes'" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 159, folio 141) and calls mass conversion "quite contrary to the Chishti mission" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 27, folio 13).

## Legacy

For the people of the Punjab, Baba Farid is not a remote historical figure but a living presence — "Farid" is a household name, his sayings are proverbs, and his verses are sung by qawwals and folk-singers alike. Through his disciple Nizamuddin Auliya and the generations that followed, the Chishti order he helped root in India became the most widespread of all the Sufi paths of the subcontinent; through his Punjabi poetry he became a father of the language’s literature and a shared inheritance of Muslims and Sikhs; and through his shrine at Pakpattan he gave the Punjab one of its enduring centres of pilgrimage. Compassion, poverty, and the sweetness that gave him his name remain the marks of his memory.

Eaton places the tomb among the first holy places of Muslim India: the tombs "of Mu'in ad-Din Chishti at Ajmer, Nizam ad-Din Auliya' at Delhi, and Baba Farid at Pakpattan—became the first Muslim holy places within India", which meant "that South Asian Muslims were no longer compelled to look exclusively to the Middle East for spiritual inspiration" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 236). Pakpattan is one of the three "enormous cults", beside Ajmer and Delhi, on which the order's wealth and power centred (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 265). For the devotees "The shrine was Baba Farid": "many murids referred to the saint and his shrine in the same terms, sometimes defining themselves as murids of Baba Farid, and sometimes referring to themselves as murids of the gaddi, or shrine" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241). "The shrine, on the other hand, has been there all along, sustaining the powerful baraka of the saint through its line of diwans" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 228). A landholder of Ferozepore District told the court, "As the Sajjada Nashin in office is a representative of Baba Farid, the same sanctity and reverence is shown to the Gaddi Nashin as is shown to Baba Farid" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 247, n. 32). In Eaton's words, "this saint has remained for many centuries an immensely popular 'invisible friend' among millions of villagers inhabiting the southwestern Punjab" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 238), and Rozehnal quotes Eaton's judgement that "The shrine of Baba Farid in Pakpattan provides a striking example of how Islam, the religion par excellence 'of the Book,' has been in one instance mediated among common villagers most of whom were illiterate" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 35, folio 25).

Many clans claim him as the one who made them Muslim. Witnesses before the court named "the Wattu, the Siyal, the Dogar, the Kathia, the Bhatti, and the Tiwana" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241, n. 9). A cultivator of Lyallpur said, "Our Tiwana tribe was converted by Baba Farid" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241, n. 10); another, "Baba Farid converted us Bhattis into Islam. Since that time we are the followers of the gaddi and respect the gaddinashin [i.e., sajjada-nishin, or Diwan] in office" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241, n. 11); and a Wattu villager, "Khewa, one of my ancestors, was converted into Islam by Baba Farid, and since that time we have been following the gaddi in dispute" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 248, n. 35). His cult went with Punjabis far from home: the Mughal officer Mirza Nathan in Bengal was a "faithful disciple" of Farid al-Din Shakarganj, "probably because the writer's ancestors had come from the Punjab where Baba Farid's cult was especially prominent" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 265, n. 10).

He belongs to more than one faith. "The same Shaykh Farid ad-Din is so highly respected by Sikhs that they have incorporated his Punjabi verses for their holy scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 18, folio 3). Abbas: "Although Baba Farid" was "a Muslim Sufi saint who wrote devotional poetry in Panjabi, his texts are revered among the Sikhs because he influenced the founder of their own religion" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 87, folio not stated); "Thus, he is a revered Sufi among the Sikhs as well as among his Muslim devotees" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 89, folio not stated). "Being part of the Granth, Baba Fareed is also given a special status in the Sikh religion and revered like the Gurus" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 188, folio not stated). Khalid writes that Nanak "like Farid, also chose Punjabi as his medium of expression" and was "impressed by the fact that Baba Farid lived a life of simplicity and shunned violence" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 153, folio 135), and that "There is a picture of Baba Farid accompanying the picture of Guru Nanak at the shrine of Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). Rizvi explains the Janamsakhis' meeting of Nanak and Farid by "the sufi and Nath belief that great saints did not die but remained accessible to important mystics in later ages through spiritual conversation" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 413, folio 389), and rejects the suggestion that Nanak met a namesake descendant as "far-fetched" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 413, folio 389). Khalid asks "why our heroes cannot be people like Baba Farid, Waris Shah and Bulleh Shah, who spread the message of peace and brought several religious communities together instead of shedding blood" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 14, ch. 8, folio not stated).

His line reaches far. Shaykh Salim Chishti of Fatehpur Sikri belongs to "the Faridi line" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 111, folio 98), and Hazrat Inayat Khan was "from the lineage of Farid ad-Din and Nizam ad-Din" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 18, folio 3). Kugle finds him the only South Asian saint in the ascension oath that Khidr teaches Muhammad Ghawth, sworn "by the Intimacy of Farid al-Din [Ganj-i Shakar] Ajhodani" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 159, folio 138). For the Chishti Sabiri order of today, "the contemporary silsila places the tomb of Shaykh Baba Farid ad-Din Mas'ud Ganj-i Shakkar in Pakpattan at the center of Sufi sacred geography in Pakistan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 206, folio 198); one of its shaykhs, Shahidullah Faridi, took the name Faridi "to mark his special relationship with the saint in Pakpattan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 77, folio 67), and its murids contemplate him daily (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 206, folio 198). "Sufi shrines such as Pakpattan serve as vital centers of popular piety—nodal points of local identity and culture." (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 47, folio 37). Ernst and Lawrence's headnote calls him "an extraordinary ascetic, noted for his controlled ecstasy; yet unlike Qutb ad-Din, he was also a loyal father and husband", whose life yields "the three characteristics of pious Chishtis: eschewing all stable income, engaging in meditation, often abetted by music, and training worthy disciples" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 167, folio 155). Schimmel quotes the judgement that "no saint excelled him in his devotions and penances." (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 378, folio 347).

He has drawn a long literature. Lahori's editor lists seventeen sources on him, among them *Fawaid al-Fawad*, Amir Khurd's *Sair al-Auliya*, *Akhbar al-Akhyar*, K. A. Nizami's *Life and Times of Sh. Farid-u-Din* (Aligarh, 1955) and Muslim Nizami's *Anwar al-Faridiya*, printed at Pak Pattan in 1965 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 89–90, folios 77–78 [markers 87–88]). Ernst and Lawrence give him twelve entries in their European-language bibliography, the earliest an account by Munshi Mohana Lala in the *Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal* of 1836 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 223, folio 212), and list Miles Irving's article on the shrine in the *Journal of the Panjab Historical Society* of 1911–12 beside Eaton's essay on its authority (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 227, folio 216). Khaliq Ahmad Nizami's biography of the saint is listed by Schimmel (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 293, folio 293), by Rizvi in its Aligarh edition of 1955 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 454, folio 430) and by Rozehnal in its Delhi edition of 1973 (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 241, folio 234). Shackle lists Gurbachan Singh Talib's *Baba Sheikh Farid Shakar Ganj* (New Delhi: National Book Trust, 1974) (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 204, folio 179), and Rafat cites Muhammad Asaf Khan's study of the provenance of his poetry, published by the Pakistan Punjabi Adabi Board, Lahore, in 1978 (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222). For the Chishti Sabiri order the book about him is Wahid Bakhsh Sial Rabbani's *Maqam-i Ganj-i Shakkar* (Lahore: al-Faisal Publishers, 1994), in which Rabbani translated "the discourses of Farid al-Din Ganj-i Shakkar" into Urdu (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 111, folio 102; Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 250, folio 243).

Description:
## Overview

The shrine of *Hazrat Shah Daula Daryai* stands in the city of Gujrat, in the fertile plain between the Chenab and Jhelum rivers in the Punjab. It commemorates a Sufi saint of the Mughal period, remembered above all as a builder of bridges, wells and *sarais* (rest-houses) and as a benefactor of the poor, the traveller and the afflicted. His epithet *Daryai* — from *darya*, "river" — is traditionally explained by his works of construction across the region's torrential streams. For nearly four centuries the *darbar* has been a focus of popular devotion in central Punjab; it is also, more painfully, the site around which one of South Asia's most persistent and troubling folk traditions grew up — that of the so-called "Shah Daula's mice" (*chuhas*), children affected by microcephaly who were historically associated with the shrine. The account below treats the saint first, and then addresses that tradition factually and with the medical understanding it requires.

Three books speak of the saint and his tomb directly, each from a different century and a different vantage. Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* describes him, in its account of the suba of Lahore and the town of Gujrat, as once the slave of a man of Sialkot who became the town's great builder and benefactor, and records that near that city ("درنزدیکی ان شهر") his tomb is a place of visitation for people of every class, "بزرگوار زیارتگاه طبقات خلایق است" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 515–514). Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, a nineteenth-century register of the saints of the Punjab, gives him entry no. 124 under the name "شاہ دولا دریائی گجراتی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 18, folio 6), with a spiritual chain, a death date in a chronogram, and a picture of his household in his lifetime. And Jamal Malik's chapter in Pnina Werbner and Helene Basu's *Embodying Charisma* prefaces its reading of Ahmad Nadîm Qâsimî's Urdu story 'Bain' ('Dirge'), which is set at this shrine, with a historical sketch of the saint and his cult drawn from colonial and *malfûzât* sources; the volume also carries a photograph captioned "The shrine of Shâh Daulah" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 8, folio not stated).

The three books spell the name in their own ways. Bhandari writes شاه دولا; Lahori's entry writes "دولا", while the editor's source list and index in the same edition write "دولہ" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 317, folio 305); Malik writes "Shâh Daulah", and inside Qâsimî's story the saint is "Sân'în Daule Shâh" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 210, folio 199).

## The Life of the Saint

Reliable dates for Shah Daula are difficult to fix, and the sources differ; he is traditionally said to have lived roughly between 1581 and 1675, and to have settled in Gujrat in the early seventeenth century — some accounts placing this in the reign of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, others in that of Akbar. He is said to have travelled in his youth to the neighbourhood of Sialkot, where he became the disciple of a Suhrawardi *faqir* remembered as Shah Saidan Sarmast, serving at his master's *khanqah* with great devotion before being entrusted with its care. He later established his own *khanqah* at Gujrat, at the place formerly known as Garhi Shah Daula.

## Descent and Early Years

Malik gives the saint a birth name: "Shâh Daulah—whose birth name was Qâsim —lived in Mughal times and died at an advanced age around AH 1676 in Gujrat" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). His descent, Malik writes, is contested: "His ancestors were Afghans, but it is also claimed that he was a Sayyid (descendant of the Prophet)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). Of his youth he writes: "After a turbulent childhood he became supervisor of the treasury of a local official, and also worked as a mendicant and an ordinary labourer for some time" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

Bhandari's account, which he introduces with "گویند" (it is said), begins differently. At first, he writes, Shah Daula was the slave ("غلام") of a resident of Sialkot whose name is printed "کهابدهره[OCR?]", the reading uncertain in the printed text. He loved the faqirs and served "حضرت میان سیدنا(۱)" devotedly; the editor's footnote gives the variant "سیدنام[OCR?]" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515).

## The Master and the Turning

In Bhandari's telling, the change in Shah Daula came at his master's deathbed. When Mian Sayyidna was about to die, he cast "نظر فیض اثر" on Shah Daula; Shah Daula's state changed and "بانوار عرفان شبستان باطن روشن گشت". He then left Sialkot and settled in Gujrat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Bhandari adds: "از بس که روشن دل بود خزاین غیب نمودار مے گشت": because his heart was so illumined, treasures of the unseen became manifest to him (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515).

Malik's sketch gives a longer apprenticeship and a quarrel: "He then spent twelve years at the feet of a Suhrawardi Sufi, but it is recorded too that he was initiated into the Qadiri order" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). "Due to some disputes with the local people of Sialkot, he migrated from there and, after some years, moved to Gujrat", Malik continues, 'in obedience to divine instructions' (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

## The Spiritual Chain

Lahori sets the saint at the end of a long chain that runs back, through Rajan Qattal of Uch, to Baha al-Din Multani. Shah Daula, he writes, was the disciple and *khalifa* of Shaikh Sina Sarmast; he of Shah Monga; he of Shah Kabir; he of Shaikh Shahr Allah, a name whose reading is uncertain in the printed text; he of Shaikh Yusuf; he of Pir Burhan; he of Shaikh Sadr al-Din; he of Shaikh Badr al-Din; he of Shaikh Ismail Qureshi; he of Shaikh Sadr al-Din Rajan Qattal Uchi; he of Shaikh Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath Multani; he of Shaikh Sadr al-Din Arif; and he of Shaikh Baha al-Din Multani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184). He adds that the saint also received grace from the Chishti line: "خاندان چشت اہل بہشت سے بھی ان کو فیض کامل حاصل ہوا", complete *faiz* from the Chishti family too (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184).

Lahori counts him "پنجاب کے مشہور بزرگوں میں سے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186), a man of lofty stations and marvels, of *jazb*, *ishq*, *zuhd* and *riyazat*, and "جامع فتوحات ظاہری و باطنی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184).

## The Saint's Household

Lahori pictures the saint's establishment in his lifetime as a royal one: "ان کی سرکار بادشاہوں کی سرکار کے مانند تھی۔ ہزاروں نوکر چاکر گھوڑا پالکی دروازہ پر حاضر رہتے تھے" — a court like the court of kings, with thousands of servants, horses and palanquins waiting at his door (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184). And "اہل حاجت کا ہجوم ہر وقت رہتا تھا": the crowd of those in need was there at every hour (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184).

Bhandari describes the same throng and the saint's open hand. In his lifetime "عالم عالم خلایق" came from every quarter for *ziyarat* and offered "از نقد و جنس فراوان نذورات"; he gave visitors and petitioners more than they had brought, a generosity such that "سخاوت تمام عمر حاتم عشر عشیر ان نشود" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik, from his sources, records the breadth of the saint's following and a refusal: he was popular among "Muslims as well as Hindus, became famous for his miracles and received large gifts" in kind, "but refused to accept land grants" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

## The Death of the Saint

The books give the year of his death in several ways. Lahori writes: "وفات حضرت کی سال ایک ہزار پچھتر میں واقع ہوئی اور مادہ تاریخ لفظ خدا دوست ہے" — he died in the year 1075 AH, and the chronogram of his death is the phrase "خدا دوست" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). The edition's modern editor, in a footnote on the same entry, gives instead "۱۰۸۷ھ [OCR?] / ۱۶۷۶ع [OCR?] میں انتقال کیا", with both figures uncertain in the printed text, citing Mushtaq Ram Gujrati's *Karamat Nama*, owned by Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184, folio 182). Bhandari dates the death by the reign of Alamgir: "بالآخر درسنه هفدهم[OCR?] عالمگیری بعالم بقا رحلت فرمود", in the seventeenth regnal year of Alamgir, the ordinal uncertain in the printed text (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik's sketch says he "died at an advanced age around AH 1676 in Gujrat" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). The site's own account gives 1675.

## The Builder of Bridges

What is most consistently remembered of him is not doctrine but works of public benefit. He is credited with constructing bridges over seasonal watercourses — including, by tradition, a bridge over the Nala Dek — together with wells, mosques and rest-houses along the routes of travel, at a time when such infrastructure eased both trade and pilgrimage across the Punjab. He is also remembered for his *langar*, his charity to the destitute, and his care for animals and for people living with disabilities. In this he embodies a distinctively practical, service-oriented sanctity: a saint honoured less for miracles than for the tangible relief of hardship.

Bhandari makes this the heart of his account. Shah Daula settled in the *qasba* of Gujrat ("دران قصبه استقامت اختیار کرده"), built tanks, wells and mosques ("تالاب ها و چاهها و مساجد احداث نموده"), and bridged ("قنطره بست") the Chenab, which came down from the hills and used to damage the town (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). He raised buildings and bridges in many places, above all a bridge on the highway ("درشاهراه") over the river Deg, five *kos* from Eminabad in the direction of Lahore ("پنجگروهی امن اباد جانب لاهور"), a work so solid "که از احدی صاحب دولتان چنین عمارت متین نشود" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). The bridge became a landmark: in his description of the Deg's course, Bhandari has the river pass "پایان پل شاه دولا که برشاهراه واقع است" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516).

Bhandari credits the saint with the making of the town itself. Gujrat, he writes, "از ابتدا این قصبه چندان رونق نداشت" until Shah Daula settled there (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515), and his settling "موجب ازدیاد ابادی و افزونی رونق گشت" — made the town grow in people and prosperity (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515).

Malik reads the saint's two titles through the same works. During his life, he writes, the saint devoted himself to "works of public utility" and to the construction of religious buildings, and this is why he was called *Daulah*, which Malik glosses 'wealth'; his building of bridges, especially, earned him the second title, glossed 'one affiliated to water' (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). At that point in the text the printed form of the second title is uncertain; elsewhere in the chapter it is *Daryâ'î*.

## The Shrine

His tomb, surmounted by a dome and set beside a spacious mosque, dates in its essentials from the seventeenth century, though the structure was substantially rebuilt in the late nineteenth century (traditionally 1898) and has been repaired and extended since. Since the mid-twentieth century the shrine has been administered by the Punjab Auqaf (Religious Affairs) Department, which now organises the annual three-day *urs* with arrangements for *langar*, sanitation and security, and with gatherings devoted to the saint's life and teaching.

Lahori, writing in the 1870s, calls the tomb a living place of pilgrimage: "مزار گوہر بار شہر پنجاب گجرات میں زیارت گاہ خلق ہے" — his mazar in the city of Gujrat, Punjab, is a place of pilgrimage for the people (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). Bhandari had placed it "درنزدیکی ان شهر", near the town, as a place of visitation for people of every class (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 515–514).

Malik gives the reconstruction one date: the shrine "had been reconstructed (1898)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). It is the only date for the building in his chapter, which names no founder, no *sajjada nashin* and no custodian family.

## Endowment and Administration

The shrine, Malik writes, held no land: "the lack of regular income at the dargâh, since no land was attached to it, resulted in the holy men's total dependence on the alms and offering of the followers", and colonial authors also suspected the followers of trafficking in women, a suspicion Malik reports from Ibbetson and Maclagan (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). He quotes the editor of the *Indian Antiquary* on "the absence of landed property in possession of the band, or any recognized right to succession to the leadership, and the entire dependence on the earnings" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).

Of the modern administration he writes of "this Sufi tomb, which was taken over by the Pakistan Auqaf Department in the 1960s" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 204, folio 193). The takeover, in his reading, did not displace the older authority on the spot: "even the nationalisation policy of the Auqaf Department since the 1960s could not totally change the perceptions deeply rooted in the minds of the rural population and the authority exercised by the shrine administrator, the mujâwir, who ideally represents state power" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).

## Fertility, Justice and Punishment

Malik sums up the shrine's reputation in a phrase: "The sanctuary of Shâh Daulah thus has a particular reputation—fertility, justice and punishment" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). He observes too that "the dargâh is a female domain, at least in quantitative terms—in contrast to mosques, which are frequented by men" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 208, folio 197), while adding elsewhere that "the power in shrines is usually held by men" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 214, folio 203).

## Devotion and Practice

The site's account describes an annual three-day *urs* under Auqaf administration, with *langar*. The books consulted give no date, month or duration for the *urs*.

Malik, writing of the shrine's older practice, describes the vow of a child. "The custom used to be to leave the child, as soon as it was weaned, at Shah Daulah's khanqah [Sufi lodge], as an offering to him"; after the saint's death, devotees "would make a vow either to present the child when born or make an offering to the shrine" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). He analyses the exchange at the tomb as "a kind of a bargain between the parents and the mujâwir, like the mahr (bridewealth): the parents are declared dwellers of paradise (jannatî—without intercession of any authority) by the shrine administrator. In response they leave the child—the present (ni‘mat) —as a trust (amânat) at the dargâh" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 211, folio 200).

## The "Chuhas" of Shah Daula: Folklore and the Medical Reality

No account of this shrine can avoid the tradition of the *chuhas* — a word meaning "mice" or "rats" in Punjabi — the name long given to microcephalic children associated with the *darbar*. This tradition must be approached with care, both because it concerns vulnerable and disabled human beings and because it has frequently been sensationalised. The essential facts, as documented by observers and scholars since the nineteenth century, are these.

Microcephaly is a medical condition in which the head and brain are abnormally small, typically accompanied by intellectual disability; it has recognised genetic and environmental causes and occurs in populations everywhere. At Gujrat, individuals with this condition came to be linked with Shah Daula's shrine through a folk belief — first recorded in print in January 1839 by the observer Shahamat Ali — that childless women who prayed for offspring at the *darbar* would be granted a child, the first of whom must, according to the legend, be dedicated to the shrine and would be born with the characteristic small head. Such dedicated children were called *chuhas* and were often maintained at, or associated with, the shrine.

From the mid-nineteenth century onward the phenomenon attracted European medical and ethnographic attention, and with it arose the sensational speculation that the small heads were produced deliberately, by binding or by fitting clamps or vessels to the skulls of infants. This claim has never been substantiated: no such instrument has ever been found, no such procedure has ever been witnessed, and medical authorities regard the intentional production of microcephaly in this manner as implausible without causing fatal injury. The modern consensus is that the *chuhas* were, and are, individuals with naturally occurring microcephaly whose condition was interpreted through the lens of local religious belief and who were, in effect, drawn into the economy of the shrine — historically, in some periods, being sent out as itinerant beggars. It should be stressed that the folk belief linking the condition to the saint's blessing or curse has no basis in fact and is not endorsed here; it is recorded only as a documented social phenomenon.

Malik's chapter, drawing on colonial sources, records the same tradition in the words of its time. The shrine, he writes, "is particularly known for its Chûhâs or Rat-children, who are without understanding or the power of speech. After some initial training they are passed on to a faqîr (religious mendicant) and made to beg in the name of Shâh Daulah" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). A further passage describes a band or order of faqirs living off these children and "the convenient existence of an important shrine" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). Malik reports, without endorsing it, the colonial suspicion that the children were "artificially produced after their birth as ordinary infants", citing Ibbetson and Maclagan (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). He also reports a physiological explanation from Sharif Kunjahi's modern life of the saint: "the bad conscience of parents, particularly mothers, set free certain chemical reactions that caused this peculiarity" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).

Malik argues that the cult is late. Because it is absent from "contemporary and even later malfûzât and biographical accounts" of the saint, he concludes: "It therefore seems likely that this cult arose only later, by the end of the nineteenth century—after the shrine had been reconstructed (1898)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).

Reform came in the twentieth century. When the Auqaf Department assumed control of the shrine in the mid-twentieth century, it acted to forbid both the abandonment of such children to the *darbar* and the alleged deforming practices, and the population of *chuhas* associated with the site steadily declined. By the early twenty-first century observers reported that only one or two remained. The episode endures chiefly as a cautionary study for historians of medicine, disability and popular religion, in which a genuine medical condition, human vulnerability, exploitation and folk piety became tragically entangled.

## Legends and Miracles

The legend behind the *chuhas*, as Malik quotes it from colonial sources, runs: "Shah Daulah, like other saints, could procure the birth of a child for a couple desiring one, but the first child born in response to his intercession would be a Chuha—brainless, small-headed, long-eared and rat-faced" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). "After the saint's death the miracle continued, but in a modified way": where a promised gift was withheld, "the spirit of the offended saint so worked on the parents that the next child was born a Chuha, and all subsequent children as well, until the original vow was fulfilled" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). These are the words of the legend as the colonial sources recorded it, not a description of any person.

Malik attributes to the same colonial sources a second miracle: "through his charismatic or miraculous powers (karâmât) Shâh Daulah was able to control female infanticide, which was widespread in Jammu State at the time" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

Bhandari's single marvel is an inward one: because the saint's heart was so illumined, treasures of the unseen became manifest to him (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Lahori calls him a man of marvels and of *jazb*, ecstatic attraction (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184).

## The Shrine in Fiction: Qâsimî's 'Bain'

Ahmad Nadîm Qâsimî's Urdu story 'Bain' ('Dirge'), as Malik reads it, "deals with the activities in and around the dargâh (court, shrine) of Shâh Daulah Daryâ'î in Gujrat" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 204, folio 193), although the story does not mention the *chuha* cult, to "which Nadîm's story does not, however, refer directly" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 204, folio 193). What follows is the story's world, not a report of the shrine.

In the story the shrine "had become an institution of justice, symbolised by the holy hand of Shâh Daulah, which, in order to judge, would rise from the grave" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 207, folio 196). Malik gives the passage in full: "The upper part [sar bâne kî taraf se] of the holy grave opened and the Pîr stretched out his holy hand [dast-e mubârak]. The culprit then was drawn to the shrine [mazâr sharîf] from wherever he was, laid his neck into the holy hand of the Sân'înjî [the pîr] and died on the spot [dher honâ]" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 210, folio 199). "Therefore, nobody dared to neglect Sân'în Daule Shâh's orders" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 210, folio 199).

The *mujâwir* rules through a dream. He demands that the girl Rano recite at the *dargâh* for three days, which "Shâh Daulah had ordered in a dream" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 207, folio 196); otherwise, the villagers are warned, "Sân'în Daule Shâhjî would put all villagers to fire and ash" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 209, folio 198).

The *urs* frames the story's crisis: "the girl's maturity or sexualisation and the marriage proposal coincide with the anniversary of the holy man's death, ‘urs, the unification of the pîr with God" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 209, folio 198), and "During the ‘urs the girl falls victim to the corrupted society" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 211, folio 200). The shrine's kitchen and bath-house become the scene of defiance: Rano flings the skirt her parents bring "into the burning coals of the public kitchen (langar)", and her father later throws the *mujâwir*'s shroud "into the burning coals of the fire heating the water for the great ablution (ghusl)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 212, folio 201).

Malik's verdict on what the story shows is severe: "It shows that the shrine cult has become a falsehood void of any mysticism, or, in other words, an expression of corrupt political power" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 208, folio 197), and "fear is the prime motivational force inducing the villagers and adepts to be loyal to the moral authority emanating from the shrine" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 210, folio 199).

## In Verse

The books carry little verse on Shah Daula. What they hold is a chronogram. Lahori's entry closes the saint's life with a two-word *tarikh*, "خدا دوست", which he gives as encoding the year of death, 1075 AH; in his words, "مادہ تاریخ لفظ خدا دوست ہے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186).

The same book closes with a verse chronogram of its own, by Mufti Ghulam Safdar Lahori, which gives the year 1292 AH. It speaks of the scope of the whole book, the saints of the Punjab, and not of this saint:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

*A chronogram on the book's own subject, the saints of the Punjab; the book gives no English.* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 282, folio 270)

## The Saint in Writing

The books point to a small literature on the saint. The *Hadiqat al-Awliya*'s editor catalogues, as his source for the death date, item no. 64, "مشتاق رام گجراتی : کرامت نامہ ۱۱۳۲ھ (حالات شاہ دولہ دریائی گجراتی) مملوکہ سید شرافت نوشاہی", a *Karamat Nama* of 1132 AH on the life of Shah Daula, by Mushtaq Ram Gujrati, owned by Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 296, folio 284). The same list has item no. 235, "نسیم ایم ایس : تذکرہ شاہ دولہ گجراتی۔ لاہور ۱۹۷۰ء" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 304, folio 292).

Malik names his own sources as "historical and biographical accounts as well as on malfûzât literature (namely, the imputed speeches and utterances of holy men)", among them Ibbetson's *Glossary* and the work of Sharîf Kunjâhî (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). Kunjâhî's book, *Hadrat Shâh Daulah Daryâ'î Gujrâtî: Hayât o ta'lîmât*, was published in Lahore in 1985 by the Punjab Auqaf Department's imprint, Markaz Ma'ârif Awliyâ Mahkamah Awqâf Punjâb (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 217, folio 206). It is in this title alone that Malik's chapter calls the saint *Gujrâtî*.

## Setting: Gujrat

The books that describe the town of Gujrat speak of the place, not of the shrine.

Bhandari places it in the Chaj doab between the Chenab and the Bihat: "در دوابه چونهت گجرات قصبه ایست". It was settled ("اباد شده") under the emperor Akbar, and villages were taken out of the pargana of Sialkot to make it a pargana of its own (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Under the heading "در بیان مقرر گردیدن پرگنہ گجرات و امن آباد" he tells how the pargana was made: "این تمام سرزمین داخل سیالکوت بود و قوم جت ورائچ[OCR?] متسلط بودند" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 177). In the regnal year 37 or, by another account, 42, as the emperor was travelling from Lahore to Kashmir, a body of Gujars came to him after the Chenab crossing to complain of oppression by the Jats and the Raich, a name uncertain in the printed text (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 176–177). The villages of their *zamindari* were separated off as "پرگنہ موسوم بگجرات[OCR?]", and a small fort and a town were founded, "قلعچہ و قصبہ احداث نموده" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 176). Bhandari does not name Shah Daula in this passage.

The town in Bhandari's own day was a market of the province: "انقصبه پیشگاه هرگونه مردم و جامع اجناس هر دیار و اشیاے نادره روزگار است". Rare swords and *jamdhars* were made there, and "کار چکن زیاده از سیالکوت می شود"; the district bred Iraqi horses, some worth up to "ده هزار روپیه" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Bhandari also sets an imperial episode in the neighbourhood. When the prince Khusrau rebelled and was turned back at the Chenab, he was seen at the ford at dawn, and "میر ابوالقاسم خان و هلال خان خواجه سرا که در حدود گجرات بودند" seized him and carried him to Gujrat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 146–145). He says nothing there of the saint or the shrine.

Usborne's annotator to Waris Shah ties the town's name to a tribe: "The Gujars are a famous tribe of the old Punjab who keep animals and sell their milk. They also engage in agriculture on a large scale. A number of Punjab towns, such as Gujranwala, Gujrat and Gujar Khan are named after the Gujar tribe" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 19, folio 18, note 3). Haroon Khalid's informant Iqbal Qaiser dates the town's rise to Akbar: "Gujrat became an important city during the tenure of Akbar. Before that it was a small village. One of Akbar's wives is also buried here" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). Khalid's account of the Punjab after the Mughals also has the governor Meer Manu waiting 'near the city of Gujrat' (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 15, ch. 9).

Gujrat has other saints. Khalid writes of a crow saint who "seemed to have quite a following in this historic city", and of the city's major shrines put "on high alert" after a blast in Sindh (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). A poster reproduced in *Embodying Charisma* names a 'Sain Kanwan Wali (Gujrat)' (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 160, folio 149).

The Chenab country around the town is the land of Punjabi romance. Shemeem Burney Abbas begins the tale of Sohni with a potter "who lived in the Gujrat district of the Panjab" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 125, folio not stated), and places Ranjha's clan at Takht Hazara, "now Gujrat District of Pakistan" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 122, folio not stated). Usborne's annotator likewise has Sohni belong to Gujrat, "on the river Chenab", the town's name garbled in the printed edition (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 12, folio 11, note 5).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of death.** The site's account gives 1675, with a birth year of 1581. Lahori gives 1075 AH, with the chronogram "خدا دوست" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). His modern editor gives 1087 AH / 1676, both figures uncertain in the printed text, citing Mushtaq Ram Gujrati's *Karamat Nama* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184, folio 182). Bhandari gives the seventeenth regnal year of Alamgir, the ordinal uncertain in the printed text (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik gives "around AH 1676" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **His master's name.** The site's account names Shah Saidan Sarmast. Lahori names Shaikh Sina Sarmast (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184). Bhandari names "حضرت میان سیدنا(۱)", with the editor's variant "سیدنام[OCR?]" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik names no master, speaking of twelve years "at the feet of a Suhrawardi Sufi" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **His order.** The site's account makes his master a Suhrawardi *faqir*. Lahori traces his chain to Baha al-Din Multani through Rajan Qattal of Uch, and adds complete *faiz* from the Chishti line (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184). Malik gives a Suhrawardi teacher but records "too that he was initiated into the Qadiri order" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **His early life.** The site's account has him travel in his youth to the neighbourhood of Sialkot to become a disciple. Bhandari says he was first the slave of a resident of Sialkot (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik says he became supervisor of a local official's treasury and worked as a mendicant and labourer (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **Why he left Sialkot.** The site's account has him entrusted with his master's *khanqah* before establishing his own at Gujrat. Bhandari has him leave Sialkot after his dying master's glance transformed him (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik has him leave "Due to some disputes with the local people of Sialkot", moving to Gujrat after some years in obedience to divine instructions (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **His descent.** Malik gives both accounts himself: Afghan ancestors, and the claim that he was a Sayyid (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **The great bridge.** The site's account names, by tradition, a bridge over the Nala Dek. Bhandari names a bridge over the river Deg on the highway five *kos* from Eminabad toward Lahore, and a bridge on the Chenab at Gujrat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515).
- **Where the tomb stands.** The site's account and Lahori place it in the city of Gujrat (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). Bhandari places it "درنزدیکی ان شهر", near the town (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 515–514).
- **When the chuha tradition began.** The site's account says the folk belief was first recorded in print in January 1839 by Shahamat Ali. Malik, from its absence in the early lives of the saint, judges that the cult "arose only later, by the end of the nineteenth century—after the shrine had been reconstructed (1898)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).
- **The cause of the children's condition.** The site's account holds that they had naturally occurring microcephaly and that deliberate deformation was never substantiated. Malik reports the colonial suspicion that they were "artificially produced after their birth as ordinary infants", and Kunjahi's explanation that the bad conscience of parents set free "certain chemical reactions that caused this peculiarity" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).
- **What the Auqaf takeover changed.** The site's account dates the takeover to the mid-twentieth century and says the Department forbade the abandonment of children, after which their number declined. Malik dates it to the 1960s and writes that it "could not totally change the perceptions deeply rooted in the minds of the rural population and the authority exercised by the shrine administrator" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).
- **The spelling of the name.** Lahori's entry writes "دولا" and his editor's lists "دولہ" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 317, folio 305); Bhandari writes شاه دولا (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515); Malik writes "Daulah", and in one sentence the second title's printed form is uncertain where elsewhere it is *Daryâ'î* (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

## Legacy

Shah Daula Daryai is remembered in the Punjab as a saint of works and mercy, whose bridges and wells served the living and whose shrine remains a busy centre of devotion in Gujrat. The disquieting tradition of the *chuhas* that attached itself to his name in later centuries belongs to the social history that grew up around the shrine rather than to the saint himself, and is best understood today through the twin lenses of medical fact and compassion for those who were affected. The *darbar* continues to draw pilgrims, to feed the poor at its *langar*, and to hold its annual *urs* under Auqaf administration.

The books add three witnesses across three centuries. For Bhandari, writing in the fortieth regnal year of Aurangzeb, the saint was the man who made Gujrat grow in people and prosperity, the builder of a famous bridge on the Lahore highway, and the saint whose tomb drew people of every class (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). For Lahori in the 1870s he was a saint of the Punjab whose tomb was a place of pilgrimage and whose death was remembered in a chronogram (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). For Malik, writing on Qâsimî's story in a volume of 1998, his shrine had a particular reputation for "fertility, justice and punishment" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195), and had become the setting of one of Urdu fiction's critiques of shrine power.
