## Overview

At Uch Sharif, the ancient town near the confluence of the Chenab and the Sutlej in southern Punjab, lies the shrine of Sayyid Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari (1192–1291), the saint who made Uch one of the great centres of Sufism in the subcontinent and the founding father of the celebrated Bukhari sayyids. 'Surkh-Posh', the Red-Robed, came from Bukhara to settle at Uch, where he propagated the Suhrawardi order and founded a spiritual dynasty whose descendants — among them Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht — would shape the religious history of the region for centuries. His shrine anchors the remarkable cluster of tombs that has made Uch Sharif a place of pilgrimage and a treasury of Islamic architecture.

The histories and studies consulted for this article fill out that outline and, in places, contradict it. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* makes him a khalifa of Bahauddin Zakariya, gives him a year of birth, a death date exact to the day and five sons, and places his mazar at Uch (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 162–163, folios 150–151). Zahur ul-Hasan Sharib brings him from Bukhara to Multan, where he became Bahauddin Zakariya's *murid*, and then to Uch at his pir's command (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). Annemarie Schimmel calls him "the forefather of a long line of devout mystics and theologians" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354), and Haroon Khalid, visiting Uch Sharif, found the shrine of 'Pir Jalaludin Bokhari' the goal of almost every visitor there (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 282, folio 256). The books differ over whether his migration ended at Uch or at Multan, over the year of his death, over the number and names of his sons, and over the epithet itself, which several of them give as Surkh alone, without Posh.

A further difficulty runs through the whole record. His grandson, whom the site's account names Sayyid Jalaluddin known as Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht, bore the same name, and several books speak of a Jalal Bukhari in terms that do not settle which of the two they mean. What each of those books says is given below as that book's own account, with its uncertainty beside it, and the question is set out under 'Where the Sources Disagree'.

## The Life of the Saint

Sayyid Jalaluddin was born in 1192 at Bukhara, in Central Asia, into a family of Sayyids tracing descent from the Prophet. Migrating southward in the age of the Mongol upheavals, he came by way of Bhakkar in Sindh and settled at last at Uch, which he made the base of his mission. He is remembered as 'Surkh-Posh' for the red garment he habitually wore, and as a propagator of the Suhrawardi way, connected to the great Multan line of Bahauddin Zakariya. From Uch he preached and guided, and he founded the family of the Bukhari sayyids that would become one of the most influential religious lineages of the Punjab and Sindh. He died at Uch in 1291, full of years, and was buried there.

Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* gives him entry no. 103 and dwells on his descent. It makes him a khalifa of Bahauddin Zakariya and ties the standing he held in Hindustan to his lineage: "ہندوستان جنت نشان میں تمام سادات و مشائخ و امرا و سلاطین بسبب صحت و نسب ان کے ان سے باادب پیش آتے" — a precedence, as the book presents it, resting on pedigree rather than on office or wealth (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 162, folio 150). The notice sets out a genealogy of ten links, by name, back to Imam Muhammad Taqi, and records the branching of two families from it, the Bukhari sayyids (خاندان سادات بخاری) and the sayyids whose name is printed بھاکھری, its reading uncertain: "سید علی اصغر، ساتواں جد حضرت کا دو صاحبزادہ سید عبد اللہ و سید اسماعیل رکھتا تھا اور سید عبد اللہ کی اولاد سے خاندان سادات بخاری اور سید اسماعیل کی اولاد سے خاندان سادات بھاکھری [OCR?] ظاہر ہوا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 162, folio 150). For the saint's early life Lahori names his source in the words "صاحب مظہر جلالی لکھتا ہے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 162, folio 150).

The books trace his road out of Bukhara in different ways. Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi writes that "Shaikh Baha'u'd-Din Zakariyya had many famous disciples, one was Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Bukhari, also called Jalal Surkh (Red)", and gives the route the site's account follows, with a reason for its last stage: "He first migrated from Bukhara to Bhakkar, however local jealousy forced him to migrate to Uch. He remained there until his death" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203). These three sentences, for which Rizvi cites a single source, are the whole of what his book says of the saint in his own right: it prints no date for him and names no tomb, shrine building or khalifa (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203). His index, which files this saint under 'Surkh', sends the shorter 'Jalalu’d-Din Bukhari' to Makhdum Jahaniyan (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 470, folio 446).

Sharib, in a chapter whose subject is the saint's grandson, brings him to Multan first: "آپ کے دادا شیخ جلال الدین سرخ بخاری اپنے وطن بخارا سے ہجرت کر کے ملتان آئے۔ حضرت بہاء الدین زکریا رحمۃ اللہ علیہ کے مرید ہوئے اور ان ہی سے خرقہ خلافت پایا' اپنے پیرو مرشد کے حکم سے اوچہ میں سکونت اختیار کی" — he migrated from Bukhara to Multan, became Bahauddin Zakariya's *murid* and received from him the *khirqa* of *khilafat*, and took up residence at Uch (اوچہ) by his pir's order (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). In Sharib's telling, then, the settlement at Uch was an instruction from Multan.

A later note in Lahori's book gives the migration a year and the same end as Sharib: "۶۳۵ھ/۱۲۲۷ء کو بخارا سے ہجرت کر کے ملتان آ گئے تھے" — in 635 AH / 1227 CE, as the years are printed, he migrated from Bukhara to Multan (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 349, folio 337). That note names Multan, not Uch, gives no year of death, and leaves the word 'Posh' out of his name (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 349, folio 337). Schimmel's sentence on him reads: "One of Zakariya's disciples, Sayyid Jalaluddin Surkhpush" ('Red-dressed', d. 1292) "from Bukhara, settled in Ucch, northeast of Multan, and is the forefather of a long line of devout mystics and theologians" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore, which names him only as the forebear of Mauj Darya Bukhari, says that he lived at Uch and that his tomb is there: "اسکا بزرگ سید جلال الدین میر سرخ بخاری اُوچ مین قیام پذیر تہا اور وہین اُسکا مقبرہ ہے" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 279, folio 282). Kanhaiya Lal gives him no date and no silsila (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 279, folio 282).

Of the Mongol age into which the site's account sets his migration, the books speak only of the Punjab at large and do not name him. Richard Eaton writes that Mongol pressures "forced waves of Turkish settlers into the subcontinent, many of them settling permanently in the urban centres of the Punjab, such as Lahore, Dipalpur, and Multan" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 217, folio 205), and that Balban's garrisoning of the Punjab's cities drew in "thousands of refugees fleeing before the advancing Mongols—artisans, merchants, petty officials, and the like" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 222–223, folios 210–211). Rizvi writes that "The Mongol invasions between the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries had devastated portions of the Panjab" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 408, folio 384), and that in that age the Qalandariyyas and Jawaliqis who passed through Multan "often came into conflict with Shaikh Baha'u'd-Din Zakariyya" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 325, folio 303). Eaton, who names Zakariya as Baha' al-Haqq Zakariya and gives his death as 1263, writes of him "whose tomb is in Multan city" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 227, folio 215).

Lahori dates the saint's life exactly, and here, unusually for this book, the editor adds no correcting footnote: "ولادت باسعادت حضرت کی سنہ پانچ سو پچانوے اور وفات انیسویں جمادی الاول سنہ چھ سو نوے میں واقع ہوئی اور مزار اوچ میں ہے" — born in the year 595, died on 19 Jumada al-Awwal 690, his mazar at Uch (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 163, folio 151). The year 690 AH corresponds to the site's 1291; Lahori's year of birth, 595, stands beside the site's 1192. The notice also carries a chronogram, which gives the date ۶۹۰ھ twice (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 163, folio 151). Omar Kasmani's note on "Jalaluddin Surkhposh Bukhari (d. 1291) of Uchh" gives the same year as the site (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 17), while Schimmel gives 1292, both in her text and in her index (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 518, folio 487). Sharib gives neither a birth nor a death year (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). Khalid says only that "Jalaludin had lived in the thirteen century", and, in a passage whose printed text is damaged, that he had died before "the end of the century" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated).

## His Names

The epithet by which the site's account knows him, Surkh-Posh, the Red-Robed, for the red garment he habitually wore, appears in only some of the books, and in varying forms. Schimmel prints 'Sayyid Jalaluddin Surkhpush' and glosses the epithet as 'Red-dressed' (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). Kasmani writes 'Jalaluddin Surkhposh Bukhari' and 'Uchh' (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 17). Khalid's travelogue has 'Syed Jalaludin Surkh Posh Bokhari' (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 276, folio 250), and beside it the shorter 'Pir Jalaludin Bokhari' (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 282, folio 256) and 'Syed Jalaludin Bokhari' (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). Rizvi prints 'Jalal Surkh (Red)' and never the longer form (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203), and indexes him as "Saiyid Jalalu’d-Din Surkh (Bukhari), 203, 277" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 483, folio 459).

The Urdu and Persian histories give him fuller names. Lahori heads his notice "سید جلال الدین شیر شاہ المخاطب بہ میر سُرخ بخاری اوچی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 162–163, folios 150–151), and his table of contents lists "سید جلال الدین شیر شاہ سرخ بخاری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 17, folio 5). The index of the same book files him under the epithet "سرخ بخاری اوچی", with the personal name "جلال الدین شیر شاہ [OCR?]" in parentheses, the reading of that name uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 318, folio 306), and his later notices give him the nisba "میر سرخ بخاری اوچی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 168, folio 156). Kanhaiya Lal has "سید جلال الدین میر سرخ بخاری" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 279, folio 282). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti calls him "میر سید جلال الدین المشہور بہ پیر سرخ [OCR?]", Mir Sayyid Jalal al-Din known as Pir Surkh (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 101), and on another page gives a different form, "سید سلطان جلال الدین حیدر سرخ [OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 106). Sharib's form, "شیخ جلال الدین سرخ بخاری", lacks the word Posh (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129).

Two books give him only the name Jalal and the nisba of Bukhara. Waris Shah's romance of Hir and Ranjha, in Charles Frederick Usborne's English, says 'Sayyad Jalal of Bokhara' (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 50, folio 49) and 'Sayyid Jalal Bokhari' (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 52, folio 51), and its later annotator 'Jalal Bukhari' (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 11, folio 10, note 2); Surkh-Posh never appears there, nor Uch Sharif as his seat, nor any date or order. Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* has only "سید جلال بخاری", without the epithet (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527).

## Uch Sharif and the Bukhari Sayyids

Through Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh and his descendants, Uch Sharif became a spiritual capital of the southern Punjab — rivalling Multan as a seat of the Suhrawardi order and producing a succession of saints of the first rank. Chief among his descendants was his grandson, Sayyid Jalaluddin known as Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht, one of the most revered Suhrawardi saints of the fourteenth century, and the line continued through generations of sajjada-nashins who carried great religious and worldly authority. The town they made holy is today a dense and evocative landscape of shrines and tombs — among them the exquisite tiled mausolea of Bibi Jawindi and others — and it is counted among the most important heritage sites of Pakistan.

Lahori, on the authority of reports he calls "روایات صحیحہ", gives the saint five sons and names their mothers. The first two, Sayyid Ali and Sayyid Jafar, were both sons of the daughter of the king of Bukhara; Jafar settled in Bukhara and never came to Hind. The third, Sayyid Ahmad Kabir, was the son of Bibi Fatima, daughter of Sayyid Badr al-Din Bhakkari, the reading of whose name is uncertain in the printed text. The fourth was Sayyid Sadr al-Din Muhammad Ghaus, and the fifth, Sayyid Baha al-Din Ahmad, famous as Muhammad Masum, is named with his mother, Bibi Tahira Sayyida (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 163, folio 151). Lahori thus records three wives, a royal marriage, and a branch of the family that stayed in Central Asia.

Sharib gives three sons, named and ranked: "ان کے تین لڑکے تھے' سب سے بڑے لڑکے کا نام سید احمد کبیر ہے۔ دوسرے لڑکے کا نام سید بہاء الدین ہے۔ ان کے سب سے چھوٹے لڑکے سید صدر الدین المعروف بہ محمد غوث ہیں" — Sayyid Ahmad Kabir the eldest, Sayyid Baha al-Din, and the youngest, Sayyid Sadr al-Din, known as Muhammad Ghaus (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). Sharib names no order for the saint himself; the Suhrawardi affiliation his chapter does name belongs to the grandson's *bay'a* from the saint's son (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 135, folio 131). Rizvi, too, gives three sons: "He was a grandson of Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Surkh (Red), a disciple of Shaikh Baha'u'd-Din Zakariyya. Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Surkh had three sons: Saiyid Ahmad Kabir, Saiyid Baha'u'd-Din and Saiyid Muhammad" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277). On the same page Rizvi writes of the Suhrawardiyya in the time of Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Bukhari, Makhdum-i Jahaniyan, whose birth he gives as 15 Sha'ban 707/9 February 1308, that the order "spread from Uch to Gujarat, the Panjab and Kashmir even extending its influence to the Delhi of Sultan Firuz Shah" Tughluq (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277).

Bhandari names the saint only in the genealogy of Makhdum Jahaniyan, where he stands as grandfather: "خوابگاه شیخ جلال پور سید محمود بن سید جلال بخاری مشهور بمخدوم جهانیانست" — the man buried at Uch, Shaikh Jalal, son of Sayyid Mahmud, son of Sayyid Jalal Bukhari, is known as Makhdum Jahaniyan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527). Bhandari thus makes Sayyid Mahmud the son through whom the line ran to Makhdum Jahaniyan, a name that appears in none of the other books' lists of the saint's sons; he gives the grandfather no tomb, no place, no date and no epithet (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527).

In two later notices Lahori names him only as the head of the Uch Bukhari line: as the grandfather of Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht in the heading of entry no. 107 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 168, folio 156), and as the ancestor of Sayyid Haji Abd al-Wahhab Bukhari Dehlvi in entry no. 114 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 176, folio 174 as printed). A later note in the book, naming a father as "ان کے والد سید جلال سرخ بخاری (رک شمارہ۔ ۱۰۳)", refers back to his notice by its number (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 349, folio 337). Two other histories know him as an ancestor. Kanhaiya Lal names him as the forebear of Mauj Darya Bukhari (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 279, folio 282). Chishti, on the page where he calls Mauj Darya "سجادہ نشین خانقاہ عالیجاہ [OCR?] اپنی اجداد بزرگوار کے", the sajjada-nashin of his forefathers' khanqah, writes of a hazrat descended from Mir Sayyid Jalal al-Din known as Pir Surkh, and of a mazar at Uch, which he here calls Uch Miran: "یہ حضرت اولاد حضرت میر سید جلال الدین المشہور بہ پیر سرخ [OCR?] ہیں [OCR?] اور اوچ میراں میں اُنکا [OCR?] مزار ہے" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 101). Elsewhere Chishti writes of "اولاد سید سلطان جلال الدین حیدر سرخ [OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 106), and in a sequence of names on a later page a "سید جلال الدین بخاری" stands just before "حضرت سید رکن الدین ابو الفتح ملتانی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 154).

Two books connect Bibi Jawindi with a Jalal Bukhari. Khalid writes that the tomb of Bibi Jawindi, whom he calls Bibi Jiwindi, "belonged to the great granddaughter of Syed Jalaludin Bokhari" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). Robert Rozehnal, writing of the same tomb, calls Bibi Jawindi "the wife of the renowned fourteenth-century Suhrawardi shaykh, Sayyid Jalal ad-Din Bukhari (1303–1383)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10); his dates are not the site's dates for this saint, and the question of which Jalal is meant is taken up below.

Of the town's later standing in the Suhrawardi order, the books speak of Uch rather than of this saint. Schimmel writes that "Ucch was, for a while, the center of the Suhrawardiyya, thanks chiefly to the active and pious Jalaluddin Makhdum-i Jahaniyan", 'whom all the inhabitants of the world serve', "a prolific writer in almost all religious fields" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). Michel Boivin speaks of "the second Sohrawardiyya period, then based in Utch near Bahawalpur in Punjab" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 56, folio 43). Kasmani, naming the saint as the third of three figures who met Lal at Chothanbi, adds: "Their shrines are spread across southern Punjab in Pakistan." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 17).

## The Shrine

The shrine of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari at Uch is a working darbar and the ancestral seat of the Bukhari sayyids. Standing amid the celebrated monuments of Uch Sharif, the shrine is at once a place of living devotion and a link to the deep medieval history of Sufism in the subcontinent.

Lahori and Kanhaiya Lal place his grave at Uch but say nothing of its building. Lahori writes "مزار اوچ میں ہے", his mazar is at Uch (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 163, folio 151), and nowhere in his account of the saint does he describe the shrine's fabric, its *ʿurs*, its custodians or its economy. Kanhaiya Lal says that his tomb is at Uch and gives no description of it (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 279, folio 282). Chishti speaks of the mazar at Uch Miran (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 101). Sharib records no mazar, *ʿurs*, custodianship or endowment for him (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129), and neither Rizvi nor Schimmel names a tomb (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). One book buries him elsewhere. Usborne's annotator, glossing the romance's Jalal of Bukhara, writes: "Jalal Bukhari, who originally came from Uch, is also buried at Multan" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 11, folio 10, note 2); the romance itself never calls him Surkh-Posh or gives Uch as his seat.

The one description of the shrine in the books consulted is Khalid's, from a visit on which Iqbal Qaiser was with him. The pages of his travelogue that describe the shrines on the mound do not themselves name the town; Uch Sharif is clear from the shrines he names and from his later 'shrine of Jalaludin Bokhari at Uch Sharif'. He writes: "The shrine of Pir Jalaludin Bokhari was also situated on this mound. It was protected by a thick wall with barbed wire on top, which was constructed recently to protect it from terrorist attacks". "Almost all the visitors here, who numbered in the hundreds, were heading towards this shrine"; there was an "old Banyan tree in the centre"; and a banner "depicted Pir Jalaludin, Bahauddin Zakariya, Baba Farid and Lal Shahbaz Qalandar. Once again there was no Nanak" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 282, folio 256).

A mosque stands "next to the shrine, within the same compound", and Khalid calls it "a historical building" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 283, folio not stated). Of the interior, in a passage whose printed lines are damaged and run into one another, he writes: "Women were not allowed here either. It was a dark room", with "wooden pillars" "intricately carved with floral designs"; there were "several graves here, of people who must have paid hefty amounts of money to get buried next to the saint"; and "The grave of the saint" was "enclosed in glass" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 283, folio not stated).

A board of the Archaeology Department, as Khalid reports it, records that Baha-ul-Halim taught "at the madrassa that used to run at the shrine of" Jalaludin Surkh Posh Bokhari (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). In the market at the Gilani shrine, Khalid saw a poster of Pir Jalaludin on sale (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 277, folio 251).

## Devotion and Practice

The shrine is visited throughout the year by pilgrims who come to honour the founder of the line and to seek his blessing. It keeps the round of prayer, qawwali, and the free kitchen, and its annual urs draws devotees from across the region. The books consulted record no date for the *ʿurs*.

Khalid's account is of the visitors' devotion as he saw it. "Women it seemed were not allowed as they looked on from the boundary" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 283, folio not stated). A man showed him "three rooms" where, he said, Baba Farid, Bahauddin Zakariya and Lal Shahbaz Qalandar had meditated; Khalid writes, "I was sure that this was an apocryphal story". The man put a green shawl "with Quranic verses on it" round Khalid's neck and offered him water; expecting to be asked for a donation, Khalid walked off (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 283, folio not stated). People stood by the grave "for blessings"; another man waited "with a green box"; and devotees "offered their donations to the saint" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 283, folio not stated).

## Guru Nanak and the Shrine

Khalid's travelogue brings the shrine into the story of Guru Nanak. "According to Sikh tradition, Nanak was invited here [Uch Sharif] by the saint Syed Jalaludin Surkh Posh Bokhari when he met him in Kandahar, on the way back from Haj" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 276, folio 250). The visit, as he places it, took place on Nanak's way to Sindh, "after he had settled down" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 278, folio 252).

Khalid himself doubts the tradition. The Sikh "tale of Nanak and Jalaludin meeting" cannot hold, he argues, for "Jalaludin had lived in the thirteen century"; in a heavily damaged passage, Iqbal Qaiser suggests that Nanak may have met a descendant "of the saint but not Jalaludin" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). He writes that "once Nanak had been invited to visit this place at the behest of the saint himself but today there is no trace of his heritage" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 277, folio 251).

Khalid then imagines the visit. "Uch Sharif was one of the most famous Muslim shrines in Southern Punjab and Nanak had arrived here only a day ago, travelling from Kartarpur"; "At the shrine of Jalaludin Bokhari at Uch Sharif, Nanak saw an overwhelming number of dervish and ascetics", some "selling beads", some selling the leaves of trees "as sacred entities with magical properties", some pretending "to practise black magic", and others selling prayers; and Nanak sat "under the shadow of the banyan tree which was in the centre of the courtyard" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 288, folio 262). In the reconstruction a jogi prepares *bhang*; near the entrance is "a man selling bhangwale pakore (fritters with the addition of cannabis)"; and a jogi "carrying an ektara" sings in praise of the intoxicant, "one of the main attractions of a festival like this" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 287, folio 261). Nanak says, "Mardana, play Raag Ashta Padya", forgetting that his companion was his best friend's son; the hymns Khalid then gives are drawn, his note says, from Singh's translation, *Hymns of the Gurus* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 289, folio 263).

Of Nanak's traces in the town itself, Khalid found little. Iqbal Qaiser asked him, "Do you want to see the well of Nanak?", and warned, "There is nothing left there anyway"; the well "was hidden within the field, shielded by a grove of trees. It was abandoned and juice tetrapaks and wrappers were floating in the black water", and beside it was a grassy mound: "This was the Gurdwara of Nanak", and "Now nothing remained" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 286, folio 260). Of the river, he writes that the "River Sutlej, the lost river of Pakistan, used to flow from here before it was lost forever after the Indus Water Treaty was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960", and that "Nanak must have seen these buildings intact with a mighty river flowing next to it" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 281–282, folios 255–256).

## Legends and Miracles

Lahori's notice, which names its source for the saint's early life (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 162, folio 150), also tells of a miracle of his childhood; its details are not given in the material consulted for this article.

Sharib's chapter on Bahauddin Zakariya names a "حضرت سید جلال الدین سرخ بخاری" among Zakariya's khalifas, with no place, no date and no shrine (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 52, folio 48), and has a man of that name receive the *khirqa* of *khilafat* at Multan after the miracle of the hail, again with no town of burial, no year of death and no silsila (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 53–54, folios 49–50). The name and the link to Zakariya resemble this saint's, and the *khirqa* agrees with the chapter in which Sharib names him as a grandfather; but the book itself gives nothing more to tie these passages to this saint.

In Waris Shah's romance a Jalal of Bukhara lends his name to two relics, a cudgel and a dagger, and his dagger becomes a weapon against a lion; the passages are given under 'In Verse'.

## In Verse

Waris Shah's *Hir and Ranjha*, in Usborne's English, counts a Jalal of Bukhara among its five Pirs, and names him in the same sentence as Makhdum Jahanian:

*he smelt the sweet savour that came from the cudgel of Sayyad Jalal of Bokhara, -and he grasped the dagger given him by Makhdum Jahanian.* (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 50, folio 49)

Two pages later it is Jalal's dagger that is used against the lion:

*he drove the dagger of Sayyid Jalal Bokhari into his belly.* (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 52, folio 51)

The cudgel is Jalal's and the dagger Makhdum Jahanian's in the first passage; in the second the dagger is Jalal's. The inversion is the book's own. The romance gives this Jalal no epithet, no seat, no date and no order; the only thing in it that sets him apart from Makhdum Jahanian is that the two are named side by side as separate members of the five.

Lahori's notice on the saint carries a chronogram that gives the date ۶۹۰ھ, the year of his death, twice (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 163, folio 151); the verse itself is not quoted in the material consulted for this article.

## Setting: Uch Sharif

The books' accounts of the town speak of Uch as a whole, not of this shrine. Rozehnal, who visited "the nearby town of Uch Sharif" in April 1996, "spent a day wandering through the magnificent blue and white tiled mosques and desolate tombs of this ancient center of learning, trade, and pilgrimage built on a hill overlooking the confluence of the Sutlej and Chenab rivers"; of its tombs he names only Bibi Jawindi's (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10). He places it as "an ancient city located seventy miles southwest of Multan in Pakistan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 210, folio 202); Schimmel places 'Ucch' 'northeast of Multan', and gives no district or province (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). Usborne's annotator describes it as an ancient town "in Bahawalpur, now part of West Pakistan", and adds: "It is famous for its Gilani and Bukhari Saints, who hailed originally from Gilan (Iraq) and Bukhara (Central Asia) respectively" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 11, folio 10, note 2).

Shemeem Burney Abbas calls the place "the city of saints in Bahawalpur", writing of Bulleh Shah's family as "Syeds who had settled in Uch Gilanian, the city of saints in Bahawalpur, where Bulle Shah was born" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 107, folio not stated). She quotes the words "Thou art an inhabitant of Uch city [Uch literally means high/great]", and, in prose, that "Bulle Shah's mentor Inayat Shah, he--he belonged to Uch city" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 104, folio not stated). At Kasur, Muhammad Bakhsh, of a hereditary family of qawwals, told her: "We came with Bulle Shah's family from Uch Sharif, and we have learned his poetry from our ancestors, who have always sung here" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 112, folio not stated). Bahawalpur, with Multan, is in her account the seat of the landowning Syeds who "support the shrines of their ancestors" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 168–169, folios not stated).

Rizvi tells a foundation legend of the town in connection with Shaikh Safiu'd-Din Kaziruni. In it an order "to mount a camel and travel in whatever direction the animal led him; he was then to remain where the camel finally halted" ends with a halt "in the middle of a desert", where "the Shaikh founded a town later called Uch"; Rizvi's verdict is: "Although this story would appear mythical, it is typical of medieval tales relating to sufis." (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 129, folio 111). He also tells of a flying contest with a yogi at Uch (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 129–130, folios 111–112), and observes that all the stories of three generations of the sufis of Uch 'recount conflicts with Hindu Yogis' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 304, folio 282).

The town's other great family is that of the Gilani Qadiris. Rozehnal calls Shaykh Muhammad al-Husseini al-Jilani "the founder of the first Qadiriyya khanaqah at Uch", and writes: "A native of Turkey, Shaykh Muhammad traveled to Khurasan and then Multan before settling with his family in Uch" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 259, folio 252). His son 'Abd al-Qadir Jilani Thani (d. 1533) is "the famous Qadiri saint of Uch Sharif", yet "there seems to be no extant archive of the saint, no textual record to document his life and legacy" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 210, folio 202). Lahori, writing of the arrival of the Qadiri line in the Punjab, says "حضرت کے سلسلہ میں سے حضرت سید محمد غوث اوچی جیلی گیلانی اول پنجاب میں آئے", and has Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus come by way of Khurasan to Multan and settle at Uch; the modern editor's footnote, citing Ali Asghar Gilani, gives "بقول علی اصغر گیلانی آپ ۸۸۷ھ میں اوچ میں داخل ہوئے", a date that is the editor's and not the author's (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 40, folio 28). Chishti, following a genealogy he names as "کتاب نسب نامہ حضرت پیر محمد شاہ صاحب", writes of a Gilani ancestor who came "اوچ شریف سے … بعہد اکبر شاہ", from Uch Sharif in the time of Akbar Shah (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 525), and of an ancestor who came to Multan, was given a man's daughter, "مسمات فاطمہ", in marriage, was presented with "علاقہ اوچ[OCR?]", and settled there (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 526). Schimmel writes that "It was in Ucch that the first missionaries of the Qadiriyya settled in the late fifteenth century; from there this order spread into the Subcontinent, where it soon gained a firm footing and was carried to Indonesia and Malaysia" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354), but elsewhere that "the order was introduced in the late fourteenth century" into the subcontinent (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 278, folio 247). Rozehnal, against the site's account, calls Bahauddin Zakariya himself "the well-known Suhrawardi saint of Uch Sharif" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 57, folio 47).

Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* records the reputation of the sayyids of Uch. The سادات اوچ are famous, he writes, and where a dispute over descent arises and they accept a man as صحیح النسب, the matter is closed: "پھر کسکی مجال نہیں کہ دم مار سکے" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 526–527). The four sons of Hazrat Muhammad Ghaus lie at Uch Sharif, "بمقام اوچ شریف آسودہ ہیں", beside the tomb of Shah Muhammad Ghaus, and some of Abd al-Qadir Sani's descendants are "صاحب سجادہ اوچ میں" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 527). The elders of the Faqir family lived at Uch Sharif Sayyidan and served the sayyids of Uch (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 584). Chishti also tells a story of the time of a Nawab whose title is printed نواب خان بہادر[OCR?], the reading uncertain: at Uch Sharif the Nawab had a boil on his cheek that would not heal, went to the sayyids of Uch Sharif for prayer, and was directed by them to Ghulam Muhyi-ud-Din, the reading of whose name is uncertain, as a skilled physician, "حکیم حاذق"; the Nawab took him to Lahore and was cured. Chishti attributes the account to Hazrat Shah Sardar, son of Pir Muhammad Shah Gilani (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 584).

Bhandari's history knows Uch as a town (قصبه اوچ) on the roads of armies (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527). Shihab al-Din's first campaign took it and left a deputy there, and his second came again to Multan and Uch and went on to Gujarat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 405); Mirza Pir Muhammad crossed the Sind and took Uch and Multan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 333); and on one march toward Jodhpur, Uch appears as "a dependency of Multan" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 285). In his account of suba Thatta, the province runs from "حدود ملتان و اوچ" to Thatta and Kach Makran (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 529).

Khalid, driving to Uch Sharif, writes that "The boundary between Sindh and Punjab becomes a blur as we drive through Bahawalpur", and that "This is where the cultures of Punjab and Sindh merge. Some of the roadside hotels are called Punjab Hotel, while others are Sindh Hotel"; the language, Siraiki, is "an amalgamation of the two languages", and Iqbal Qaiser adds that "The Siraiki spoken in Multan is closer to Punjabi, while here it is more like Sindhi" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 276, folio 250). Boivin, too, notes that "The Siraiki language is mainly spoken in Southern Punjab, with Multan as capital. Interestingly, this area was a part of Sindh during the Middle Ages" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 216, folio 203). Khalid found the older city on a mound, with the 'massive havelis' "of the current caretakers of the shrine, the Gilanis and the Makhdooms" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 276, folio 250); the group of 'thirteenth and fourteenth century shrines' was reached through the market, and Iqbal Qaiser remarked, "This place has changed since the last time I came here" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255). On the mound were several graves "which were covered arbitrarily with the blue and white Multani tiles that had been recovered from these historical shrines" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated).

For further reading on the town, Rozehnal points to Mas'ud Hasan Shahab's *Khitta-i pak Uch* (Bahawalpur: Urdu Academy, 1967/1993) and to the second volume of Rizvi's *A History of Sufism in India* (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 259, folio 252).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Which Jalal: the indexes and chapter headings.** The site's account distinguishes this saint from his grandson, Sayyid Jalaluddin known as Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht, and several books name a Jalal Bukhari in terms that could fit either. Rizvi indexes this saint as "Saiyid Jalalu’d-Din Surkh (Bukhari), 203, 277" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 483, folio 459), but sends the shorter form to the grandson: 'Jalalu’d-Din Bukhari, see Makhdum Jahaniyan' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 470, folio 446). Sharib's table of contents lists a chapter as "باب ۲۲ حضرت سید جلال الدین بخاری ۱۲۹", a name both men share (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 15); within it this saint appears only as the grandfather of its subject (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). Bhandari's "سید جلال بخاری" is a bare name in Makhdum Jahaniyan's genealogy, with no epithet, tomb or date (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527). In two later notices Lahori names him only as the head of the Uch Bukhari line (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 168, folio 156).
- **Which Jalal: a fourteenth-century Jalal ad-Din Bukhari.** Carl Ernst and Bruce Lawrence write that Qiwam ad-Din "is best known for his spiritual initiation, as a Chishti through Chiragh-i Dihli, and as a Suhrawardi through Jalal ad-Din Bukhari (d. 1383)", and that Sa'd ad-Din compiled his master's discourses after the *Khizana-yi Jalali*, "in the style of a Suhrawardi malfuzat text of Jalal ad-Din Bukhari, The Jalalian Treasury" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 71, folio 57); they name neither Uch nor Surkh-Posh nor Makhdum. Rozehnal's "Sayyid Jalal ad-Din Bukhari (1303–1383)", the husband of Bibi Jawindi, is likewise given no epithet (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10). Their dates stand against the site's 1192–1291 for this saint; Ernst and Lawrence name no place, and neither book uses the epithet Surkh-Posh.
- **Which Jalal: the five Pirs of the romance.** Waris Shah's *Hir and Ranjha* names 'Sayyad Jalal of Bokhara' and Makhdum Jahanian in one sentence as two of its five Pirs (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 50, folio 49); it gives Jalal no epithet, seat, date or order, and that sentence is the only thing in the book that sets its Jalal apart from Makhdum Jahanian.
- **Which Jalal met Guru Nanak.** Sikh tradition, as Khalid reports it, has Syed Jalaludin Surkh Posh Bokhari meet Nanak at Kandahar and invite him to Uch (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 276, folio 250). Khalid answers that "Jalaludin had lived in the thirteen century", and Iqbal Qaiser suggests that Nanak met a descendant "of the saint but not Jalaludin" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated).
- **Where his migration ended, and where he lies.** The site's account has him settle, die and be buried at Uch. Lahori's notice puts his mazar at Uch (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 163, folio 151), Kanhaiya Lal his tomb (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 279, folio 282), and Chishti a mazar at Uch Miran (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 101); Rizvi has him remain at Uch until his death (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203), and Schimmel has him settle in Ucch (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). A later note in Lahori's book brings his migration from Bukhara to Multan and names no Uch (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 349, folio 337). Sharib has him come to Multan and move to Uch at his pir's order (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). Usborne's annotator says that he "originally came from Uch" and "is also buried at Multan" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 11, folio 10, note 2).
- **The road from Bukhara.** The site's account brings him by way of Bhakkar in Sindh to Uch. Rizvi agrees on Bhakkar and adds that "local jealousy forced him to migrate to Uch" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203). Sharib and the later note in Lahori's book take him from Bukhara to Multan instead, the latter in 635 AH / 1227 CE as the years are printed (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129; Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 349, folio 337).
- **His dates.** The site's account gives 1192–1291. Lahori gives his birth in the year 595 and his death on 19 Jumada al-Awwal 690, the year that corresponds to the site's 1291 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 163, folio 151). Kasmani gives 1291 (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 17); Schimmel gives 1292, in her text and in her index (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 518, folio 487). Rizvi prints no date for him at all (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203), Sharib gives no birth or death year (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129), and Khalid says only that he lived in the thirteenth century (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated).
- **His sons.** Lahori gives five: Sayyid Ali, Sayyid Jafar, Sayyid Ahmad Kabir, Sayyid Sadr al-Din Muhammad Ghaus and Sayyid Baha al-Din Ahmad, called Muhammad Masum (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 163, folio 151). Sharib gives three: Sayyid Ahmad Kabir, Sayyid Baha al-Din and Sayyid Sadr al-Din, known as Muhammad Ghaus (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). Rizvi gives three: Saiyid Ahmad Kabir, Saiyid Baha'u'd-Din and Saiyid Muhammad (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277). Bhandari makes Sayyid Mahmud the son through whom the line passed to Makhdum Jahaniyan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527).
- **His order.** The site's account makes him a propagator of the Suhrawardi order. The books make him a khalifa, *murid* or disciple of Bahauddin Zakariya (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 162, folio 150; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129; Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354), but none of those that give him the epithet Surkh or Surkh-Posh names his order: Rizvi does not use the word Suhrawardiyya of him (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203), and the Suhrawardi affiliation Sharib names is his grandson's (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 135, folio 131). The Suhrawardi Jalal ad-Din Bukhari of Ernst and Lawrence and of Rozehnal is the man whose identity is in question above.
- **His epithet.** The site's account calls him Surkh-Posh, the Red-Robed, for a red garment. Schimmel glosses Surkhpush as 'Red-dressed' (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354); Rizvi has 'Jalal Surkh (Red)' only (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 223, folio 203); Sharib's form has no Posh (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129), nor has the later note in Lahori's book (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 349, folio 337); Lahori's notice has "میر سُرخ" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 162–163, folios 150–151); and Chishti has 'Pir Surkh' and, on another page, "سید سلطان جلال الدین حیدر سرخ [OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 101; Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 106).
- **Bibi Jawindi.** Khalid calls her "the great granddaughter of Syed Jalaludin Bokhari" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated); Rozehnal calls her the wife of "Sayyid Jalal ad-Din Bukhari (1303–1383)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10).
- **The relics in the romance.** In Waris Shah's *Hir and Ranjha* the cudgel is Jalal's and the dagger Makhdum Jahanian's (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 50, folio 49); two pages later the dagger is Jalal's (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 52, folio 51).
- **Bahauddin Zakariya's seat.** The site's account speaks of the Multan line of Bahauddin Zakariya; Sharib has the saint come to Multan to become his *murid* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129), and Eaton puts the tomb of Baha' al-Haqq Zakariya, as he names him, "in Multan city" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 227, folio 215). Rozehnal calls Zakariya "the well-known Suhrawardi saint of Uch Sharif" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 57, folio 47).
- **Where Uch lies.** The site's account sets Uch near the confluence of the Chenab and the Sutlej, and Rozehnal on a hill overlooking it (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10). Rozehnal puts it "seventy miles southwest of Multan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 210, folio 202); Schimmel puts it 'northeast of Multan' (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354).
- **The Qadiriyya at Uch.** Schimmel has the first Qadiri missionaries settle in Ucch "in the late fifteenth century" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354), and elsewhere has the order introduced into the subcontinent "in the late fourteenth century" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 278, folio 247). Lahori's editor, citing Ali Asghar Gilani, has Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus enter Uch in ۸۸۷ھ (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 40, folio 28).

## Legacy

Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari holds a foundational place in the spiritual history of the Punjab and Sindh: the Bukhara-born saint who rooted the Suhrawardi way at Uch and fathered a dynasty of saints whose influence endured for centuries. Through his descendants — above all Jahaniyan Jahangasht — his line shaped the religion and society of the region, and through the shrines of Uch Sharif his memory is bound to one of the great sacred landscapes of Pakistan.

The books carry that memory in their own ways. To Schimmel he is "the forefather of a long line of devout mystics and theologians" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354); to Kanhaiya Lal, the ancestor of Mauj Darya Bukhari (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 279, folio 282); and on the banner Khalid saw at his shrine he stands beside Bahauddin Zakariya, Baba Farid and Lal Shahbaz Qalandar (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 282, folio 256). Lahori's notice records a standing in Hindustan that rested on his lineage (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 162, folio 150), and Chishti's book records the authority of the sayyids of Uch in questions of descent (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 526–527).

Khalid sets the shrine in the southern Punjab of his own day. "The southern region of Punjab, where Uch Sharif lies, has more traces of religious and cultural syncretism compared to the northern and central region, where there is a greater prevalence of education and hence religious intolerance" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 277, folio 251). At the shrine itself he wrote: "Standing at this shrine and observing such blatant religious oppression, it became clear to me why such extremist organisations were becoming popular in this region" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 284, folio 258). He reports the view of Ayesha Siddiqa, who "belongs to Bahawalpur, which is only about seventy kilometres from here", that organisations of the Ahl-e-Hadith school "have seeped into the social fabric of southern Punjab, a region that has historically rejected such strands of Islam and adopted a syncretistic version of religion. Such Sufi shrines are a symbol of that strand of Islam", and Tahir Kamran's, that such organisations are popular with the young because "they offer an explanation for their current oppression", and that their first step is "to target such shrines and their guardians, who have become immensely rich feeding off the oppressed classes" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 284, folio 258).

## Overview

At Uch Sharif rests Sayyid Jalaluddin Bukhari (1308–1384), universally known by his honorifics *Makhdoom-i-Jahaniyan* — 'the Master of the World' — and *Jahangasht*, 'the World-Traveller.' Grandson of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari, he was among the most learned and widely revered Suhrawardi saints of fourteenth-century India, a tireless traveller and preacher whose authority was sought by sultans and commoners alike. His shrine is one of the principal darbars of Uch Sharif and a major centre of pilgrimage in the southern Punjab.

The histories and studies consulted for this article fill out that portrait in unusual detail, and in places contradict it. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* gives him a full notice, with the night of the week on which he was born and the festival on which he died, and places his *roza* at Uch as a place of pilgrimage (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 169, folio 157). Zahur ul-Hasan Sharib gives him a whole chapter, from his birth at Uch to his death, with his teachings, his sayings and the wonders told of him (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 133–142, folios 129–138). Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi prints his birth, his death and his burial: "Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Bukhari died on 10 Zu'lhijja 785/3 February 1384 and was buried in Uch" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 303, folio 281). Rizvi writes that after the death of Shaikh Ruknu'd-Din the Suhrawardi order "declined in Multan only to be rejuvenated in Uch" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277), and Annemarie Schimmel writes that "Ucch was, for a while, the center of the Suhrawardiyya, thanks chiefly to the active and pious Jalaluddin Makhdum-i Jahaniyan" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). The books differ over the year of his death, over his father's name, over how often and how far he travelled, over the orders into which he was initiated, and over whether he lies at Uch or at Multan.

A further difficulty runs through the whole record. His grandfather, Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari, bore the same name, and several books speak of a Jalal Bukhari, or join the title Makhdum Jahaniyan to that name, in ways that do not settle which of the two men they mean; others give the title to a saint of Multan, or the epithet Pir Jahanian to a man of another name. What each of those books says is given below as that book's own account, with its uncertainty beside it, and the question is set out under 'Where the Sources Disagree'.

## The Life of the Saint

Born at Uch in 1308 into the Bukhari sayyid family founded by his grandfather Surkh-Posh, Jalaluddin was schooled in the religious sciences and the Suhrawardi discipline and grew into a scholar-saint of vast reputation. He earned the title *Jahangasht* — 'he who has roamed the world' — through his extraordinary travels: he journeyed across the Muslim world, performed the Hajj many times, and visited the great centres of learning and sanctity of his age, gathering knowledge and spiritual connection wherever he went. Honoured as *Makhdoom-i-Jahaniyan*, he was held in the highest esteem by the rulers of the Delhi Sultanate, particularly in the Tughluq age, and his counsel and blessing were widely sought. He died in 1384 and was buried at Uch, where his shrine became a focus of devotion.

Sharib makes him one of the Husaini sayyids, of a respected family of Bukhara: "آپ سادات حسینی سے ہیں۔ بخارا کے ایک معزز خاندان سے تھے" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). He names his father as سید احمد کبیر and his grandfather as شیخ جلال الدین سرخ بخاری (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129), and his younger brother as سید صدر الدین المعروف بہ راجو قتال (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 137, folio 133). Rizvi gives the same line in English: "He was a grandson of Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Surkh (Red), a disciple of Shaikh Baha'u'd-Din Zakariyya. Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Surkh had three sons: Saiyid Ahmad Kabir, Saiyid Baha'u'd-Din and Saiyid Muhammad. Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Bukhari and his younger brother, Raju Qattal, were the sons of Saiyid Ahmad Kabir" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277). Lahori's heading to his notice names the same three generations (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 168–169, folios 156–157), and the editor's appendix to it makes the line one of succession: "ان کے جانشین ان کے فرزند سید احمد کبیر تھے", the grandfather's successor was his son Sayyid Ahmad Kabir (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 349, folio 337).

Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* names another father. Its genealogy reads "خوابگاه شیخ جلال پور سید محمود بن سید جلال بخاری مشهور بمخدوم جهانیانست": the man whose resting-place is at Uch, Shaykh Jalal, son of Sayyid Mahmud, son of Sayyid Jalal Bukhari, is known as Makhdum Jahaniyan; and Bhandari calls him "مرید و خلیفه پدر بزرگوار خود است", the disciple and khalifa of his own revered father (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527). Bhandari does not call the grandfather Surkh-Posh, does not place his tomb at Uch and gives him no date (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527).

The editor's appendix to Lahori's notice is about the father, not the son. "مخدوم جہانیاں جہاں گشت بخاری کے والد گرامی سید احمد کبیر الدین بھی ایک بزرگ صوفی تھے": the revered father of Makhdum Jahaniyan Jahangasht Bukhari, Sayyid Ahmad Kabir al-Din, was also a venerable Sufi. Of his training it adds "وہ شیخ جمال خنداں رو کی خدمت میں بھی حاضر رہتے تھے۔ مخدوم احمد کبیر کی باطنی تربیت شیخ صدرالدین عارف ملتانی نے کی تھی": he attended Shaykh Jamal Khandan Ru, and his inward training was given by Shaykh Sadr al-Din Arif Multani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 349, folio 337).

The same editor dates the father's death twice, and differently. A footnote to the notice makes Sayyid Ahmad Kabir a murid of Shaykh Sadr al-Din Arif who "۷۱۳ھ [OCR?] کے بعد انتقال کیا", died after 713 AH, the reading of the year uncertain in the printed text, and cites two pages of Muhammad Ayub Qadri's *Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahan Gasht Bukhari* for it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 168, folio 156, حاشیہ 1). The appendix says instead: "مخدوم سید احمد کبیر کا سال وفات تذکروں میں نہیں ملتا۔ ہم نے بعض قرائن و قیاسات کی بنیاد پر حدود ۷۳۱ھ/۱۳۳۰۔۳۱ء قرار دیا ہے". The year of his death, the editor writes, is not found in the tazkiras, and he has put it at about 731 AH / 1330–31 CE "on the basis of certain indications and conjectures", pointing to his own Danishnama article "احمد کبیر الدین" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 349, folio 337). The second date is, by the editor's own account, a conjecture.

The books date the son's birth closely, though not alike. Lahori gives it as "چہارم شعبان المعظم شب شنبہ سنہ سات سو سات", the night of Saturday, 4 Shaban, in the year 707 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 169, folio 157). Sharib writes "آپ کی ولادت باسعادت اوچہ میں 15' شعبان 707ھ کو واقع ہوئی", born at Uch on 15 Sha'ban 707 AH, citing the *Salik al-Salikin* and the Urdu translation of the *Akhbar al-Akhyar* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129, حاشیہ 1). Rizvi has "Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din, the Makhdum-i Jahaniyan, was born on 15 Sha'ban 707/9 February 1308" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277), and Michel Boivin prints his life dates as '(1308–84)' (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 56, folio 43). Bhandari puts the birth on Shab-i Barat: "شب برات هفتصد و هفت هجری بعرصه وجود آمد", on the night of Barat in the year 707 Hijri he came into existence (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527).

Sharib traces his schooling. He began it at Uch, which Sharib spells here "اونچہ", under "علامہ قاضی بہاء الدین"; after the qazi's death he came from Uch to Multan to finish the *Hidaya* and the *Bazdawi*, "ہدایہ و بزدوی", under "شیخ موسیٰ اور مولانا مجد الدین"; and then "مدینہ جا کر مزید تعلیم حاصل کی", he went to Medina and studied further (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 134, folio 130). Rizvi writes that "he received a formal religious education, and then became his father's disciple" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277).

Sharib records "آپ نے شادی کی تھی", that he married, but names no wife and gives no number of children (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 137, folio 133); a youngest son of four years appears in one of the stories told of him (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 140–141, folios 136–137). Rizvi names a son, Saiyid Mahmud Nasiru'd-Din, who "too lived in Uch and attracted disciples from Multan and neighbouring areas. He had a very large family and is believed to have died in 847/1443-44" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 304, folio 282), and his index lists a 'Muhammad b. Makhdum Jahaniyan' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 476, folio 452).

Of his death the books give more than one year. Lahori writes "دہم ماہ ذی الحجہ روز عید اضحیٰ سنہ سات سو پچاسی", the tenth of the month of Zil-Hijja, the day of Eid al-Adha, in the year 785 AH, and his editor's footnotes dispute neither this date nor that of the birth (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 169, folio 157). Rizvi gives the same day and year with its Common Era equivalent, 3 February 1384, and buries him in Uch (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 303, folio 281); his index has him "(b. 1308, d. 1384)" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 474, folio 450). Bhandari, too, puts his death on the Id-i Qurban of 785, a Wednesday, in the words "چهارشنبه عید قربان هفتصد و هشتاد و پنج اخشیجی پیکر برانداخت", he cast off his elemental frame; he prints no era word with this year, as he does with the year of the birth (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527). Sharib gives a later year: "کچھ روز بیمار رہ کر 10' ذی الحجہ 788ھ کو آپ رحمت حق میں پیوست ہوئے", after some days' illness he passed into God's mercy on 10 Zi al-Hijja 788 AH, again on the authority of the *Salik al-Salikin* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 137, folio 133, حاشیہ 10). On another page Boivin prints '(d. 1383)' (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 189, folio 176), and Schimmel gives '(d. 1383)' in her text and 'd. 1382-83' in her index (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 518, folio 487). Carl Ernst and Bruce Lawrence call him only "the famous fourteenth-century Suhrawardi saint of the Punjab" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 95, folio 81).

## His Names and Titles

Sharib gives his name, kunya and titles together. "آپ کا نام سید جلال الدین حسین ہے": his name is Sayyid Jalal al-Din Husain; his kunya is ابو عبداللہ; his laqab is "مخدوم جہانیاں جہاں گشت"; and some, Sharib adds, call him simply Makhdum Jahaniyan (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). The chapter opens by calling him "حضرت سید جلال الدین بخاری سیاح بادیہ تجرید [OCR?] و تفرید ہیں", a traveller of the wilderness of *tajrid* and *tafrid*, the reading of the first of the two words uncertain in the printed text (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129). Rizvi's fullest form is "Saiyid Abu 'Abdu'llah Jalalu'd-Din Husain bin Ahmad Bukhari, better known as the Makhdum Jahaniyan" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 22, folio 8); elsewhere he writes "the Makhdum Jahaniyan, Saiyid Jalal Bukhari" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 24, folio 10) and 'Makhdum-i Jahaniyan Saiyid Jalal Bukhari' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 251, folio 231), and his index gives the headword 'Makhdum Jahaniyan, Saiyid Abu ‘Abdu'llah Jalalu’d-Din Husain b. Ahmad Bukhari' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 474, folio 450).

Lahori heads his notice, entry no. 107, "سیّد جلال الدین بخاری الملقّب بمخدوم جہانیاں جہاں گرد بن سیّد احمد کبیر بن سیّد جلال الدین شیر شاہ میر سُرخ بخاری اوچی": Sayyid Jalal al-Din Bukhari, entitled Makhdum Jahaniyan Jahan-gard, son of Sayyid Ahmad Kabir, son of Sayyid Jalal al-Din Sher Shah Mir Surkh Bukhari of Uch (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 168–169, folios 156–157). The heading's second title is جہاں گرد, the world-roamer; the book's index of persons has instead "مخدوم جہانیاں جہاں گشت بخاری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 330, folio 318). The notice gives him a chain of praise-titles: "چراغ خاندان مظہر انوار ربانی مطلع تجلیات سبحانی کاشف رموز طریقت ہادی طرائق حقیقت صاحب ارشاد پیشوائے اوتاد" — the lamp of the family, the manifestation of the lights of the Lord, the dawning-place of the epiphanies of the All-Glorious, the unveiler of the mysteries of the Path, the guide on the ways of Reality, the master of guidance, the leader of the *awtad* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 168, folio 156).

The books gloss the titles differently. Rizvi writes "the Makhdum-i Jahaniyan (Lord of the Mortals)" and 'the Jahangasht (World Traveller)' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 299–300, folios 277–278), and explains the second: "So well-travelled did he become that Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din was called the Jahangasht (World Traveller)" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 300, folio 278). Schimmel renders the first 'whom all the inhabitants of the world serve' (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). Sharib tells a story of how the first title was conferred, given under 'Legends and Miracles' below.

Other books join the title to the name in their own ways. Boivin writes 'Jalal al-Din Bukhari Makhdum-i Jahaniyyan Jahangasht' (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 56, folio 43) and "Sayyid Jalal al-Din Bukhari, better known under the name of Makhdum Jahaniyyan Jahangasht" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 189, folio 176), and indexes him under 'Jahangasht' (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 244, folio 231). Ernst and Lawrence have 'Makhdum-i Jahaniyan Jahangasht' (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 93, folio 79) and 'Jalal ad-Din Bukhari Makhdum-i Jahaniyan' (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 95, folio 81); Robert Rozehnal 'Sayyid Jalal ad-Din Bukhari Makhdum-i Jahaniyan' (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 57, folio 47); Schimmel 'Jalaluddin Makhdum-i Jahaniyan', to which her index sends the bare title (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 520, folio 489); and Christopher Shackle, in a note to Bulleh Shah, 'Jalal ud Din Makhdum Jahaniyan of Uch' (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 186, folio 161, n. 2 on 122). Waris Shah's romance of Hir and Ranjha, in Charles Frederick Usborne's English, has "Sayyid Jalal of Bukhara, whom men also call Makhdum Jahanian" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 11, folio 10), and later the shorter 'Makhdum Jahanian' (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 50, folio 49) and bare 'Jahanian' (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 52, folio 51); the title Jahangasht never appears in it, nor Uch Sharif, nor any date or order. Bhandari's form is "مشهور بمخدوم جهانیانست", known as Makhdum Jahaniyan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527).

The epithet is not his alone in Lahori's book. Its index gives 'Pir Jahanian' to a Kamal Bukhari (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 326, folio 314; Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 316, folio 304), and so do two of its notices. Shah Kamal Bukhari, the maternal grandfather of Muhammad Nur, is 'famous as Pir Jahanian', with a mazar at qasba Chunian (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 51, folio 39), and a later notice speaks of "پیر سید کمال المشہور پیر جہانیاں" of Chunian, of the Bukhari sayyids, "سادات بخاری", with living descendants there (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 266, folio 254). The book gives this Pir Jahanian the name Kamal, not Jalal al-Din, and a mazar at Chunian, not Uch; whether he is another saint who shared the sobriquet, or a second site claimed for the saint of Uch, these passages do not say.

Sharib spells the saint's town three ways: "اوچہ" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 133, folio 129), "اونچہ" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 134, folio 130) and "اوچ" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 146, folio 142).

## Masters and Initiations

Lahori sets out four stages of his formation, in order. He took his first *bai'at* at the hand of his father, Sayyid Ahmad Kabir, and received from him the *khirqa* of *khilafat* of the Suhrawardi path; he then drew inward *faiz* from Shaykh Sadr al-Din, famous as Muhammad Ghaus; at Sadr al-Din's direction he became the murid of Shaykh Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath Multani, completed his course and received the khirqa of khilafat from him; and he then made the Hajj, and at Mecca stayed with the Shaikh al-Islam, Shaykh Afif al-Din Abdullah Matri, for outward and inward benefit (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 168, folio 156). A footnote in the edition names him among the "نامور خلفا", the famous khalifas, of Shah Rukn-e Alam, with Maulana Zahir al-Din, Sultan Hamid al-Din Hakim, Shaykh Fakhr al-Din Iraqi and Shaykh Sama al-Din Dehlvi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 165, folio 153, حاشیہ 1). Another quotes him on the teaching of Shaikh al-Arif at Multan, "شیخ العارف ہر مبتدی و منتہی کو بلا کسی امتیاز کے تعلیم دیتے تھے": Shaikh al-Arif taught every beginner and every advanced student without any distinction (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 161, folio 149, حاشیہ 1).

Sharib's account runs along the same line and goes further. "آپ اپنے والد ماجد سے سلسلہ سہروردی میں بیعت ہوئے": he took bai'at from his father in the Suhrawardi silsila (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 135, folio 131). Then, "پھر آپ نے اپنے چچا حضرت سید صدر الدین المعروف بہ محمد غوث سے خرقہ پہنا۔ حضرت شیخ رکن الدین ابو الفتح رحمۃ اللہ علیہ سے بھی آپ نے خرقہ خلافت پہنا": he put on the khirqa from his uncle, Hazrat Sayyid Sadr al-Din, known as Muhammad Ghaus, and from Hazrat Shaykh Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath, God's mercy be upon him, he also put on the khirqa of khilafat (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 135, folio 131). He took bai'at and khilafat, Sharib adds, in fourteen *khanwadas*: "آپ نے چودہ خانوادوں میں بیعت اور خلافت حاصل کی" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 135, folio 131, حاشیہ 4).

Sharib records khirqas of other kinds as well. He claimed the *khirqa-yi siyadat*, the robe of his sayyid descent, from Hazrat Ali, "کہ جو خرقہ ان کو سرور عالم حضرت محمد مصطفیٰ صلی اللہ علیہ وسلم سے ملا تھا", the khirqa that had come to Ali from the Prophet; and he wore the khirqa of Baha al-Din Zakariya, which he had received from his father (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 135, folio 131). Two khirqas came to him in dreams, from Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath and from Nizam al-Din Auliya, and each was found on his head when he woke (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 135, folio 131). On his return he received a further khirqa of khilafat from Nasir al-Din Chiragh Dehlvi (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 137, folio 133).

A footnote lists, without stories, the men from whom the khirqa came to him: Shaykh Qawam al-Din, the khalifa of Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath; Qutb al-Din Munawwar; Nasir al-Din Chiragh Dehlvi; "شیخ مکہ امام عبداللہ یافعی، شیخ مدینہ حضرت عبداللہ المطری", the shaykh of Mecca, Imam Abdullah Yafi'i, and the shaykh of Medina, Hazrat Abdullah al-Matri; a qutb of Aden whose name is uncertain in the printed text; Shaykh Ishaq Kazaruni; Shaykh Amin al-Din; Shaykh Hamid al-Din; a khalifa of Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, Shaykh Sharaf al-Din Mahmud Shah, whose name is uncertain in the printed text; Sayyid Ahmad Rifa'i; Shaykh Najm al-Din Kubra; Hazrat Khizr; and Shaykh Nur al-Din, among others (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 135–136, folios 131–132, حاشیہ 5).

Rizvi, too, has him become his father's disciple and take initiation from Rukn al-Din, and then adds a second order: "he received a formal religious education, and then became his father's disciple. Later he obtained initiation into the Suhrawardiyya order from Shaikh Ruknu'd-Din" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277), and "After his return to Uch, Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Bukhari went to Delhi and was initiated personally into the Chishtiyya order by Shaikh Nasiru'd-Din" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277). Rizvi makes him the man who began in India the practice of initiation into more than one order: "The practice seems to have been started in India by the Suhrawardi, Makhdum Jahaniyan Saiyid Jalal Bukhari who, as we shall see, also obtained initiation in the Chishtiyya order" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 292, folio 272). Elsewhere he calls him 'the famous Suhrawardi' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 429, folio 405) and 'the celebrated Suhrawardi saint' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 22, folio 8).

Rozehnal, quoting the *Sirat-i Zauqi*, says that Jalal ad-Din "completed his training under Shaykh Rukn ad-Din Abul Fatah Suhrawardi and Nasir ad-Din Chirag-i Delhi. Thus both the Suhrawardi and Chishti systems were followed in the family." (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 57, folio 47). Ernst and Lawrence call him a Suhrawardi "who also had close ties to the Chishtiyya" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 95, folio 81). Bhandari, after making him his father's disciple and khalifa, writes "از شیخ رکن الدین ابو الفتح سهروردی نیز خلافت یافت", he received khilafat also from Shaykh Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath Suhrawardi, and "در دهلی شیخ نصیر الدین چراغ دهلی را دیده فراوان فیض اندوخت", at Delhi he saw Shaykh Nasir al-Din Chiragh-i Dihli and gathered abundant grace (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527). Boivin calls him "the great Sohrawardi Sufi" and "one of the masters of the second Sohrawardiyya period" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 56, folio 43).

## The Hijaz and the Travels

Lahori follows the stay at Mecca with a wider journey: "بقدم تجرید سیر تمام روئے زمین کی کی", he toured the whole face of the earth on the foot of detachment, drawing *faiz* from hundreds of guiding saints (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 168, folio 156). Rizvi reports a like figure from Jamali: "According to Jamali, during his travels the Saiyid was met by more than three hundred important sufis" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277).

Sharib gives the Hijaz years a length and an end: "چھ سال مدینہ اور مکہ میں رہ کر 752ھ میں وطن واپس ہوئے", after six years in Medina and Mecca he returned home in 752 AH (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 137, folio 133, حاشیہ 7). On that journey he met "سید صدر الدین کماش [OCR?]" and "شیخ حمید الدین بن محمود الحنی [OCR?] سمرقندی", both names uncertain in part in the printed text (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 137, folio 133, حاشیہ 8). At Medina, leading the prayer in the Prophet's mosque in the imam's absence, "آپ بپاس ادب اس جگہ سے جہاں سرور عالم صلی اللہ علیہ وسلم کھڑے ہوتے تھے۔ ایک صف پیچھے کھڑے ہوئے": out of reverence he stood one row behind the place where the Prophet used to stand (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 136, folio 132).

Rizvi doubts the wider travels. "Although it is believed that the Saiyid went abroad on three different occasions, the validity of such an assertion is doubtful. His travels mentioned in the Safar Nama-i Makhdum Jahaniyan (Book of the Travels of Makhdum Jahaniyan) are mostly legendary and all of a later date" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 300, folio 278). He also writes that "It seems likely that for most of the reign of Sultan Muhammad bin" Tughluq "the Saiyid lived abroad and his" khanqah "was administered by his brother" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 299–300, folios 277–278). The wonders that the *Mahbubiyya* attaches to his journeys are given under 'Legends and Miracles'.

## The Sultans of Delhi

Three books record that Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq gave him office. Sharib writes "سلطان محمد تغلق شاہ کے عہد میں آپ کو منصب شیخ الاسلامی و مسند خانقاہ محمدی پیش کیا گیا۔ آپ نے عہدہ قبول فرمایا۔ کچھ عرصے تک منصب شیخ الاسلامی و مسند خانقاہ محمدی پر سیوستان اور اس کے مضافات میں فائز رہ کر اپنے فرائض بحسن و خوبی انجام دیتے رہے": in the reign of Sultan Muhammad Tughluq Shah the office of Shaikh al-Islam and the seat of the Khanqah-i Muhammadi were offered to him; he accepted, and for a time held them at Siwistan and its dependencies, discharging his duties well; he then resigned them at the order of Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 136, folio 132). Rizvi: "It would seem that Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq appointed him the Shaikhu'l-Islam and made him the head of a" khanqah "in Siwistan (Sehwan) known as the Khanqah-i Muhammadi to which several villages were attached. However, Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din did not remain there long" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277). Boivin: "He was named shaykh al-islam by the sultan of Delhi Muhammad bin Tughluq." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 56, folio 43).

Under Muhammad's successor, Firuz, the books bring him often to the court. Sharib writes "سلطان فیروز تغلق آپ کا معتقد و منقاد تھا۔ اس کے عہد حکومت میں آپ کئی دفعہ اوچہ سے دہلی تشریف لائے": Sultan Firoz Tughluq was his devotee and obedient to him, and in his reign he came several times from Uch to Delhi; Sharib's footnote cites the Urdu translation of the *Akhbar al-Akhyar* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 137, folio 133, حاشیہ 9). Rizvi writes: "During the time that Sultan Firuz Shah Tughluq ruled in Delhi the Saiyid remained mainly at Uch, only visiting the capital periodically. One of his known visits took place between 8 Rabi' II 781/24 July 1379 and Muharram 782/April 1380" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 300, folio 278), and elsewhere he dates that visit to the day: "The account dates from Sunday 8 Rabi' II 781/24 July 1379 and ends on Tuesday 17 Muharram 782/23 April 1380, during the time of Shaikh's visit to Delhi." (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 22, folio 8).

Rizvi describes the Sultan's regard. "the Sultan gave Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Bukhari a royal reception and continued to visit him in his" khanqah "throughout his stay. So great was the Saiyid's hold with the Sultan that all his recommendations were granted"; and "His assistance was also sought by the governors of Sind" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 301, folio 279). A letter that Rizvi quotes in S.H. Askari's translation says of the Sultan: "When for some days his holiness, Syed Jalalu'd-Din (Bukhari) may his resting place be blessed! came to him, he met him and derived many benefits from his association with the Syed"; and "He learnt to say the 'Chasht' or the morning prayer and 'Tahajjud' (night prayer) from the saintly saint after the latter's arrival (at Delhi from Uch, near Multan)" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 258, folio 238).

He used that regard for others. Rizvi relates that Sultan Firuz, advised by the *'ulama*, summoned "Shaikh Sharafu'd-Din from Bihar to account for his conduct. A farman was issued authorizing this, but was cancelled at the request of Makhdum-i Jahaniyan Saiyid Jalal Bukhari" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 251, folio 231); "It would, however, seem that the strong recommendations of Makhdum-i Jahaniyan, which the Sultan and the 'ulama' were unable to ignore, saved Shaikh Sharafu'd-Din from the axe" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 251–252, folios 231–232). "The abolition of about twenty-eight taxes by Sultan Firuz Shah largely imposed on towns throughout the empire may be ascribed to the influence of the Saiyid" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 301, folio 279).

The books credit him with the peace of Thatta. Rizvi: "In 763/1362 accompanied by a large army Sultan Firuz marched on Thatta"; "The Sammah ruler, Jam Jauna bin Babinya (756/1355—770/1369), sought to arrange peace-terms through Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din. It was finally agreed that Jam's son, Mani, should rule as a tributary of Sultan Firuz of Delhi. The peace was generally hailed as a triumph for Makhdum Jahaniyan" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 301, folio 279). Boivin dates the siege otherwise and calls the peacemaker a saint of Multan: "In 1367, his successor, Firuz Shah Tughluq, returned to lay siege to Thatha; Jam Juna I Samma would have to ask for the intercession of a saint of Multan", Sayyid Jalal al-Din Bukhari, "better known under the name of Makhdum Jahaniyyan Jahangasht (d. 1383)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 189, folio 176).

Sharib tells of an intercession with the Sultan's minister. Khan Jahan, the wazir of Firoz, had imprisoned the son of a *muharrir*, a clerk, and the saint "انیس بار سفارش کرنے تشریف لے گئے", went nineteen times to plead for him and was not received. The twentieth time Khan Jahan sent word, "اے سید تم کو غیرت نہیں آتی", O Sayyid, have you no shame? He answered: "اے عزیز! میں جتنی بار آتا ہوں' مجھ کو ثواب ملتا ہے۔ میں چاہتا ہوں کہ مظلوم کو تیرے ہاتھ سے چھڑاؤں' تاکہ تو بھی درجہ ثواب کو پہنچے", O dear one, every time I come I earn merit; I wish to free the wronged man from your hand, so that you too may reach the rank of merit. Khan Jahan came to him "نگے سر' گلے میں رسی ڈالے ہوئے", bareheaded, with a rope round his neck, asked his pardon and became his murid, and "محرر کے بیٹے کو خلعت اور گھوڑا دے کر رہا کر دیا", released the clerk's son with a robe of honour and a horse; and when he offered the saint a *nazrana*, "آپ نے وہ نذرانہ محرر کے بیٹے کو دے دیا", he gave that offering to the clerk's son. Sharib's footnote cites the *Salik al-Salikin* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 138, folio 134, حاشیہ 14).

In two passages on one page where Rizvi names him by the title alone, with no personal name, he is the measure of other men's standing at Delhi. "At that time the Makhdum Jahaniyan had gone to Delhi. The Sultan and his nobles used to pay their respects to the famous Suhrawardi and great glamour surrounded his personality. The Baba suggested to Shaikh Ahmad that he should become the disciple of the great Shaikh, but Ahmad refused to leave his pir"; and "At that time Makhdum Jahaniyan also happened to visit Delhi. He called on Ahmad-i Khattu and hugged him, telling him he reminded him of his friend, Baba Ishaq" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 429, folio 405).

## Teachings and Rulings

Rizvi gives his rulings. "A notorious puritan, Makhdum Jahaniyan strongly opposed the tradition which had developed around the Shab-i Barat festival which was held in the evening of the middle of Sha'ban, the eighth month in the Muslim Calendar, when fire works were exploded, graves were white-washed and lighted lamps were placed on them" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 302, folio 280). Muslims, he taught, "should pray and give the money, which otherwise would be used on crackers and lamps, to the poor"; "Only in India, he added, was there such a blatant disregard of the holy law, for such innovations were not to be found in Ghazna, Khurasan or Arabia"; "He also sternly disapproved of giving Allah such Hindi names as Thakur (Lord), Dhani (Rich) and Kartar (Creator)"; and he advised the *a'imma* "not to accept any payment which came from illegal sources of revenue" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 302, folio 280).

His rule on sufis and rulers set the direction of the visit. "Makhdum Jahaniyan urged that dervishes, sufis and the 'ulama' visit rulers, government officials and the rich in order to elicit assistance for the deprived and justified his own visits to Sultan Firuz on these grounds. Dervishes, however, should never allow such people to visit them at their" khanqahs; "if this did occur, the time should be beneficially used by preaching on the significance of the Shari'a" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 302, folio 280). Of royal stipends he ruled that "according to the books of Fatwas, it was makruh (disapproved) however it was not invalidated by the Shari'a" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 301, folio 279).
