Description:
## Overview

Tilla Jogian — the "Hill of the Ascetics" — crowns the highest peak of the eastern Salt Range, rising to some 975 metres above sea level, in the Jhelum District of the Punjab. On its summit lie the ruins of an ancient temple and monastic complex that was, before 1947, the foremost centre of Hindu yogis in the whole of the Punjab. Cooler and greener than the parched country below, the hilltop has for many centuries been a retreat for renunciants seeking solitude, and its long association with the *Nath* order of yogis, with Guru Nanak, and with the lovers of Punjabi legend has made it one of the most storied heights in the region.

The books bear out that reputation from several sides. Christopher Shackle, annotating the lyrics of Bulleh Shah, calls the hill the headquarters of the order of *Kanphat* yogis (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 10 on 122). Haroon Khalid calls it the most important pilgrimage site for jogis in the Punjab (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 21, folio 3). Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, in its account of the suba of Lahore, sets on the salt mountain the place of austerity of the jogi Bal Nath (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514), and records a gathering there on the day of Shivrat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 514–513). And in Waris Shah's romance of Heer and Ranjha, in Charles Frederick Usborne's English, Tilla is the hill to which Ranjha comes to take *jog* from Bal Nath, whom Usborne spells Balnath (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30).

## Gorakhnath and the Nath Yogis

Tradition traces the sanctity of Tilla Jogian back some two thousand years and links its foundation to *Gorakhnath*, the revered yogi and organiser of the *Nath* tradition — though this popular chronology is internally inconsistent (scholarship usually places the historical Gorakhnath centuries later, c. 11th–12th century CE) and should be read as legend rather than settled history.

Shackle's notes to Bulleh Shah place Gorakhnath at the head of the order the hill housed. Where the poet names 'guru Gorakh', Shackle explains "Gorakhnath, the head of the Kanphat yogis" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 12 on 122); the name on which the poem's initiate meditates is "Presumably the name of the yogis' guru Gorakhnath" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 11 on 122); and his glossary describes "the great yogi Gorakhnath, from whom Ranjha sought initiation as a yogi" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 198, folio 173). Shackle gives Gorakhnath no date and no lineage.

Michel Boivin, whose study names no Nath site in Sindh or in the Salt Range, describes the Nathpanthis as "the followers of Gorakhnath, who is believed to be an avatar of Shiva" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 77, folio 64). He observes that "in the Persian sources, the main Hindu figure is the jogi", a term "usually employed for the Nathpanthis, a Shivaite school of renunciants who were the followers of Gorakhnath" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 21, folio 8); he speaks of "an ascetic order founded by Gorakhnath" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107); and his glossary defines the jogis as "wandering Shivaite ascetics who meditate on One, usually affiliated with the Nathpanth" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206). In one tradition he reports, "Gorakhnath would have sent an invisible army to help Goga Pir against Rai Pithora" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 188, folio 175).

Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi's history of Sufism in India, which nowhere mentions Tilla Jogian, says of the Naths in general that they "lived in forests, wandered in towns and also established permanent monasteries" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 376, folio 354). Harish Dhillon notes that in the Puratan Janamsakhis the account of the anointment of Guru Angad has Gorakhnath "in conversation with Guru Nanak", and comments: "Historically, Gorakhnath lived and preached long before Nanak's time (in the eleventh century)" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 10, folio not stated).

Gorakhnath's name also reaches the cult of the goddess Hinglaj, the subject of Jürgen Schaflechner's study: "Tradition has it that Hinglaj was very fond of the Nath community, especially of Guru Gorakhnath. So the Goddess waited day after day in Thatta for Gorakhnath to come to meet her" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 205, folio not stated). Schaflechner records 'the dhūnī of Guru Gorakhnath' there (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 256, folio not stated) and writes that "The fireplace of Goraknath dates back to the long-standing tradition of Nath Yogis who made the journey to Hinglaj", citing Briggs's study of 1938 (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 256–257, folio not stated); "two texts describe the pilgrimage of Guru Gorakhnath to Hinglaj: the Gorakh Caritra and the Gorakhpurāṇa" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 257, folio not stated). What Boivin, Rizvi, Dhillon and Schaflechner say here is said of Gorakhnath and the Naths, not of this hill; Boivin and Rizvi name no Nath site in the Salt Range at all.

## The Seat of the Jogis

Tilla Jogian became the principal seat of the *Kanphata* yogis — the 'split-eared' ascetics, so called from the great rings inserted through the cartilage of their ears at initiation — an order that looked to Gorakhnath as its master. On the hilltop the *jogis* maintained shrines, cells, and reservoirs of water, and the complex is said at its height to have sheltered hundreds of ascetics who came to meditate in its heights. The site formed the easternmost of a string of ancient Hindu sanctuaries strung along the Salt Range, a chain that also includes the temples of Katas Raj and, at its western end, the Amb temples above the Soon Valley.

Shackle's note on the 'Tilla' of Bulleh Shah's lyric reads: "Tilla Jogian high up in the hills of District Jhelum was the headquarters of the order of Kanphat ('split-eared') yogis, who were initiated by having the cartilage of their ears pierced to allow the insertion of a wooden ring" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 10 on 122). It describes the order rather than the buildings: Shackle names no temple, building, date, custodian or endowment.

Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* places the hill on the salt mountain. "بالاے همین کوه بهفت کروهے قلعه رهتاس": on top of this same mountain, seven kos from the fort of Rohtas, is the place of austerity of the jogi Bal Nath (بالناتهه[OCR?] جوگی, the reading of the name uncertain in the printed text), called تله[OCR?], for which the editor's footnote gives the variant بله[OCR?]; the book gives its height in kos as چهار کروه بلند (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Waris Shah's romance, in Usborne's translation, calls the hill simply 'Tilla' and 'your hill of Tilla'; it never writes 'Tilla Jogian', and it names neither the Salt Range nor Gorakhnath. Beyond the name Tilla, its chief tie to this hill is a note by a later, unnamed annotator: "According to tradition, Balnath was the fourth Guru of 'Tilla Guruan' (the mound of the Gurus) on the banks of the river Jhelum" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1). The same note goes on, in the annotator's own present tense: "The place is still preserved, and the 'Jog Mat' or the cult of the wandering mystics, with its emphasis on pantheism, is still practised there" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1). It gives no building, structure, custodian, date or district.

The poem peoples the hill with Bal Nath's *chelas*, who keep the jogi's house and kitchen. When Ranjha arrives, "They were all engaged in religious contemplation and prayers. They were reading Gayan Gita Bhagvat and Bharat" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). Their service runs for a fixed term, and they complain of it: "For eighteen years we have been serving him. We have given up all and live by begging. All day and night we remember God. Yet he does not give us Jog" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). The annotator explains the guru by his Muslim counterpart: "Guru — the Hindu holy man, the teacher, the Hindu counterpart of the Muslim Murshid" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 5).

## Festival and Practice

Bhandari records the one festival that any of these sources sets on the hill. On the appointed days, and above all on the day of Shivrat, "روز شیورات که روزه است منسوب بمهادیو[OCR?]", at the end of winter (دربرامد[OCR?] زمستان), the book says, "خلایق کثیر و طوایف جوگیان" gather there "و نمایش گری بکاری برند" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 514–513). The sources consulted record no other festival there.

Shackle's notes, which speak of yogis at large rather than of this hill, gloss the rest of the yogi's equipment as Bulleh Shah's lyrics present it: the ochre dress (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 165, folio 140); the bonfire and its ashes, for "Yogis sit in front of a bonfire (dhūāñ) and rub its ashes (bhabūt) on their bodies" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 190, folio 165, n. 3 on 137); the deerskin, skull-cup, matted hair and ashes (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 156, folio 131); the forehead mark (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 190, folio 165, n. 1 on 137); and the horn, bowl and beads (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, pp. 124, 141; folios 99, 116). He explains, too, that "The tenth door is the hidden aperture in the skull that is opened at the climax of the yogic process" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 173, folio 148, n. 2 on 63).

## Guru Nanak and the Hill

Such was its renown as a place of Hindu spiritual power that it drew, in the early sixteenth century, *Guru Nanak*, the founder of the Sikh faith, who is remembered in tradition as having spent forty days in meditation upon the hill during his travels. The episode became part of the sacred memory of the site for Sikhs, adding another layer to a place already venerated by yogis and by Hindu pilgrims from across the Punjab.

The books consulted add no account of Nanak's own stay on the hill. Haroon Khalid's reconstruction in *Walking with Nanak* brings the hill into the story by another road: Tripta accompanied her husband "to Tilla Jogian, the most important pilgrimage site for jogis in the Punjab. There the couple paid for the jogis' food for one day, as a result of which the jogis prayed all night to bless this young couple" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 21, folio 3).

## Ranjha Takes Jog

Tilla Jogian occupies a special place in Punjabi folklore through the tragic romance of *Heer and Ranjha*, immortalised in the eighteenth century by the Sufi poet *Waris Shah*. In the tale, Ranjha, parted from his beloved Heer, climbs to Tilla Jogian in his grief and there renounces the world: the ascetic *Bal Nath*, master of the hill, pierces his ears and initiates him into the order of the *jogis*, granting him *jog*, the discipline of renunciation. Through this episode the hill entered the imaginative life of the Punjab as the very emblem of the lover-turned-ascetic, and generations who never climbed its slopes knew its name from the recitation of Waris Shah's verses.

Waris Shah dates his poem "in the year 1180 Hijri" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 56, folio 55). In Usborne's English, Ranjha sets out for Tilla telling himself that "Balnath surely knows the way of salvation", and "after many days' journeying, Ranjha reached Tilla the hill on which Balnath lived" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). He "bowed his head and placed a piece of gur" before the guru "as an offering, and clasped the feet of all the Jogis" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). The annotator explains the gift: "Gur is raw sugar. It is well known as a ceremonial offering in the Punjab countryside" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32).

The poem sets caste against the vocation: "You Jats cannot attain Jog" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30), and "What can a Jat do with a beggars bowl or horn, whose heart is set only on ploughing?" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). Ranjha's own name, the annotator notes, is a caste: "Ranjha is still a well-known caste of the Jats in the old Punjab" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 3, folio 2). Bal Nath sets out the conditions of *jog*: "You will have to dress as a Jogi, to wear dirty clothes, long hair, cropped skull and to beg your way through life. You will have to give up the pleasures of birth, to cease to rejoice when friends come or to grieve when they die. You will have to abstain from casting eyes on women. You will have to become divinely intoxicated by taking kand, mul, post, opium and other narcotic drugs" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). A jogi must travel as well: "You will have to go on long pilgrimages to Jagannath, Godavari, Ganges and Jamna" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). Ranjha, for his part, admits that the vocation is a means to his love: "Had I been only a lover of God, I should have sought only Him… Hir has captivated my heart. That is why I have become a Jogi" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31).

The rite of initiation is the fullest ritual description in the book. "They obeyed the orders of their Guru and brought Balnath the earrings as he had told them, and the razor wherewith to shave Ranjha. And the Guru took off Ranjha's clothes and having rubbed him in ashes and embraced him, made him sit by his side. Then he took the razor of separation and shaved him completely. Then he bored his ears and put earrings on him. He gave him the beggar's bowl, the rosary, the horn and the shell in his hands", and last he taught him the word Allah (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). With the rite came a moral rule: "An old woman should be treated as your mother and a young woman as your sister" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31).

The annotator stresses what the scene shows of its time: "Here Ranjha, a Muslim, becomes a spiritual disciple of Balnath, a Hindu yogi. This may seem strange today, but was by no means unusual at the time" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 4). In the same note he adds that "A Murshid is a spiritual teacher" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 4).

The *chelas* turn on their guru: "They left the Jogi's house and kitchen. They pierced the Guru with their shameless taunts" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). Bal Nath himself comes to regret his gift: "Verily I repent and am sorry for having given Jog to this youth. He has got the treasures of jog without spending a single farthing" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). A protest in the poem names the hill again: "Had I known that you would try to keep me from my Love, I would never have set foot on your hill of Tilla" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). At last "Ranjha made haste to leave Tilla and he collected strange herbs and potent roots from the woods" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 34, folio 33).

Ear-boring is the act that makes a jogi, and the poem returns to it again and again after Ranjha leaves the hill: "Perhaps he has obeyed my word and got his ears bored" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 40, folio 39); "He went to Tilla and got his ears bored and became a Jogi. He has today entered your village" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 41, folio 40); "Fate has shaved your beard and bored your ears" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 43, folio 42); "He has bored his ears and has become a Jogi for my sake" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 45, folio 44). At the end the marks are removed: "They took the Jogi's rings out of his ears" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 54, folio 53).

## Legends and Miracles

Waris Shah's guru commands by enchantment. When the *chelas* rebel, "Whereupon the Guru rebuked them and his anger blazed from his eyes. The Chelas instantly obeyed him, so powerful was the enchantment that the Guru laid upon them. All ill feeling vanished from their minds" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31).

At the hill, too, a prayer is answered aloud. Bal Nath "prayed and poured ashes over his body and plunged his soul into the deep waters of meditation"; then "there came a reply from the Darbar of God": "Hir has been bestowed on Ranjha and his boat has been taken ashore" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32).

The annotator denies the guru two powers. "Balnath obviously could not read Ranjha's thoughts", he writes, as jogis often claim to do (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 6); and "Balnath apparently had no power to take back what he had given" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 34, folio 33, note 16). He also records a popular belief: "According to popular superstition in the Punjab countryside", Pirs, Fakirs and Jogis can, by the force of their piety, "make the Moving Finger of Destiny cancel what it has written" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30, note 7).

## In Verse

Bulleh Shah's lyric, in Shackle's translation, follows the initiate to Tilla step by step:

*Casting aside his drum, he goes toward Tilla, he sits and meditates on his name. He has his ears split and the earrings inserted, and is initiated by the guru* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 123, folio 98)

The lyric then names the authority a Pir must satisfy:

*My Pir gains the approval of guru Gorakh. He keeps crying 'Hir, Hir.'* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 124, folio 99)

Shackle glosses the yogic vocabulary of Bulleh Shah's verse: "The 'unstruck music' (anhad nād) is the mystical sound heard at the climax of the yogic process"; "The 'circle of nectar' (amrit manḍal) is another traditional image for the ecstatic state that is the goal of yoga"; and the phrase 'make the Ganges flow backward' (ulṭī gangā bahāio) is "an idiom meaning 'to do the opposite of the usual,' which here refers to the drawing up of psychic energy during the yogic process" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 155, folio 130). Again: "The 'fourth state' (cauthā pad, Skt. turīyāvasthā-) is a yogic term that denotes the state of liberation achieved through transcending the three guṇas that govern worldly existence" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 176, folio 151, n. 2 on 71).

Waris Shah's poem, in Usborne's English, defines *jog* in its own terms:

*Jog means to be dead while alive. One has to sing the song of nonentity using ones meagre body as a guitar. One's self has to be entirely absorbed. It is no child's play.* (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30)

*God has made his abode in this body of dust He is in every thing as a thread runs through the beads.* (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30)

The annotator reads the 'Song of Nonentity' through Sufi eyes: "this is the doctrine of annihilation in God (fana fillah) as practised by the Muslim Sufis, which has strong spiritual affiliations with the 'Nirvana' of the Hindus and Buddhists" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 10). The poem also names a degree of *jog* called Chit Akas, reached "after passing through the stages of Bhut Kas and Juda Kas" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31), which the annotator glosses only as "The three different planes of Jog Philosophy" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 13).

## Setting: The Salt Mountain

Bhandari's account of the salt mountain on which he places Tilla speaks of the range, not of the hill itself. In the Sind Sagar doab (دوابه سندساگر), rock salt (نمک سنگ) is dug at the foot of the hills near Shamsabad, famous above all other salts and called نمک سندهه[OCR?] because it is produced in that doab (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514). The miners, called الاشه کش[OCR?], dig tunnels "زیاده از دو صد سیصد درعه[OCR?] عمیق"; each goes in naked with a lamp in his hand and a pick on his shoulder, cuts a lump of about سه من and carries it out on his back; he is paid, "از ناظمان این امر اجرت گرفته", and the men feel no fear. The tunnels, the book adds بحکمت الهی, are not hot in summer or cold in winter (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Two large tunnels near Shamsabad, کهوهره[OCR?] و کهیوره[OCR?], yield "هر سال چندان لکهه من نمک", and their revenue, with that of other places, "بسرکار بادشاهی ضبط می شود" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514). Craftsmen make trays, dishes, covers and lamp-stands of salt; the گچ شیرین found next to it is used for whitewash inside the houses of the great; and the stone is also made into dishes and انجوره[OCR?] (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Bhandari also reports a Hindu belief. The Kahyala pool, "کهنتا[OCR?] چهه[OCR?] کولابی[OCR?]", whose depth no one can tell, is held to be an ancient temple; on great days such as the sun's entry into Aries, Hindus crowd there بقصد تغسل[OCR?]. They believe the earth has two eyes: the right is the pool of بهکر[OCR?] near Ajmer, the left this pool (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514). He cites the *Zafarnama* and the *Akbarnama*, "درظفرنامه و اکبرنامه ان راکوه جوده نوشته اند"; Jud was رئیس قوم جنجوهه, whose descendants still live and rule at the foot of the hills in the parganas "کرچاک[OCR?] و نندنه[OCR?] و کهیاله(۱)[OCR?]", the editor giving کهتاز[OCR?] as a variant for the last (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Writing of the Sind Sagar doab as a whole, Richard Eaton notes: "Only in the extreme western Punjab, in the Sind Sagar doab, where the Janjua Rajputs and Ghakkars dominated, were the Jats conspicuously absent as zamindars" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 225, folio 213). Lukas Werth, whose chapter in Werbner and Basu's *Embodying Charisma* studies the anonymous saints' shrines of a village in the range to which he gives a pseudonym, sets that village "In the mountains dividing the plains of the Punjab from the slightly elevated plateau of the Potwar" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 88, folio 77), and writes of "the salt range where there is no irrigation" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 93, folio 82).

## Decline and Present State

The complex flourished until the Partition of 1947, when the departure of its Hindu and yogi custodians for India left it without a resident community. Deprived of care, the buildings fell into decay; the reservoirs silted, the shrines crumbled, and in the decades since the site has been steadily overgrown — by the early twenty-first century much of it lay beneath a spread of wild olive and scrub, its masonry slipping into ruin. Conservationists and writers have repeatedly warned that this remarkable monument, at once archaeological site, sacred summit, and literary landmark, risks being lost altogether without deliberate protection. Its remoteness has spared it the crowds that press upon lower shrines, but that same isolation has hastened its neglect.

Against this stands the present-tense note of Usborne's later, unnamed annotator: "The place is still preserved, and the 'Jog Mat' or the cult of the wandering mystics, with its emphasis on pantheism, is still practised there" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1).

For the fate of such places after the division of the Punjab, Haroon Khalid, writing of the country at large and not of this hill, says: "I have seen several gurdwaras and temples being taken over and destroyed by the migrants" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Who initiated Ranjha.** The site's account names Bal Nath, master of the hill. Usborne's translation of Waris Shah agrees, and its annotator calls Bal Nath "the fourth Guru of 'Tilla Guruan'" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1). Shackle's glossary to Bulleh Shah instead names "the great yogi Gorakhnath, from whom Ranjha sought initiation as a yogi" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 198, folio 173), and Bulleh Shah's lyric says that the initiate "is initiated by the guru" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 123, folio 98).
- **Gorakhnath's date.** The site's account says that tradition traces the hill's sanctity back some two thousand years and links its foundation to Gorakhnath, while scholarship usually places him c. 11th–12th century CE. Dhillon puts him "in the eleventh century" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 10, folio not stated), while the Puratan Janamsakhis, as he reports them, set him in conversation with Guru Nanak.
- **Gorakhnath's place in the order.** The site's account calls him the organiser of the Nath tradition. Boivin speaks of "an ascetic order founded by Gorakhnath" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107) and reports the belief that he is an avatar of Shiva (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 77, folio 64); Shackle calls him "the head of the Kanphat yogis" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 12 on 122).
- **The name of the hill and where it stands.** The site's account gives Tilla Jogian, the "Hill of the Ascetics", on the highest peak of the eastern Salt Range in Jhelum District. Shackle has Tilla Jogian "high up in the hills of District Jhelum" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 10 on 122). Usborne's translation says only 'Tilla', and its annotator gives 'Tilla Guruan', "the mound of the Gurus", "on the banks of the river Jhelum" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1). Bhandari calls the place تله[OCR?], with the editor's variant بله[OCR?], and sets it on the salt mountain seven kos from the fort of Rohtas (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).
- **The ear-ring.** The site's account speaks of great rings through the cartilage of the ear; Shackle of the cartilage pierced "to allow the insertion of a wooden ring" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 10 on 122).
- **The hill since 1947.** The site's account has the complex abandoned at Partition, without a resident community, and its buildings in ruin. Usborne's annotator, writing in the present tense, says that "The place is still preserved" and that the 'Jog Mat' "is still practised there" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1).

## Legacy

Tilla Jogian gathers into one windswept hilltop several of the great strands of Punjabi religious and cultural history: the antiquity of the *Nath* yogis and their Kanphata order; the pilgrim memory of Guru Nanak; and the deathless romance of Heer and Ranjha. As one of the trio of Salt Range sanctuaries alongside Katas Raj and the Amb temples, it testifies to a landscape once dense with Hindu holiness. For the modern traveller it offers a rare and melancholy grandeur — ruined shrines amid olive groves, commanding a vast prospect over the Jhelum plains — and stands as a reminder of a plural sacred past that survives now chiefly in stone and in song.

Writers on the romance, who speak of the tale rather than of the hill, show how it lives on in song. Shackle writes: "The greatest of these local legends is the story of Hir and Ranjha, which is set in the world of the Jat pastoral tribes of western Panjab" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 20, folio xix). Annemarie Schimmel writes that the romance, "elaborated in more than a hundred versions in Panjabi, Urdu, Sindhi, and Persian, was given its final form in the late eighteenth century by Warith Shah. It is his verse which is sung, time and again, wherever Panjabis meet" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 171, folio 153), and that "The visitor who stays in a Panjabi village will certainly find somebody to sing for him the old romance of Hir Ranjha in the classical form given it by Warith Shah" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 414, folio 383). Shemeem Burney Abbas records that Waris Shah "is said to have recited it with great emotion among his speech communities in the Panjab", and that "Many renowned folk artists in the Panjab, such as Reshma, Zahida Parvin, Nazir Begum, Sabiha Khanum, Tufail Niazi, and Iqbal Bahu, have sung it" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 123, folio not stated). Scott Kugle compares its place in Punjabi devotion with that of Radha and Krishna: "Punjabi poets and their eager audiences poured into Hir and Ranjha the same erotic emotion that was invested in Radha and Krishna in regions closer to the Ganges. The story of Hir and Ranjha became a favorite Sufi device for conveying the value of erotic passion in spiritual life" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 228, folio 207). Bhandari, in his account of the suba of Lahore, already records that wonderful verses and designs on the love of Heer and Ranjha were composed and sung there (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 512–511).

## Overview

Tucked amid the crowded lanes of Aibak Road in the Anarkali quarter of Lahore, a modest garden tomb marks the burial place of Sultan Qutb ud-Din Aibak, founder of the Mamluk, or "Slave," dynasty and the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. A slave who rose through service to the Ghurid ruler Muhammad Ghori, he established independent rule based in Lahore after Ghori's death, laying the foundations of Muslim dynastic government in the subcontinent, and he is remembered too as the patron who commissioned Delhi's Qutb Minar. He died in Lahore in November 1210 after a fall from his horse while playing *chaugan*, an early form of polo. The tomb is not a Sufi shrine: it hosts no *ʿurs*, no pilgrimage tradition and no ongoing devotional practice, and it is maintained as a protected historical monument, valued chiefly for its symbolic role marking the thirteenth-century founding moment of Muslim dynastic rule in South Asia, centred, briefly, on Lahore itself.

The tomb's physical history has been anything but continuous. Historians dispute whether a substantial mausoleum ever stood over the grave in the medieval period; for long the site was a simple, informal grave hemmed in by the houses of the Anarkali bazaar; and the structure visitors see today is essentially a reconstruction of the 1970s, though one official account dates it to 1990.

The books consulted add a good deal to this picture. Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's survey of the tombs and buildings of Lahore, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, is the only one of them to describe the grave itself: he places it in the Sadr Bazaar of Anarkali, records a lost two-storey dome of marble that old people remembered, and says the Maharaja of his day demolished the buildings and sent their stone to Amritsar (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 271). Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* gives the fullest account of the life: the purchased slave made viceroy, his campaigns, his accession at Lahore, his generosity, his name and his death at *chaugan* (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400; Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 401–402). Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* places his death at Lahore and explains his title Lakh Bakhsh, but names no grave for him (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Naveed Alam's translation of Madho Lal Hussein, Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi, Shemeem Burney Abbas and Annemarie Schimmel mention him in passing, and the year of his death is given in more than one way.

## The Life of the Sultan

Aibak was born around 1150 in Turkestan and sold into slavery as a child. He rose through service to the Ghurid ruler Muhammad Ghori, and came to command Ghurid territories in northern India following the decisive Second Battle of Tarain in 1192.

Bhandari calls him plainly 'سلطان قطب الدین ایبک غلام زرخرید سلطان شهاب الدین نیابتاً حکومت هندوستان داشت', the Sultan's purchased slave, governing Hindustan as his deputy (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). After the victory at 'نراین', he writes, Sultan Shihab al-Din left 'ملک قطب الدین ایبک را که غلام برگزیده او بود درقصبه کهرام هفتاد کروهے دهلی نایب سلطنت': his chosen slave was made viceroy at the *qasba* of Kuhram, seventy *kos* from Delhi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 402). Rizvi's history of Sufism tells it differently: "Mu‘izzu’d-Din Muhammad bin Sam had conquered Delhi and, departing for Ghazni, left his favourite slave, Qutbu’d-Din Aibak, as head of his forces in the occupied city" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121).

As deputy, 'نیابتاً', after the Sultan went back to Ghazni, Bhandari continues, he 'دراسرع اوقات قلعه دهلی ومیرته تسخیر نموده بهرجا حکام نصب گردانید', in the shortest time took the forts of Delhi and Meerut and set governors in every place; in the second year he took 'قلعه کول', and then the forts of Gwalior, Budaun 'ودیگر قلاع', and other forts (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 401–402). He marched on Gujarat and took revenge on 'راۓ بهیم دیو گجراتی' for the Sultan's earlier defeat, 'انتقام شکست سلطان که سابقاً بتحریر درامده', plundered the country, returned to Delhi and 'خطبه وسکه بنام سلطان رواج داد', put the *khutba* and the coin into currency in the Sultan's name (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). In the Sultan's tenth campaign, against the Khokhars near Lahore, 'ملک قطب الدین نیز از دهلی بخدمت سلطان رسیده باتفاق یکدیگر گوشمال انجماعت ... کردند': Malik Qutb al-Din too came from Delhi to the Sultan's service, and together they chastised that tribe (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401).

Rizvi describes the occupation: "Occupying troops stationed at Indraprastha near Delhi under Qutbu’d-Din Aibak were forced to make several invasions in the Doab and the regions around Ajmer to consolidate their power" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 140, folio 122). In the same account he records that "Qutbu’d-Din had appointed Saiyid Husain Mashhadi as the darogha (military governor) of the area. The Saiyid served the Khwaja with great devotion" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 140, folio 122).

His captains carried the conquest east. In Bhandari's words, 'در بلاد بنگاله آغاز ظهور اسلام از ملک محمد بختیار که از امراے بزرگ سلطان قطب الدین ایبک بود گردیده وازان زمان آن ولایت درتصرف[OCR?] سلطان دهلی گشت': Islam in Bengal began with Malik Muhammad Bakhtiyar, one of Aibak's great amirs, and from that time the province was in the hands of the Sultan of Delhi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 208). Chishti tells of a general who sent his booty from Bihar 'اپنے مالک کی پاس دہلی مین', to his master at Delhi, of a 'مست ہاتہی', a rutting elephant, and of the governorship of Bihar and an order to take Bengal (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809).

Delhi was his seat. Bhandari records that 'سلطان قطب الدین ایبک و سلطان شمس الدین التمش در قلعه رائے پتهورا می بودند', he and Iltutmish lived in Rai Pithora's fort (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 561), and that 'ازان تاریخ شهر دهلی دارالخلافت سلاطین مسلمین مقرر گردیده', from then on Delhi was the capital of the Muslim sultans (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). He is remembered as the patron who commissioned Delhi's Qutb Minar, and Alam's note calls him "known for the famous Qutb Minar" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185). Schimmel, writing of the death of Muʿinuddin in 1236, places it "not far from the beautiful mosque" that Aibak, whom she calls 'of Delhi', "had erected in Ajmer" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346).

## The Accession

After Ghori's assassination in 1206, Aibak established independent rule based in Lahore. Chishti's history gives Muhammad Ghori's death as 'سن بارہ سو چہہ [OCR?]', the year twelve hundred and six, and says he died without a son; 'قطب الدین حاکم دہلی', Qutb al-Din the ruler of Delhi, then claimed Hindustan (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Elsewhere Chishti sets the accession in 'چھ سو دو[OCR?]', six hundred and two, with the figure ۶۰۲ in the margin, when he 'تخت دہلی پر جلوس فرمایا', took his seat on the throne of Delhi; before that, he writes, 'ملک ہندوستان ... بے چراغ تھا', the land of Hindustan was without a lamp (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 267). Kanhaiya Lal states his status plainly: Shahab-ud-Din Ghori 'دہلی کا تخت سلطان [illegible] قطب الدین ایبک اپنے غلام کے سپرد کر دیا', handed the throne of Delhi to Qutb al-Din Aibak, his own slave (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 24, folio 19).

Bhandari puts the moment of sovereignty at Lahore: 'بعد ازانکه سلطان درجه شهادت یافت از دهلی برامده درلاهور رسید اصالتاً سریراراۓ خلافت گشت ویازدهم ربیع الاول سنه ۶۰۳[OCR?] سکه وخطبه بنام خود کرد'. After the Sultan attained martyrdom, he came out of Delhi, reached Lahore and took the throne in his own right, and on the eleventh of Rabiʿ al-Awwal of the year 603 had the coin struck and the *khutba* read in his own name; the reading of the year is uncertain in the printed text (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). 'سلطان غیاث الدین محمود[OCR?] برادرزاده سلطان شهاب الدین از فیروزه کوه', Sultan Ghiyas al-Din Mahmud, Shihab al-Din's nephew, sent him from Firozkoh 'چتر وتجملات بادشاهی', the parasol and the trappings of kingship, and 'بخطاب سلطانی مخاطب ساخت', addressed him with the title of Sultan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 400–401).

## The Contest with Yildiz

His rival for the Ghurid inheritance was Taj al-Din Yildiz, whom the books spell variously. Bhandari calls 'تاج الدین یلدوز' one of Shihab al-Din's 'بندهاۓ خاص', his special slaves, who had been given the name of sultan in Ghazni after Shihab al-Din's death; a dispute arose between the two 'برسر لاهور', over Lahore, and they fought a pitched battle: 'بالآخر تاج الدین تاب مقاومت نیاورده منهزم گشته درکرمان اقامت ورزید وسلطان مظفر ومنصور شده باستقلال کمال بسلطنت پرداخت'. At last Taj al-Din could not hold out, was routed and settled in Kirman, and the Sultan, victorious, gave himself to rule in complete independence (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400).

In Kanhaiya Lal's history Yalduz, having seized Ghazni, 'پھر پنجاب کو آیا', came on to the Punjab to take the throne of Hind from Qutb al-Din (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Aibak defeated him in the field and pursued him to Ghazni, and then 'قطب الدین وہاں سے لاہور کو آ گیا', Qutb al-Din came from there to Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Chishti, for his part, has him defeat 'الدوز [OCR?]' and be crowned at Ghazni, where he grew 'آرام طلب', a lover of ease, and was driven back (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809).

## His Rule and His Household

Chishti says he ruled 'بہت لیاقت سی', with great ability, and lived five years after his master, the reading of the number being uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Bhandari reckons the whole of his government thus: 'مدت بست سال حکومت هندوستان نمود ازانجمله سلطنت غزنین چهار سال', he governed Hindustan for twenty years, the sultanate of Ghazni among them for four (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Rizvi's index gives the bracket "(1206-1210)" after his name (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 481, folio 457).

Iltutmish, who would follow him, was his slave before he was his son-in-law. Rizvi writes that "Sultan Qutbu'd-Din Aibak, also a former slave, during a visit to Ghazna after his Anhilwara expedition in 1196, took a fancy to Iltutmish and was able to buy him in Delhi, and between 1197 or 1198 to 1206 Iltutmish rose to prominence" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 153, folio 135, footnote 2). In Bhandari's account, 'اورا سلطان قطب الدین ایبک به[OCR?] لک جیتل خریده بفرزندی گرفته دختر خود را درمناکحت او درآورده بود': Aibak bought him for a lakh of *jitals*, adopted him and married him to his daughter. 'بعد فتح گوالیار امارت انجا باو ارزانی داشت', after the conquest of Gwalior he granted him its command; then he gave him 'برن[OCR?]' and its region and, step by step, Budaun, until Iltutmish rose to be *amir al-umara* and 'خط آزادی از سلطان یافت', received his letter of manumission from the Sultan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 399). Shemeem Burney Abbas, recounting her own ancestors' appointment as muftis of Lahore under "the Muslim slave king Shamsuddin Iltutmish", adds that "Qutubuddin Aibek was himself a slave king" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated).

He was succeeded eventually by his son-in-law Iltutmish. The books differ on what came between. Bhandari writes that 'سلطان مرحوم پسر صلبی که سزاوار جهانبانی تواند بود نداشت', the late Sultan had no son of his own body fit to rule; the nobles therefore seated 'آرام بخش پسرخوانده سلطان', Aram Bakhsh, the Sultan's adopted son and the only heir, 'درسنه ۶۰۷[OCR?] درخطه دل کشاۓ لاهور', in the year 607 in the delightful region of Lahore, as Sultan Aram Shah (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400); but 'از سلطان آرام شاه امور خلافت تمشیت نیافت', under Aram Shah the affairs of state did not prosper (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 399). Chishti calls 'آرام' his son, deposed after a year by 'شمس الدین', who was Aibak's slave and son-in-law (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Kanhaiya Lal names his successor on the throne of Delhi as 'سلطان شمس الدین التمش' (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20), and Abbas has Iltutmish ascend the throne of Delhi "after the death of his master, Qutubuddin Aibek" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated).

A different Qutbuddin must not be confused with him. On the same page as her mention of Aibak's mosque, Schimmel writes of Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki of Farghana, who died in 1235 and whose "rather modest compound in Merauli near the Qutb Minar in Delhi is usually filled with pious pilgrims" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346); her index lists him separately (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 513, folio 482).

## Lakh Bakhsh: His Names and His Giving

Bhandari explains the name Aibak: 'چون انگشت خنصر او شکسته بود ازینجهت اورا ایبک گفتندے', because his little finger was broken, he was called Aibak (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401).

His title Lakh Bakhsh, the giver of lakhs, is explained by his largesse. Kanhaiya Lal ties it to Lahore: there he 'بہت [illegible] رعایا کو [illegible] خوش کیا اور کثرت داد و دہش سے سلطان لکھ بخش خطاب لیا', pleased the subjects and, by the abundance of his giving, took the title Sultan Lakh Bakhsh (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Bhandari gives a long passage in praise of his giving, 'دست جود وسخایش گرد افلاس ازچهره مفلسان برافشاندی', which ends 'چون لکها باهل احتیاج انعام دادی ازینجهت درهند اورا لکهه بخش گفتندی': because he gave lakhs to the needy, in Hind they called him Lakh-bakhsh (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). A couplet in his praise follows:

باهمت او حوصله دریا تنگ
بارفعت او مرتبه گردون پست

The couplet closes Bhandari's praise of the Sultan's generosity (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400).

The books write his name in several forms: 'قطب الدین ایبک' in Kanhaiya Lal and Bhandari (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 24, folio 19; Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401), "Sultan Qutub-uddin Aibak" in Alam's note (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185), Qutbu’d-Din Aibak in Rizvi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121), Qutubuddin Aibek in Abbas (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated) and Aybek in Schimmel (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346).

## Death at Chaugan

He died in Lahore in November 1210 after a fall from his horse while playing *chaugan*, an early form of polo. Kanhaiya Lal tells it in one line: 'اور لاہور ہی کے مقام پر گیند کھیلتے ہوئے گھوڑے سے گر کر مر گیا', and at Lahore itself, playing ball, he fell from his horse and died; he gives no year (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Bhandari has 'درسنه [illegible] درچوگان بازی از اسپ افتاده گوۓ زندگی بجولانگاه آخرت رسانید', that he fell from his horse at *chaugan* and died; the year cannot be read, and Bhandari names no place of death (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Chishti gives the year as 'سن بارہ سو دس [OCR?]', twelve hundred and ten, the reading flagged as uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809).

Naveed Alam's translation of Madho Lal Hussein recalls the death in a note on the game itself: "The game was brought to the subcontinent by the Central Asian armies. Sultan Qutub-uddin Aibak, known for the famous Qutb Minar, died playing polo in Lahore in AD 1210." (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185). The verse is Hussein's own, a *kafi* that watches a polo match and does not name the Sultan:

*Let me stand and watch for a few days / the polo tournament. Who wins, who loses, / whose brisk horse makes a clever move? … Let's see who hits the ball / across the field. The crowd cheers and jeers* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 113, folio 113, kafi 90)

## The Tomb

Chishti's survey of Lahore's tombs is the only book consulted that describes the grave. He places it 'دروازہ لاہوری کے باہر بطرف شمال', outside the Lahori Gate on the north side, east of a 'گودام [OCR?] شراب', a liquor godown, 'واقعہ صدر بازار انار کلی', situated in the Sadr Bazaar of Anarkali. In his day a 'قصاب [OCR?] خانہ', a butcher's house, stood on its land, and 'طوائف لوگوں', courtesans, occupied it (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 271).

He records what had been lost. Under Sikh rule there stood 'عمارات عالیشان سنگ [illegible]', lofty buildings of stone; 'مہاراجہ نے سب مسمار کرکے روانہ امرتسر کر دین', the Maharaja demolished them all and sent them off to Amritsar; and there remained 'ایک قبر خشتی [OCR?] بلند چبوترہ پر', a single brick grave on a raised platform. Old people, he writes, had seen a 'گنبد دو منزلہ سنگ مرمر کا', a two-storey dome of marble, unmatched anywhere round Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 271).

Chishti judged that no building near Lahore was older than this grave, because Qutb al-Din was '[illegible] سی', and because 'سلطنت عوریہ یہاں چغتائی [OCR?] سے بہت مدت پہلے تھی', the Ghurid sultanate was here long before the Chaghatai; for the fuller story he refers the reader to 'تواریخ ہند', the histories of Hind. He left more unsaid on purpose: because of the courtesans, what might have been written, '[illegible] لکھا جاوے قلم انداز کیا گیا', was omitted (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 271–272).

The modern accounts tell the story another way. Punjab's Directorate General of Archaeology states that the grave was "originally... only one grave without any tomb or structure," that a marble tomb was later "pulled down by Ranjit Singh," and that the department itself "built the present tomb over the grave in 1990." Earlier still, according to Dawn's "Harking Back" column, Sultan Iltutmish had ordered "a simple small room, one barely able to enclose the grave": at first a mud room, it was later bricked in during Akbar's reign. For long the site was a simple, informal grave hemmed in by the houses of the Anarkali bazaar.

The same column dates the present mausoleum's actual construction to 1972, ordered by Prime Minister Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto after the Bangladesh war, who is quoted remarking that Aibak "was a great and kind ruler and deserved the respect of the poor"; the design was led by the architect Kamil Khan Mumtaz. Daily Times likewise places the rebuilding "during the 1970s," rather than in 1990 as the Archaeology Department's own page states. The structure visitors see today is essentially this 1970s reconstruction by Pakistan's Department of Archaeology and Museums, deliberately evoking early Sultanate-period style within a small walled garden.

The other books are silent on the tomb. Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore names no grave for him, and its table of contents lists no tomb of his (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 2–5); Bhandari names no burial (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400); and Rizvi, Abbas, Schimmel and Alam mention none.

## The Tomb Today

Unlike Lahore's Sufi shrines, the tomb hosts no *ʿurs*, no pilgrimage tradition and no ongoing devotional practice. It is maintained purely as a protected historical monument, and none of the books consulted records any observance at the grave.

## Setting: Anarkali and Ghurid Lahore

What the books say of the quarter and the city is context, not a description of the tomb. Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* knows Anarkali only as a cantonment and a bazaar (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 34–35, folios 37–38). Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail* says that the Anarkali market "is named after the legendary lover of the Mughal Emperor Jahangir", that the area "over the years has become the largest tyre market in the city", and that "The Pak Tea House, just a few shops away, once famed for its gatherings of the leading intelligentsia of the city, is now on its way to becoming yet another tyre shop" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 66, folio not stated).

Aibak's Lahore was a city the Ghurids had only lately taken. Bhandari tells how 'خسروشاه بن بهرام شاه', driven from Ghazni by the Ghurids, took Lahore and died there in 555 (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 405); his son Khusraw Malik held it for twenty-eight years, 'مدت حکومت او درلاهور بست وهشت سال', while Shihab al-Din attacked Lahore again and again (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 405). In the campaign Bhandari dates 582, Khusraw Malik submitted and was taken to Ghazni, where he died, and the Sultan 'ودرلاهور نایب خود نصب کرد', set his own deputy in Lahore (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 404). Kanhaiya Lal marks the same turn: with Khusrau Malik's surrender, 'سلاطین غوریہ کی سلطنت کا ہند میں آغاز ہوا اور غزنویہ حکومت با اختتام پہنچی', the rule of the Ghurid sultans in Hind began and the Ghaznavid government came to its end (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 24, folio 19).

After Aibak's death Lahore was briefly a royal seat again: his heir Aram Shah was enthroned there, and when Iltutmish came, Aram Shah moved 'از لاهور', from Lahore, toward Delhi, drew up his ranks and fled 'باندک محاربه', after little fighting (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 399). In Kanhaiya Lal's account Yalduz rose again in Iltutmish's reign, took Multan and came to Lahore 'اور اُس نے دل کھول کر پنجاب کو غارت کیا', and plundered the Punjab freely (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20).

Chishti's general account of the city sets the loss of old Lahore's monuments in the Sikh period, which is the setting for his report of this tomb's demolition. In Ranjit Singh's time, he writes, red, black and marble stones 'گرد و نواح لاہور کے', in the neighbourhood of Lahore, were torn down (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 296); when the cantonments of Ranjit Singh's armies were built the bricks of old tombs and houses were pulled out, and 'ہزار ہا مقابر و گنبد و مساجد و باغات و حویلیہائے[OCR?] قدیمہ جو یادگار امرائے سلف تھیں گم گشتیں[OCR?]', thousands of tombs, domes, mosques, gardens and old mansions that were memorials of the nobles of the past were lost (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 431).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of his death.** The current account gives November 1210. Chishti gives 'سن بارہ سو دس [OCR?]', 1210, the reading flagged as uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809), and Alam's note gives "AD 1210" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185). Kanhaiya Lal gives no year (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20), and in Bhandari the year is illegible (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Schimmel's index prints "(d. 1206)" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 523). Rizvi's index prints "(1206-1210)", a span of rule, and gives no death date (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 481, folio 457). Abbas prints a year at this point that cannot be read in the copy consulted (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated).
- **Where he died.** The current account, Kanhaiya Lal and Alam place his death at Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20; Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185). Bhandari tells the fall at *chaugan* but names no place (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Rizvi places him at Delhi and Ghazni only and has no Lahore for him (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 481, folio 457).
- **Where Ghori left him.** Rizvi has Muhammad bin Sam leave him "as head of his forces in the occupied city" of Delhi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121). Bhandari has him made viceroy at Kuhram, seventy *kos* from Delhi, taking Delhi himself afterwards (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 401–402).
- **When and where he became sovereign.** The current account has him establish independent rule based in Lahore after Ghori's assassination in 1206. Chishti has him take his seat on the throne of Delhi in 'چھ سو دو[OCR?]', 602 (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 267), and elsewhere has Ghori die in 1206 and Aibak, ruler of Delhi, claim Hindustan (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Kanhaiya Lal has Ghori hand him the throne of Delhi (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 24, folio 19). Bhandari has him come from Delhi to Lahore and strike coin and read the *khutba* in his own name on 11 Rabiʿ al-Awwal 603, the year's reading uncertain (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401).
- **Yildiz and Ghazni.** Bhandari has Yildiz contest Lahore, lose a pitched battle and settle in Kirman, and gives Aibak four years of the sultanate of Ghazni (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Kanhaiya Lal has Aibak defeat Yalduz, pursue him to Ghazni and come back to Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Chishti has him crowned at Ghazni, grow 'آرام طلب', a lover of ease, and be driven back (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809).
- **How long he ruled.** Chishti says he lived five years after his master, the number's reading uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Bhandari says he governed Hindustan for twenty years (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Rizvi's index brackets his name with 1206 and 1210 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 481, folio 457).
- **His successor.** The current account has him succeeded eventually by his son-in-law Iltutmish. Bhandari has the nobles seat Aram Bakhsh, his adopted son, at Lahore as Aram Shah, saying the Sultan had no son of his own body (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Chishti calls 'آرام' his son, deposed after a year by Shams al-Din (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Kanhaiya Lal names Iltutmish as his successor on the throne of Delhi with no reign between (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20), and Abbas has Iltutmish ascend "after the death of his master" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated).
- **How he acquired Iltutmish.** Rizvi has him buy Iltutmish in Delhi, having taken a fancy to him on a visit to Ghazna after the Anhilwara expedition of 1196 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 153, folio 135, footnote 2). Bhandari has him buy Iltutmish for a lakh of *jitals*, adopt him and marry him to his daughter, and names no place (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 399).
- **Where he was called Lakh Bakhsh.** Kanhaiya Lal ties the title to his largesse at Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Bhandari says that 'درهند', in Hind, he was called Lakh-bakhsh (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400).
- **What once stood over the grave.** The Directorate General of Archaeology says it was originally only a grave without any tomb or structure, and that a marble tomb was later pulled down by Ranjit Singh. Dawn's column has Iltutmish order a simple small room, first of mud and bricked in under Akbar. Chishti reports lofty buildings of stone under Sikh rule, demolished by the Maharaja and sent to Amritsar, and a two-storey marble dome that old people remembered (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 271). The current account adds that historians dispute whether a substantial mausoleum ever stood over the grave in the medieval period.
- **When the present tomb was built.** The Directorate General of Archaeology says its department built the present tomb in 1990. Dawn's column dates the construction to 1972, under Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto, and Daily Times places the rebuilding in the 1970s.

## Legacy

The tomb is valued chiefly for its symbolic role, marking the thirteenth-century founding moment of Muslim dynastic rule in South Asia, centred, briefly, on Lahore itself. Bhandari makes the same claim for Delhi: from his time, 'ازان تاریخ شهر دهلی دارالخلافت سلاطین مسلمین مقرر گردیده', Delhi was fixed as the capital of the Muslim sultans (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). Chishti, for whom the land of Hindustan had been 'بے چراغ' before him (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 267), held his grave to be older than any other building near Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 271–272).

Aibak, according to Dawn's column, had also wanted Lahore's dead buried together, designating land south of Mozang village as a graveyard for "at least 150,000 dead," the origin of the present Miani Sahib graveyard.

Bhutto's remark, as Dawn reports it, that Aibak "was a great and kind ruler and deserved the respect of the poor" stands beside the older memory of the Lakh Bakhsh, whose giving Bhandari praises in prose and verse (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400).
